text: GILBERT. 5 v. 27 Book I. He is questioned concerning his grief. Canto i A labouring man beholds our gentle Avight, And begs to knoAV Iioav came he in such plight ; Young Gilbert hears the query meant for kind, Returns short ansAA-er, brief unfolds his mind : Confess'd that luckless love infix'd the dart, Which caus'd fresh pain to fester in his heart ! Compassion, then, the curious hind express'd, Fetch'd a deep sigh, and thus the youth address'd " Unhappy stranger, list to my sad tale, " And let my words to sooth your grief avail : " Would I Avere single, like as you are noAV, " No anxious cares should e'er affect my broAV ; " Gay Pleasure o'er my joyous hours should tend, " CroAvning my bliss with ale, a pipe, a friend. " Such bliss I knew ; but, still dissatisfied, " I courted Ruth, ah me ! and wedlock tried : " Simple, indeed, to sacrifice my peace, " And for a Avife exchange regretted ease !

title: Gilbert; or True Love rewarded: an amatory rural poem [By J. Templeman. Illustrated.]
text: GILBERT. 6 45. Book I. The labourer expresses his grievances. Canto 1. v. " When ci'oavs the cock th' umvelcome daAvn of day, " O ! I must speed the summons to obey ; " Compell'd, through poverty, to quit my rest, " And leave my bed with silent grief oppress. " The food I eat a bare existence yields ; " Fate froAvns on me, care all her wants reveals . " These, these, are mine 1 vainly do lament " The hapless hour I barter 'd my content. " Near the road-side are stony fragments laid, " To mend the ruts by loaded waggons made ; " The splinter'd lumps I in the holloAvs spread, " And throw the gravel where the horses tread. " Such toil is hard : alas ! my strength I prove ; " DoAvn runs my SAveat, and heavily I move ; " While not one drop of home-brew'd ale I taste, " To cheer my sinking spirits, Aveakly brac'd : " Ah ! sir, a Avife, two infant children small, " Whate'er I earn, they're ready for it all !

title: Gilbert; or True Love rewarded: an amatory rural poem [By J. Templeman. Illustrated.]
text: GILBERT. 7 63 Book I. Gilbert makes reply. Canto i. v. " A single doit no more my wage affords, " A penny spent excites provoking Avords ! " Go noAv, bethink, I envy such as you, " Free to act fair, and best what pleases do : " Would I Avere single ; or might choose once more, " I'd have no wife — but I in vain deplore." This Gilbert heard : his varying look bespeaks A mind perplex'd, and thus he silence breaks : " Well-taught experience makes us all grow Avise ; " Each for himself the doubtful matter tries. " My stubborn passion I would gladly close, " Set right my thoughts, and banish all my Avoes ; " From hateful strife I'd keep my temper free, " Were lovely Jenny Avedded but to me. " Were she, were Jane become my constant bride, " How rich the gift ! I'd nothing crave beside : " Able to work, industry I'd embrace, " With sweet contentment smiling on my face."

title: Gilbert; or True Love rewarded: an amatory rural poem [By J. Templeman. Illustrated.]
text: GILBERT. 9 Book I. Gilbert proceeds on his way. Canto i. v. 99. " Regret and sorrow by one act I date ; " A foolish act, Avhich I repent too late." He spoke : our swain giAres vent a piteous sigh, The tear, big-SAvelling, Avets his glistening eye ; He bids abruptly the poor hind adieu, Far on the road his journey to pursue. Depress'd, forlorn, near Tideswell tOAvn he goes, Explores the Avondrous spring that ebbs and floAvs ; Or, this side hast'ning, climbs the heavy hill, Descends the slope, and comes into the dell : Some time he stands his sufferings to bewail, Near the Avild fig-trees in the dismal vale, Where sundry elms obstruct the lightning's beam, Save, oft, the wither'd branch admits a gleam ; Or Avhere the mountain towers its lofty head, He Avalks beloAv, hard by the colonnade, Which, strung Avith floAv'rs in Avreaths, love-knots and darts, Bears nigh resemblance to the sculptile arts. c

title: Gilbert; or True Love rewarded: an amatory rural poem [By J. Templeman. Illustrated.]
text: GILBERT. 10 Discovers a tomb-stone of marble. Canto i. v. 117. Book I. Like one who fear'd a snake amidst the grass, Strives Gilbert 'neath the fig-trees' boughs to pass ; Disturbs the blinking screech-owl— loud it screams A hideous sound the vale more horrid seems. Through the entangled covert breaking way, Our weary wanderer hails the sun's bright ray ; Views the rough steep, whose brow salutes the sky ; Or loiters where the tomb-stone meets the eye ; Its chequer'd marble, smoothly wrought, stands fair, The work of time and persevering care ; With bleeding hearts supports the fluted urn, While little Cupid ever seems to mourn ; What meant these things young Gilbert sought to know, And stooping down, intently look'd below ; He, on the pedestal, some lines survey 'd, Sacred to memory of a beauteous maid : And here, for meditation well design'd, Nature's own works engross the studious mind,

title: Gilbert; or True Love rewarded: an amatory rural poem [By J. Templeman. Illustrated.]
text: GILBERT. 11 Book I. He meets with a shepherd's boy. Canto i. v. 135 A solemn spot to bless the anchorite, And bear his thoughts in ecstatic delight. But though deep solitude influence still Th' expanded soul to sooth each troubling ill, Young Gilbert ponders o'er his slighted pain, And cheerless, sighing, hastes across the plain. Along the ground the boughs' dark semblance plays ; Down airy paths he turns his mournful gaze : A course uncertain in the fields he bends, Towards where Derwent's gliding wave extends ; Onward he travels, melancholy, slow. A shepherd's boy essays his grief to know : An answer kind lorn Gilbert ne'er denies, He tells th' inquiring rustic why he sighs : " Ah me ! with scorn fair Jane my love requites, " Wounds deep my breast, and cruel pangs excites ; " A stubborn passion makes my tears to flow, " Distracts my senses, brings my spirits low.

title: Gilbert; or True Love rewarded: an amatory rural poem [By J. Templeman. Illustrated.]
text: GILBERT. 12 v. 153 Book I. The story of proud Nelly. Canto i " Far live my friends, I've from my kindred ran, " In all respects a miserable man ! " The length'ning wilds with weary steps I tread ; " My flatt'ring hopes and happiness are fled. " No situation long allures my stay ; " I wander, heedless where I shape my way : " A change of place affords a small relief, " Variety's my best solace in grief." To which the boy assum'd a friendly look, A smile o'erhung his visage while he spoke : " How much I feel for your untoward plight ! " And if I can, I'll set the matter right. " Your scornful Jane is worthy of all blame, " Another Nell — I'll warrant her the same : " That village-tyrant humbled, yonder lies, " Nor more to wound her lovers by surprise ; " No more those side-long glances cause despair, " No more young Cupid wantons in her hair ;

title: Gilbert; or True Love rewarded: an amatory rural poem [By J. Templeman. Illustrated.]
text: GILBERT. 13 Book I. The story continued. Canto i. v. 171. " Her prideful days are fled — for ever past ; " By her own weapons she's o'erthrown at last! " Long time a ploughman, Edwin was his name, " Tried every art to win the beauteous dame ; " Neglected, scorn'd, he pin'd for Nell the Proud, " Who oft express'd her sentiments aloud :" ' Stripling ! forbear ; your suit I'll still deny ; ' Think you in lime, nor place your heart so high : ' A simple cotter surely charms not me, ' Nor covet I to wed the like of thee ! ' Go now, accost some milk-maid, ruddy fair; ' Implore the like to pity your despair : ' Tis not for Nell your prayers or groans to heed ; ' Hence unregarded, from my presence speed !' " Such haughty words came Edwin oft to hear, " When, led by love, he met her look severe ; " Till, all at once, distraction seiz'd his mind, " And for a time — poor youth ! he was confin'd.

title: Gilbert; or True Love rewarded: an amatory rural poem [By J. Templeman. Illustrated.]
text: 14 GILBERT. 189, Book I. The story concluded. Canto i. v. " Meanwhile the soldiers to our village came, " To hire the service of the swains their aim ; " Some red-coat serjeant made weak Nell his prize, " Destroy'd her virtue — then commenc'd her sighs. " Vexatious strife her manner soon betray 'd ; " Her ruin'd state with horror she survey 'd : " Fall'n were her hopes, her pride all done away ; " How she repin'd ! — to gloomy thoughts a prey. " Th' unhappy girl a mother soon became ; " By which, ah me ! increas'd her open shame : " Life grew too burdensome for her to bear ; " She poison took, and bade farewell to care. " Near yonder barn four different roads are seen, " There lies the wretch of suicide between. " Long time did many intercession make, " To save the body from the driving stake : " A dreadful fate ! — deserv'dly it befell " The needless pride of our aspiring Nell.

title: Gilbert; or True Love rewarded: an amatory rural poem [By J. Templeman. Illustrated.]
text: GILBERT. 15 Book I. Day draws near to close. Canto i. v. 207. " Her slighted lover mourn'd her dire disgrace ; " He midst the rocks a marble stone did place. " Now then, young man, suspend your fruitless grief; " Let what I've told afford you full relief: " Who knows but she who treats you thus unkind, " May fall decoy 'd, and punishment soon find." He ceas'd. Poor Gilbert to reply disdains ; Renews his journey o'er the dusky plains : He lov'd his Jane — perceiv'd, though friendly spoke, The shepherd's words his anger did provoke. The sun now sunk, the lingering light fast fled ; Across the fields his quicker steps he sped. He feels arise new pangs to vex his soul ; Down his pale cheeks his tears incessant roll. Clear shines the moon — spread far, her lucid beam Reflects more bright the Derwent's silv'ry stream : Gilbert beholds, and, guided by the ray, Shapes farther south his solitary way.

title: Gilbert; or True Love rewarded: an amatory rural poem [By J. Templeman. Illustrated.]
text: GILBERT. 16 Book I, The lover's soliloquy — a sudden storm. Canto i. v. 225. Lo ! while he walks, he seems still more oppress'd ; He smites in agony his lab'ring breast ; Groan follows groan, and sigh succeeds to sigh, Loud his complaints resound the cloudless sky. " How hard I'm doom'd ! — how great the woes I feel ! " Beyond the powers of language to reveal. " Fair Jenny s slights affect my sinking heart ; " Beneath the lash of studied scorn I smart. " Ah me ! what languor steals o'er every vein, " Hope comes no more to cheer a hapless swain : " Sure I'm as weak as Jenny 's comely fair ; " Her form, her image, haunt me every where. " Blow, blow, ye winds ! blow yet more bleak and cold ! " My cause for sorrow I will hence unfold. " Oh ! for some lonely cavern 'midst the bourn, " Where answering Echo still delights to mourn ! " I'll try no more a prude's esteem to gain, " Who loves to frown, and cruel e'er remain."

title: Gilbert; or True Love rewarded: an amatory rural poem [By J. Templeman. Illustrated.]
text: GILBERT. 17 v. 243 Book I. Shelters beneath elm trees — enters into a wood. Canto i. Thus loud complaining on his way he goes ; The wind is up, it shakes the rustling boughs ; Fast from the clouds a sudden shower descends ; Full many a shrub o'ercharg'd with water bends : Big hail comes rattling 'side the neighb'ring hills, Strikes the tree tops, falls plunging the clear rills ; In clay-moist earth the dashing stream divides, Sweeps rough the soil, or down the quarries glides With hideous roar, till the strong current's force Impetuous, laves below the rocks its course. Gilbert to shelter hastens o'er the sands, Aside a row of rev'rend elms he stands, Whose tow'ring branches thicker darkness crown, While shiver'd leaves and splinters fall adown. Lone in the wood's deep solitude he's come, With weary step, unmindful of the gloom ; Disturbs the snakes, coil'd up in various folds, Alarms the frogs, and wakes the blinking owls. E

title: Gilbert; or True Love rewarded: an amatory rural poem [By J. Templeman. Illustrated.]
text: GILBERT. 19 279, Book I. The hovel. Canto i. v, A horrid gloom involves the wood profound, And night's foul bird screams frightfully around : Lo ! where he goes the track is more o'ercast, The mournful youth bewilder'd stands at last ; Vexatious tears wet either swollen eye, And his warm breast heaves many a lab 'ring sigh. Cold blows the blast : he mends his weary pace, Hies through the thorns, and finds the lonely place, Where still are laid fell'd trunks of sturdy oaks, Fell'd by the woodman's close-repeated strokes ; And nigh at hand, erected on the glade, Stood a small hut, of sapless branches made ; The driven stake rough set the plot of ground, And interwoven hung the boughs around. That Gilbert view'd, and much desir'd to know How he should act the best, or stay or go ; To seek the fields, continue to lament, Or 'midst a hovel cease his useless plaint.

title: Gilbert; or True Love rewarded: an amatory rural poem [By J. Templeman. Illustrated.]
text: GILBERT. 21 Book I. Gilbert ascends a tree. Canto i. v. 315. Ah me ! 'tis ceas'd. — Now high a tree he scales, There sits till morn illumes the dusky vales. " Sweet warbler, hail !" the list'ner station'd, cries, " Why cease your strains, that charm away my sighs ? " Come, welcome sleep ! cause me a little rest, " A little ease for my impassion'd breast ; " So when day breaks I'll tempt my fate no more, " But wind the circuit which I've wound before." He ceas'd. The dismal shades of night soon fled ; Aurora ting'd the sky with streaks of red ; A thousand chirping songsters of the grove, Awake the swain to feel fresh pangs of love : His Jennys comely figure, and her scorn, Dwell in his thoughts ; he's more and more forlorn ; The busy Avorld to him a chaos seems, His love sincere, frustrated is he deems. " Gilbert! afflict no more your pensive mind, " Nor mourn for one who treats you so unkind ;

title: Gilbert; or True Love rewarded: an amatory rural poem [By J. Templeman. Illustrated.]
text: GILBERT. 22 Book I. Descriptive of perplexity in love. Canto i. v. 333 " But set at nought the pow'r of those fine eyes, " Lest your sense fall a hopeless sacrifice." Methinks I hear our lover loud exclaim, " Go, gentle bard ! nor seek ray faults to blame ; " Beauty divine unfolds her awful charms, " Distracts my breast with violent alarms ; " Exerts her power, to waft the dang'rous storm, " Destroys my peace, enchains me to that form. " Alas ! what signs of madness vex my brain ! " My blood no longer burns in ev'ry vein : " My senses lost, outcast, forlorn I die, " Far from the glance of her disdainful eye : " Yet, cruel Jane ! one kindly tear bestow ; " Drop but one tear in sorrow for my woe." " Unhappy Gilbert ! cease this doleful strain, " Curb the wild thoughts that cause your inward pain ; " Love's hapless flame with troubles still dismays, " And wrongly balances ere judgment weighs.

title: Gilbert; or True Love rewarded: an amatory rural poem [By J. Templeman. Illustrated.]
text: CANTO II. JN OW shines the sun — enliv'ning are his beams ; Noav ev'ry leaf a sparkling treasure seems ; The dew-drops hang, reflecting various dyes, Ting'd like the rainboAv's colours 'midst the skies ; And now the woodman's measur'd strokes repeat, Spread by the busy Echo loud to beat. AdoAvn the oak our Avanderer fast descends, ToAvards the spot his eager steps he bends :

title: Gilbert; or True Love rewarded: an amatory rural poem [By J. Templeman. Illustrated.]
text: 28 GILBERT. v. 9, Book I. Canto ii Gilbert among the bushes. Beneath the trees, o'ershadoAving Avith their boughs, Through many a mazy labyrinth he goes ; VieAVS the green laurel rip'ning o'er his head, Clusters of fruit like cherries tempting red ; Rife mistletoe, which bears the pulp milk-wliite ; And ivy, cank'ring to its fatal height. With ling'ring pace, by little he proceeds ; Noav in the dingle's cavity he speeds ; Explores his way 'tween many an hazel bough, And scatters nuts of glossy brown below. Full oft the squirrels from the grove rebound, Rustling the dry leaves falling on the ground ; The nimble dormice seek the desert pass, Steal quick along, or hide beneath the grass : Aside their holds, Avhere tangled brambles grow, Near the rough blackthorn, and the cruder sloe, Rank nettles, thyme, wood-betony, henbane, Waste their known virtue and their strength in vain.

title: Gilbert; or True Love rewarded: an amatory rural poem [By J. Templeman. Illustrated.]
text: GILBERT. 29 The woodman. Canto ii. v. 27. Book I. But iioaa' our Gilbert comes Avithin the spot, Where overnight he'd seen the branch-form'd cot : He shouts amain : the Avond'ring Avoodman hears, And is confounded by unusual fears : Behind the Avail, in thoughtful mood, he stands^ Holding his axe within his trembling hands — Finds out a crevice, marks the vent'rous SAvain, Perceives his stupor and his fright are vain. The AA'oodman cries, " My son, Avhat brings you here ? " Tell me your name, Avhence come, and who you are ? " Sure in the Avood there's nothing fit to find, " Fit for a youth to please his active mind : " The nuts are Avet Avith night's returning deAV, " The crabs unripe are sure no prize to you : " Confess for why you leave your distant home, " Far in the Avilds, at peep of day, to roam. " 'Tis seen some grief affects your early fire, " Dulls every look, bespeaks affliction dire :

title: Gilbert; or True Love rewarded: an amatory rural poem [By J. Templeman. Illustrated.]
text: 30 GILBERT. v. 45, Book I. Gilbert's unhappiness. Canto ii " I feel concern'd — I Avish the cause to hear, " Nor of my friendship have you need to fear." To Avhom the youth replies, as frankly free, " Soon I'll inform you, sir, concerning me. " My name is Gilbert, o'er the wilds I rove, " A wight oppress'd by unsuccessful love. " From Bawtry toAvn Avith weary steps I came, " Strange to these parts, no home have I to claim " For three long months I've like a vagrant pass'd " From place to place, and here I come at last. " Ah me ! I ventur'd into solitude, " To mourn my slighted passion for a prude ! " Cruel infatuation ! — I adore " A giddy maid, Avho hates me more and more ! " With grief of soul my brain it stupifies, " My panting bosom heaves incessant sighs. " I've bade adieu to Janes disdainful scorn, " Leaving my friends, disconsolate, forlorn,

title: Gilbert; or True Love rewarded: an amatory rural poem [By J. Templeman. Illustrated.]
text: GILBERT. 31 Book I. He relates some particulars of his Use. Canto ii. v. 63. " Hoping through change of place some ease to find, " Haply some ease for my disorder'd mind. " And while I Avalk'd o'erborne AA'ith sad dismay, " A countryman o'ertook me on my Avay, " Ask'd Avhat I Avas ? Avhat ail'd me ? Avhence I came ? " Or Avanting Avork? I answer'd him the same. " Then, as I Avish'd, h%presently agreed " To hire my help — his boy I did succeed : " He good instruction did on me bestOAV, " And still my labour Aalued not too low. " A straAV-roof'd cottage on the moor he OAvn'd, " A thriving hedge extended far around ; " Choice shrubs and trees, with various blossoms spread, " O'er floAvers and plants, grac'd many a cultur'd bed. " Blest with a Avife industrious and fair, " A ruddy offspring claim'd his anxious care : " When clos'd at eATe his labours in the field, " Sweet rapture their lov'd intercourse would yield :

title: Gilbert; or True Love rewarded: an amatory rural poem [By J. Templeman. Illustrated.]
text: GILBERT. 32 Book I. The subject continued. Canto ii. v. 81. " Fix'd by his spouse, his children on his knees, " Near his fire-side — what luxury of ease! " On his rough stand he'd place the sparkling ale, " And joke and laugh, or tell some pleasing tale. " When I approach'd, the little rustics fled, " Scar'd at a stranger- — nothing yet they said : " Familiar grown, no more my sight they fear'd ; " Still, Avhen they play'd, sweet innocence appear'd. " Here taught to break the glebe, the dung to throw, " I've from the heap o'erspread the same beloAv ; " Enrich'd Avith nutriment the barren soil, " That better crops might crown the ploughman's toil. " When sultry heats have parch'd the stubbled earth, " Dried up the grain, and threaten'd certain dearth, " I've borne the bucket from the neighb'ring rill, " The garden troughs and Avatering-pots to fill. " At times have I, with artificial showers, " Reviv'd the plants, the herbs, and drooping flowers ;

title: Gilbert; or True Love rewarded: an amatory rural poem [By J. Templeman. Illustrated.]
text: GILBERT. 33 Canto ii. v. 99. Book I. Continued. " Propt firm the Aveaker, pluckt the useless Aveed, " And crush'd the vermin on the leaf that feed. " From end to end the garden, thus I've pass'd., " Despairing, groaning, gloomily o'ercast. " With nervous strength I've handled well the spade, " Cut through the turf, and dug the heavy glade ; " Till by the dint of force I've chang'd the scene, " And brought to broAvn Avhat late before was green. " With care, alternate ridge and dale IVe made, " To keep in earth the rising celery's head ; " Remov'd the frames, the tender shrub to breathe, " And others place the crystal bells beneath. " Pleasing employ ! but yet I felt a pain ; " Alas ! I sought for comfort still in vain. " My master kindly strove to sooth my care, " And ease the burden of my deep despair. " Full oft IVe rose at early dawn of morn, " And brush'd around the fields of rip'hing corn : K

title: Gilbert; or True Love rewarded: an amatory rural poem [By J. Templeman. Illustrated.]
text: GILBERT. 34 117 Book I. Continued. Canto ii. v " Some clatt'ring scarecroAv to erect in sight, " High on the bank, the plund'ring birds to fright. " The tall wild poppy of \ermilion hue, " And the cyanus, bright with glossy blue, " I've freshly gather 'd from the corn so green, " And Aveav'd a wreath with boxen leaves between ; " Ah, luckless wreath ! neglected, Avith'ring there, " Never to grace proud Jenny's auburn hair : " Thou still an emblem of those hopes shalt be, " Those fallen hopes, that once did flatter me. " Hoav griev'd my heart at even, when I've seen " Young lovers loit'ring o'er the level green ! " I, Avhile they danc'd on light fantastic toe, " Have found my spirits overcome Avith woe. " And when at night tir'd nature fain Avould rest, " I've kept aAvake, unhappily oppress'd, " Soft slumber hast'ning from my tearful eyes, " While my rent bosom heav'd afflicting sighs.

title: Gilbert; or True Love rewarded: an amatory rural poem [By J. Templeman. Illustrated.]
text: 36 GILBERT. Book I. Recommends labour a cure for lave. Canto ii. v. 153 " Still from experience learn one truth to know, " Love is a foible, indolent and low, " Derives its growth from weakness of the heart, " Unnerves our strength, and leaves a rankling dart. " Full thirty years ago its poAver I knew : " My wife Dorinda mark'd my passion true, " Yet would essay her fickle arts in vain ; " But I with scorn re turn'd her proud disdain, " Laugh'd when she smil'd, or angry have I frown'd, " Join'd in her songs, and made the place resound. " One morn in May how chang'd indeed was she ! " Her thoughts Avere wholly occupied by me. " Then was the time I could no more withstand ; " I shew'd the ring, and soon obtain'd her hand : " Since Avhich no more of love I ever knew, " But day by day my labour I pursue : " 'Mid sturdy trees I drive the pointed wedge, " Lop from the trunk the rough redundant ledge ;

title: Gilbert; or True Love rewarded: an amatory rural poem [By J. Templeman. Illustrated.]
text: GILBERT. 37 171 > Book I. Refreshment . Canto ii. v. " A tyrant in this forest I appear, " Who levies desolation far and near. " Were you, young man, to labour once inclin'd, " Not stupid grief could more oppress your mind : " Come try the drift, a Aveighty axe receive, " And Avhat you earn, the Avhole to you I'll gVe." The Avoodman ceas'd, Avhile stepping to the shed Clean on a block his humble fare to spread ; DraAvs his clasp-knife, divides his salted meat, Divides his bread, and bids our Gilbert eat : A taper'd horn Avith home-breAv'd liquor stor'd, Pour'd from the keg, adorns the rustic board ; With ale concludes the morning's cool repast. The Avilling youth to Avork betakes at last ; A pond'rous axe his nervous hands sustain, Behind the tree he tries his strength amain, Intently earnest, closer still he goes, Exerts his force, and gives repeated blows.

title: Gilbert; or True Love rewarded: an amatory rural poem [By J. Templeman. Illustrated.]
text: GILBERT. 38 Canto ii. v. 189. Book I. Lopping branches — tying faggots. Struck to the root, the stubborn oak must yield, Lean more and more Avith strokes the woodmen wield ; The deep incision bears its Avay all round, Till down the branches crash along the ground : Here left aAvhile to drench the moss-groAvn plain, The dripping sap through sundry channels drain, Falls drop by drop, and, gathering at the foot, O'erflows the bason of the stunted root. The timber fell'd, the youth Avith ardour glows, His poAvers reneAv'd, he lops the cumb'rous boughs ; Soon every branch the parent tree disown, And rough the trunk extends its length alone; With lesser pains the splinters he divides, And heaps on heaps he into faggots ties, A pile of fuel near the spot to raise, To cheer the Avinter by a friendly blaze. Now mid-day's come, once more the sparkling ale Exhilarates their spirits as they fail,

title: Gilbert; or True Love rewarded: an amatory rural poem [By J. Templeman. Illustrated.]
text: GILBERT. 39 v. 207, Book I. Praise of good wine. Day's labour done. Canto ii ReneAvs their strength — to Avork again they go, Long to repeat the Avide-resounding bloAV. As in the climes Avhere order'd vines extend, A sov'reign po\v'r the ills of life to mend, The grapes knoAvn virtues, squeez'd into the boAvl, Enliven better each industrious soul : But AA'ine like this the boasted cellars lack, Where viler mixtures drug in every stack, Mere Avater, cider, spirits, juice of sloes ; Preferr'd to ale its excellence Avho knows ? Ah ! Avhere such dregs the festive board disgrace, Still may the drinker boast a paler face ! The heady liquor modestly refuse, Or worse expect by this destructive juice. His toil now done, the rustic leads the swain Across the forest and the distant plain : A bunch of sticks alternate each one bears ; The woodman Avhistles while the youth despairs,

title: Gilbert; or True Love rewarded: an amatory rural poem [By J. Templeman. Illustrated.]
text: 40 GILBERT. v. 225, Canto ii. Book I. Cottage described. One sings with glee, the other's frequent sigh, Unfolds a heart divest of ev'ry joy : By bitter anguish Gilbert's much oppress'd, His heavy sorroAv throbs his pensive breast. A cleanly cottage overtops the vale, Securely fenc'd by many a sturdy pale : The Avoodman's load rebounds against the gate, The children run, and glad his smile await ; He Avelcomes heartily his lovelorn guest, Exerts his skill, and tries the merry jest. High on the hearth ascends the cheerful blaze, Illumes the room, and shines the sidelong gaze ; The oaken draAvers usurp the proudest place, Fresh gather'd flowers two shining vessels grace, Here, side to side, the chairs are fix'd around, The six old chairs for strength of years renoAvn'd ; Sweetly the linnet charms the listening ear, A few dark pictures on the walls appear.

title: Gilbert; or True Love rewarded: an amatory rural poem [By J. Templeman. Illustrated.]
text: GILBERT. 41 Book I. The matron prepares supper. Canto ii. v. 243. Rubb'd with nice art the cupboard shines more bright, Its Ararnish'd front reflects the Avav'ring light ; A curious clock repeats the cuckoo's note, And strikes each time a silver sound to float. Young Gilbert vieAv'd the woodman's humble state, A king might envy such their happy fate ; Here every face felicity express'd, Here rural life a certain charm confess'd. With kind concern the Avife her cares essays, Lifts out the board, and straight the knives she lays Brings four Avood trenchers, long esteem'd her best, Placing them round for family and guest. Her eldest son o'er distant fields returns, A lusty blade, Avho to be idle scorns ; A shepherd's boy, untaught, of manners plain, Coarse his poor garb, and Avild his oaten strain. He from the flame the heatful cover bears, Helping his mother in her anxious cares ; G

title: Gilbert; or True Love rewarded: an amatory rural poem [By J. Templeman. Illustrated.]
text: GILBERT. 42 Canto ii. v*. 261 Book I. Mention of next day's labour. Unloos'd the lid, a spiral steam issues, Tavo Avholesome dumplings nicely boil'd he vieAVS ; Plac'd in the midst, salt ham and greens invite, With savoury smell, the sharpen'd appetite ; The little group their different stations take, And all, save one, a hearty supper make : — In vain they press the stranger, vain entreat He'd end his grief, and strive his meal to eat ; In vain he strives — his tears he'd fain forego, His starting tears, expressing Avell his woe. Noav supper ends, the frugal crumbs are clear'd, The master's voice above the rest is heard : " To morroAv morn, by order, we must go " To load the timber fell'd by many a Woav ; " On the rough common- waste, as heretofore, " With sapless lops increase the 'squire's big store, " While his due rent the tenants to him bring, " And from industry all his riches spring.

title: Gilbert; or True Love rewarded: an amatory rural poem [By J. Templeman. Illustrated.]
text: GILBERT. 43 v. 279, Book I. The son has leave to help his father. Canto ii, " Just at the rising of the early daAvn, " Fetch up the team along the Avide-fenc'd laAvn ; " Prepare the bolted hooks, the clanking chains, " The levers, poles, and rollers, aid our pains. " A jovial day in labouring hard Ave'll spend, " With sparkling ale our utmost poAvers extend, " Recruit our spirits while at rest Ave stand; " Our Gilbert here Avill lend a helping hand. " But did your master, Avhen my Avish you told " Say he'd, for once, secure the sheep in fold ? " Gave he consent to your assisting me, " By taking charge of all one day from thee ? " Or by a mean, unfriendly, flat excuse, " Did he the office of your aid refuse ? " He knows full Avell I never him deny, " Whene'er he craves a little fuel dry." To which the son Avith modesty replies, " The courteous shepherd seldomer denies ;

title: Gilbert; or True Love rewarded: an amatory rural poem [By J. Templeman. Illustrated.]
text: GILBERT. 44 v. 297 Book I. Rustic mirth. Canto ii " He oft remarks my close, assiduous pains " Make full amends — by kindnesses he gains : " Sometimes he grants a holiday's advance, " I, round the Maypole, join in festive dance ; " Or, on the green to chase the rural maids, " I'm oft the foremost of the village blades ; — " In such like sports no cares e'er intervene, " The same with labour after I begin. " Just at the rising of the early daAvn, " I'll fetch the oxen o'er the deAvy laAvn ; " I'll bring the bolted hooks — the clanking chains, " The levers, poles, and rollers, aid our pains." And now the home-brew'd ale its virtue shews : BroAvn shelling nuts the humble banquet close ; The wakeful children at the sight feel pleas'd, The shells are broken, and the kernels seiz'd. O'er lively tales with laughter Mirth presides, Now here, now there, her fav'rite lore divides :

title: Gilbert; or True Love rewarded: an amatory rural poem [By J. Templeman. Illustrated.]
text: GILBERT. 45 Book I. Gilbert forgets his sorrows — retires to rest. Canto ii. v. 315 The honest Avoodman and the matron sing, The shepherd plays the bladder's sounding string. SorroAV, long cherish'd, leaves the lovers breast, He cracks his nuts to cater like the rest ; Forgets his troubles, chokes each rising sigh, Starts for a joke, and pleases menily. As Time for none will make the least delay, E'en sAvifter flies the more Ave wish his stay ; So sure the hours unheeded lightly pass'd, Then each retiring, sought SAveet sleep at last

title: Gilbert; or True Love rewarded: an amatory rural poem [By J. Templeman. Illustrated.]
text: CANTO HI XlOW sweetly sleep, amid the night's void hours, Recruits our strength, reneAvs our wasted powers ; Affords tir'd Nature vigorous supplies, Befriends our labours, renovates our joys ! Nor on the proud alone, nor tyrant kings, AAvaits the blessing — free to all it springs ; Save, in the dungeon, Avhere the wretch of ill Is chain'd on straAV — sleep may forsake him still. H

title: Gilbert; or True Love rewarded: an amatory rural poem [By J. Templeman. Illustrated.]
text: GILBERT. 50 Canto iii. v. 9. Book II. Thoughts on sleep, SjC. Happy that man, Avho, at the evening's close, With thoughts unruffled, sinks into repose ; No cares, through vice, perplex his quiet breast ; Nor frightful dreams break in upon his rest ; But rightly good, his conscience bears no stains ; He, undisturb'd, beloved sleep obtains. The morning breaks, Aurora bright appears ; Sol darts his rays, dries Nature's dewy tears : From slumber ris'n, the Avoodman wakes the swain The shepherd's boy had early sought the plain, First drove the team to wait behind the door, Then brought the chains, and rollers us'd before. Along the common to the woods they pass, Brushing the Avat'ry margin of the grass ; On every blade dependent crystals shine, High on each branch the birds in matins join : Nor yield the hedges yet a luscious food, Nor clust'ring hips and haAVS enrich the Avood ;

title: Gilbert; or True Love rewarded: an amatory rural poem [By J. Templeman. Illustrated.]
text: GILBERT. 51 Book II. Morning's repast. Manner of loading the timber. Canto iii. v. 27. But left for frost their stubborn rind to bite, When the snoAv, falling, clothes the fields in Avhite. Wise Providence divinely shoAvs his care, Provides for all on earth, in sea, in air ; His poAver sustains, his bounteous gifts supply, The little birds, from spray to spray that fly. Close up the hill the harmless oxen go, Wind through the dale, the woodland site below ; Where scatter'd lie the fallen trees around, With all their branches levell'd on the ground. And to the Avell-known hut the men repair, Unload the implements with speed, with care ; Yet, ere they work, they take an hour's regale, Eat what they list, and drink their share of ale. Fast to each trunk they bolt the rattling chain, Guide the strong poles, the rollers sweep the plain; They, orderly, by one and one proceed, Till every balk appears along the mead ;

title: Gilbert; or True Love rewarded: an amatory rural poem [By J. Templeman. Illustrated.]
text: 52 GILBERT. Canto iii. v. 45. Book Is. Invitation into the cottage. Where strength they lack, the lever lends its aid, To load the Avain Avith six firm Avheels display 'd ; The oxen slowly draAv the wain along ; The Avoodman cheerly sings a rural song. Well-pleas'd, the brave triumvirate survey 'd The lengths of timber on the common laid : And, as the Avight, Avho ploughs the ocean o'er, Encounters toils while adding to his store, The stock acquir'd reveals th' umveary'd strokes, Struck at the roots of fir-trees, pines, and oaks. Perplex'd in mind, our Gilbert quits the plain ; Dorinda kindly bids him in again. His two compeers to welcome stable lead The useful kine, on good neAV hay to feed : Give rest their limbs till noon's relaxing sun, The better half of their hard work is done ; No more remains their final task to seal, Than the dried fuel in the cart to wheel.

title: Gilbert; or True Love rewarded: an amatory rural poem [By J. Templeman. Illustrated.]
text: GILBERT. 53 7 Book II. Dinner of fried eggs and bacon. Return to labour. Canto iii. v. 63. And noAv to dine the handy dame prepares ; Withal essays to lull the stranger's cares — Ah me ! such cares that bitterly assail His anxious mind, till every succour fail. An iron pan, o'er the clear embers plac'd, Holds the fresh eggs, the bacon fine in taste^ Cut in nice slices, streak'd Avith red and Avhite, Fries crispy broAvn, true relish to excite. They fix the chairs to front Avhere trenchers stand The helpful Avife deals out Avith ready hand : By Avhich refresh'd they rise, reneAv their toil, To bring the sticks, and raise the lofty pile. Within the stable go the men apart, They link the team to draAV the lumb'ring cart Across the upland path, the verdant plain, The common field, the Avasting Avood's domain. Arriv'd, at even distances they stand, Hurling the faggots o'er the stumpy land ;

title: Gilbert; or True Love rewarded: an amatory rural poem [By J. Templeman. Illustrated.]
text: 54 GILBERT. Loading the cart with faggots. Solitude. Canto iii. v. 81. Book II. The crackling heaps upheld above the glade, High on the cart the burden's closely laid. At several times the team the treasure brings ; Then o'er the common, pile on pile upsprings : The squire's big stock the best of prices bear, The rougher lops, the balks of timber square. MeanAvhile our Gilbert seeks to ease his mind, Steals in the Avood, and loiters far behind ; Here lies the tree he'd fell'd the day before, He marks it's drying, Avithering boughs, once more In solitude he ponders o'er his fate, Lone solitude befits his hapless state : No jocose woodman cheers the solemn spot, Or pours libations in the branch-form'd cot ; No axe resounds Avhere late the sticks were pil'd, To guide him wand'ring through the mazy wild ; But dull the scene — increasing gloom prevails, Till the poor youth his destiny bewails.

title: Gilbert; or True Love rewarded: an amatory rural poem [By J. Templeman. Illustrated.]
text: GILBERT. 55 Canto iii. v. 99. Book II. Tea-drinking in the cottage. Reason aAvakes, our suff'ring sAvain to aid ; Lorn he returns along the shelving glade. Pleas'd, the blithe Avoodman and his son behold The pensive stranger near the neighb'ring fold ; Attune their holla his slow steps to haste, Till he rejoins them on the rugged waste. Lo ! now the time of drinking tea arrives : The cleanly matron seems the best of wives ; Slice after slice of home-made bread she toasts, Her butter, cream, and treacle too, she boasts. Nor china cups the beverage contain, Nor pompous tea-urn fits the humble train ; Of coarser fabric stout the set is made, And where they break, the loss is soon repaid. 'Neath humbler roofs Simplicity is found ; Lo ! Avhere she dwells contentment smiles around With less requir'd, the best is man supplied, His little wants the sooner satisfied :

title: Gilbert; or True Love rewarded: an amatory rural poem [By J. Templeman. Illustrated.]
text: 56 GILBERT. Canto iii. v. 117. Book II. Gilbert proceeds on his journey. But Avhere the mind's on more than needful bent, Adieu, simplicity ! adieu, content ! Farewell those charms, to grace a cottage left ! He's evermore of happiness bereft. While drinking tea the rustic group are plac'd, Lorn Gilbert sickens at the transient jest ; His every look unhappiness displays, Unfit to hail the social hearth's bright blaze. Lo ! he'll retire ; a reason he assigns ; To Aveep in fav'rite solitude he pines : — Starts up resolv'd — they crave his longer stay; He bids farewell, and hastens on his way. Across the common, iioav he saunt'ring goes, Grief Avrings his soul, and heaAry are his woes; He southern travels o'er the vary'd fields, Till 'side a pond, to rest aAvhile he yields. Near to the margin walking in despair, AVith sighs and groans he rends the evening air.

title: Gilbert; or True Love rewarded: an amatory rural poem [By J. Templeman. Illustrated.]
text: GILBERT. 57 Book II. He is accosted by a farmer's boy. Canto iii. v. 135. A farmer's boy comes driving doAvn his team ; To give the horses drink amidst the stream ; The lover's doleful plight attracts his eyes ; He Avhistles, shouts, dismounts, and to him flies. " Ah ! tell me, friend, Avhat you're about to do ! " The river's springs may fatal prove to you. " Near to it's brink, see, nine green aviIIoavs groAv, " Each one is carv'd with sundry hearts beloAV ; " The Avretched carver perish'd in my view, " Lo ! in the Avave himself he headlong threAv : " I instant div'd, the body brought on shore — ■ " Alas ! too late — his life-blood ebb'd no more. " KnoAvn in the vale, the father's name is John ; " His harmless mirth's for ever, ever gone ! " Tearino- his Avhiten'd locks, he beats his breast; " Ne'er look'd since, nor once essay 'd a jest; " Which on my mind a deep impression stamps, " Excites soft pity and my pleasures damps. i

title: Gilbert; or True Love rewarded: an amatory rural poem [By J. Templeman. Illustrated.]
text: GILBERT. 58 Gives afurther account of himself. Canto iii. v. 153. Book II. " Poor stranger ! come, your secret ills confess, " Explain the cause you suffer such distress ; " Why seek alone, the solitary pass, " Where the wild weeds shoot rankly o'er the grass ? " 'Tis sev'ral miles to town — 'tis evening's close ; — " And your deportment speaks your very woes." Gilbert, half angry, answers him aright ; " Farmer, forbear ; nor mock my AvayAvard plight : " I'm one, indeed, by every ill sore vex'd, " My passion slighted, and my mind perplex'd : " A cruel maiden leads me to complain, " Sets out her charms ; but trifles with my pain : " Friend, linger not ; dismiss your groundless fear, " 'TAvas merely chance that brought me Avandering here " Alas ! though sorroAv festers in my breast, " A change of place affords some little rest : " A change of place relieves my stubborn woe, " And yields the short-liv'd pleasure grief may know.

title: Gilbert; or True Love rewarded: an amatory rural poem [By J. Templeman. Illustrated.]
text: GILBERT. 59 Book II. The story of poor Susan. Canto iii. v. 171. " I've Avound my course through many a vale and grove, " O'er Avintery Avastes, o'er stubbled fields I rove ; " Parch'd up by thirst, I've sought the murm'ring rill, " And, for my food, the turnip-groAving hill : " Ah! Avhere smooth bricks are burnt, on clay-red plains, " A bak'd potatoe oft reAvards my pains ; " I lie, at night, extended on the grass ; " And such the life of misery I pass." " 'Tis misery indeed," the boy replies ; " Lo ! what you say awakens my surprise : " Such once Avas Susan's melancholy state, " Doom'd by the rigour of severer fate. " Our servant she, and well by all belov'd, " Till some young soldier cruel to her prov'd : " No more the drum's and fife's enliv'ning sound " Spread universal mirth and glee around ; " But to yon village did the blades repair, " To fist the swains, and overcome the fair.

title: Gilbert; or True Love rewarded: an amatory rural poem [By J. Templeman. Illustrated.]
text: 60 GILBERT. Canto iii. v. 189. Book II. Continued. " Alas! poor Susan bitterly repin'd, " Yet strove to hide the anguish of her mind : " Her mind's distemper every day increas'd, " Until, at length, her tears she seldom ceas'd. " Desponding cares seiz'd on the lovelorn dame, " Her senses fled — more Avretched she became. " Nightly she Avander'd in the lonely field, " A piteous sight as ever you beheld : " Beneath a stack she'd fix herself to lie, " Vent Avild her plaint, and sigh add still to sigh ; " Or by the moon's pale light AA'ould rings prepare, " And bracelets for her arms of plaited hair. " Poor hapless girl ! — but death has set her free ! " Aside her grave there groAvs the lone yeAv-tree ; " No sculptur'd stone to head the turf is found, " But grass and nettles skirt the border round : " Her fortune hard, unkind her luckless doom, " Early she sunk a victim to the tomb.

title: Gilbert; or True Love rewarded: an amatory rural poem [By J. Templeman. Illustrated.]
text: 61 GILBERT. Book II. The story concluded. Canto iii. v. 207. " Come then, young man, your stubborn cares forego, " Cheer up your spirits, and dismiss your Avoe ; " Take friendly Avarning from this tale so true, " Nor let your soitoav fatal prove to you. " Ah ! turn with me — thy lodging I'll provide " Within the loft, I'll give thee food beside ; " To morroAV morn, my master, I'll engage, " Will hire your service, and your grief assuage." This Gilbert hearing, he Avipes dry his eyes, Cheers up his sinking spirits, and replies : " My ever-grateful thanks to you are due ; " Your fair advice assur'dly I'll pursue. " Though in the fields I'd plann'd the night to spend, " Say where you go, I'll on your steps attend : " Such good, unlook'd-for, elevates my mind ; " Fruits of your friendship and compassion kind." In saying Avhich, along the bank they haste ; Both mount the team, and ride across the waste.

title: Gilbert; or True Love rewarded: an amatory rural poem [By J. Templeman. Illustrated.]
text: GILBERT. 63 Canto iii. v. 243. Book II. The farmer's boy. A full variety of useful plants, Supplying well the farmer's daily wants. Such ample store our Gilbert's fain to view, While slow the team their sluggish course pursue The farmer's boy the upland path explores, Dismounts below, and opes the stable doors ; His usual care to feed his charge bestoAv'd, He and his friend repass the narroAV road ; A strong desire his anxious breast betrays, To free the sufferer, and his spirits raise. Kind, gentle youth ! Avith education scant, He boasts a heart to help the Avretch of Avant ; A steady stripling, ever well inclin'd To follow the good dictates of his mind. Where bountifully Nature's gifts dispense, The rustic hind arrives at excellence ; Arrives at knowledge, unacquir'd from schools, And guides his actions by his self-taught rules :

title: Gilbert; or True Love rewarded: an amatory rural poem [By J. Templeman. Illustrated.]
text: ARGUMENT. Night, Reflections, fye. Gilbert takes up his lodging in a hay- loft. He gives a fuller account of his adventures ; is left alone. The amorous girl disappointed. Gilbert ruminates on the incident, and at length falls asleep. Time. One day more is employed in the second book.

title: Gilbert; or True Love rewarded: an amatory rural poem [By J. Templeman. Illustrated.]
text: CANTO IV. AS days revolve, eventful change takes place ; Some rise in poAver, some sink into disgrace : Lo ! in this Avorld, strange ups and doAvns await, Kings, princes, beggars, ministers of state. Who needs go far, one painful truth to note ? How worth is left to wear a thread-bare coat ! While the rich fool his pamper'd Avish enjoys, And foully revels 'midst of luxuries.

title: Gilbert; or True Love rewarded: an amatory rural poem [By J. Templeman. Illustrated.]
text: 68 GILBERT. v. 9, "S Book II. Gilbert in a hay-loft. Canto iv, Merit avails but little here at best, To raise the bard by poverty depress ; We are not found to pass our judgment light, Since feAv, 'tis thought, in rags can argue right. Yet oft kind Fortune fair endeavours crowns, Bestows reAvards, bids smiles succeed to froAvns : Haply the poet strives no more in vain ; But from the press encores his heavenly strain : He gains applause — the muse his lay inspires, Bids genius wake, and warms Avith all her fires. Noav the full Moon expands, the kindly ray, Shot 'thAvart, increases by departing day ; Afar and near she spreads her sacred light, And silvers o'er the heavy gloom of night. Where stands the five-bar hedge-gate near the waste The farmer's boy and Gilbert thither haste ; A scaling-ladder's fix'd against the boards, The barn a shelt'ring canopy affords.

title: Gilbert; or True Love rewarded: an amatory rural poem [By J. Templeman. Illustrated.]
text: 69 GILBERT. v. 27, Book II. Gilbert is questioned respecting his misfortunes. Canto iv. Dry useful fodder forms a shelving stack, Pil'd to the tiling o'er the stable-rack, Bags fill'd Avith oats and beans, a goodly store, Spreads the broad surface of the rougher floor. Gilbert bemoans, unhappily forlorn ; His friend's retir'd, but soon he'll back return : He comes Avith bread and cheese to show his care ; First parts the Avhole, then gives the youth a share. The rough Avind ceas'd, the sky's serenely bright, Nor clouds eclipse pale Cynthia's Avelcome light, Who darts her beams through many a chinky Avay, Shining the atoms o'er the chaffs display. And noAv the boy from Gilbert seeks to know, If other pangs than love excite his Avoe ; He, by his friends deserted, did appear As though hard fortune dealt Avith him severe : " Say, is it love affects your pensive mind ; " Or do relations treat you still unkind ?

title: Gilbert; or True Love rewarded: an amatory rural poem [By J. Templeman. Illustrated.]
text: GILBERT. 70 Book II. He confesses Jane to have slighted his affection. Canto iv. v. 45. " Once more confess Avhat mean these far-fetch'd sighs, " These groans, these tears that wet your glist'ning eyes " No base design leads me to speak these words ; " Sweet consolation friendship oft affords : " Your sev'ral cares to your true friend disclose, " Who may perchance find Avays to ease your Avoes." The other cries, " Your wish I'll not deny : " Tis luckless love occasions me to sigh : " Fair Jane, of BaAvtry's distant town, 'tis she " Whose wayward slights have long affected me : " A carrier once, I drove a tilted cart, " Conveying goods in safety to the mart : " Oft, at the turnpike, I have form'd excuse " To call and loiter, telling some rare neAvs : " Her parents kneAv ray inclination Avell, " With pleasure mark'd whate'er I stood to tell : " But scornful Jenny scarce a look would deign, " To ease the anguish of my stubborn pain.

title: Gilbert; or True Love rewarded: an amatory rural poem [By J. Templeman. Illustrated.]
text: 72 GILBERT. The ivory telescope. Canto iv. v. 81. Book II. " A ruddy maid, religiously inclin'd, " Of virtuous mould, and careful turn of mind. " She soon grew fond, by soft persuasion led, " Agreed with me at proper time to wed ; " Next with our wages some neat cot we'll rent, " And buy a pig to add to our content. " AAvhile adieu ! I noAv must home return — " Gilbert, fareAvell ! nor longer vainly mourn. " With you my ivory spying-glass I'll leave, " To view the moon, and thus the time deceive. " A Cobler, late, instructed me to spy " The num'rous specks which twinkle 'mid the sky " He'd fix'd his glass in leather, so complete, " That, when drawn out, it measur'd seven feet. " Again adieu ! nor think on Jennys scorn — " I'll be the first to call you in the morn ; " Here, on the hay, for once your lodging take ; " To-morrow night a better shift we'll make."

title: Gilbert; or True Love rewarded: an amatory rural poem [By J. Templeman. Illustrated.]
text: GILBERT. 73 Book II. Gilbert is left overcome aith grief. Canto iv. v. 99. This saying, closely shaking hands, they part ; A sincere friendship dwells in either heart ; Nor either selfish interests excite, Their minds congenial sentiments unite ; Linking in other bonds than kindred chains, Or mercenary hopes, or look'd-for gains. Noav lone and drear, young Gilbert vainly tries To cheer his spirits, to forego his sighs ; But, ah ! dire Avoes convulse his inmost soul, While, unrestrain'd, his tears incessant roD. With limbs relax'd, in agony he lay, Extended out upon the covering hay, Praying for slumber to assuage his care ; But slumber flies the Avretch of deep despair. Three tedious hours our hopeless lover's pass'd — Lo ! from his stupor he's constrain'd at last : A gentle tapping on the boards he hears ; His mind's assail'd by various doubts and fears : i

title: Gilbert; or True Love rewarded: an amatory rural poem [By J. Templeman. Illustrated.]
text: 74 GILBERT. Book II. Hears a knocking at the door. A female enters. Canto iv. v. 117. The noise continues, up he starts amaz'd ; He groAvs courageous, the trap-door is rais'd : — A damsel Avaiting, meets his stricken eyes, Confounds his thoughts, and fills him Avith surprise. No looks of softness glisten o'er her face, Nor charms express the bloom of youthful grace, Rip'ning in beauty ; nor a form complete, To keep the lover kneeling at her feet : Devoid of all, above the steps she springs, Sits on the hay, and thus to speak begins : " Young lad, dismiss your vain surprise and fear ! " The farmer's man declar'd hoAv you came here. " A sneaking kindness he forsooth pretends ; " No more of that — let you and me be friends : " 'Tis very late — the folks are all asleep, " From my Avarm bed in silence I did creep ; " All negligent myself you see IVe clad, " I flew down stairs to make your bosom glad.

title: Gilbert; or True Love rewarded: an amatory rural poem [By J. Templeman. Illustrated.]
text: GILBERT. 75 135 She speaks to the lover, and confounds him. Canto lv. v, Book II. " Hoav pleas'd am I ! — aAvay your needless fear ! " Embrace SAveet Kitty like no looby here : " My kind respects to some poor hind I've shoAvn, " Can he do less than love but me alone ?" In speaking this, on Gilbert fix'd, her eyes Shoot kinder glances — amorously she sighs : Moves nigher still, her purpose to pursue, And bares her snoAvy bosom full in vieAV. What fierce temptation for our lovelorn swain ! He strives to speak — alas ! he strives in vain : His every look, Avith wonder strange impress'd. Displays the state of his impassion'd breast. To such discourse if he should e'er attend, TVould injure cruelly his sincere friend : Still seem'd that friend in Kitty much deceiv'd ; A faithless fair, though otherwise believ'd. Noav fires his blood to burn through every vein, Noav prudence cools the fiery course again ;

title: Gilbert; or True Love rewarded: an amatory rural poem [By J. Templeman. Illustrated.]
text: 76 GILBERT. He essays an answer. Canto iv. v. 153. Book II. Confus'd he stands, nor yet he silence breaks ; — Noav more collected, thus he falt'ring speaks : " Cease, O fair maid ! to tempt a wretch forlorn, " And from the hay-loft quickly back return : " For me, poor wight, unAvorthy still I prove ; " Nor can I meet Avith ardour due your love : — " Alas ! your breast a guilty passion gloAvs, " It heats your blood, and virtue overthroAvs : " Yet better judgment still shall guide my way ; " I scorn the crime that would my friend betray. " He late confess'd, it Avere by both agreed, " Both you and him, to Aved Avith proper speed, " Adding your Avages some neat cot to rent, " Your two years' wages, none of Avhich you've spent." Then to himself: " Ah, Jane ! unlike to she ! " Were all your fond affection fix'd on me, " Nor longer as a vagrant I Avould roam, " But stay Avith thee for happiness at home.

title: Gilbert; or True Love rewarded: an amatory rural poem [By J. Templeman. Illustrated.]
text: GILBERT. 77 Book II. Resists the temptation, and is upbraided by the damsel. Canto iv. v. 171 " Ah ! not to me such joys as these belong ; " I'm doom'd to knoAV of ills a mighty throng : " My troubled soul by heavy grief's oppress'd, " Dull care corrodes my e'er desponding breast." He ceasing, dares not on her look again; One fatal smile might make his purpose vain. The maid observant, thus resumes her lore, But not in mood so jocose as before : " For shame, young SAvain, to use me so severe ! " To be insulted sure I came not here : " I heard your case, soft pity fill'd my breast, " My guilty passion finish'd all the rest : " Still not my pity, not my passion told, " Can Avarm a heart that stubborn is and cold ; " No more I'll fondly tempt a wretch forlorn, " But from the hay-loft quickly I'll return. " My proffer'd kindnesses your scorn excite ; " Add no exposure to your cruel slight :

title: Gilbert; or True Love rewarded: an amatory rural poem [By J. Templeman. Illustrated.]
text: GILBERT. 78 v. 189. She retires disappointed. Canto iv, Book II. " Disgrace attends whene'er the thing is knoAvn, " And I shall rue my meeting you alone." At Avhich, she rising, hastily retires, Her hopes all fled, and dampt her amorous fires ; Back to her bed her silent Avay she hies, Falls fast asleep, and goodly dreams enjoys. Our Gilbert by himself is left once more, To dAvell Avith solemn silence as before : The strange adventure strikes Avith new surprise, Suspends his grief, and sooths his dreary sighs : Stretch'd on the hay his weary limbs he rests ; Soft slumber comes, no more dull care molests : Forgot his griefs, and Jenny's slights and scorn, He lies asleep, nor wakes till rising morn.

title: Gilbert; or True Love rewarded: an amatory rural poem [By J. Templeman. Illustrated.]
text: ARGUMENT. The return of day. Mistake cleared up. Character of the far- mer; his family described. Gilbert is disappointed ; proceeds on his journey. Stubbled field, fye. Burning the brakes. Advantages, fye. attendant on cleanliness. Time. One day more is employed in the third book.

title: Gilbert; or True Love rewarded: an amatory rural poem [By J. Templeman. Illustrated.]
text: CANTO v AURORA Avakes the rosy dawn of day Our mournful lover quits his bed of hay, Shakes of dull sloth, and thence his steps to bend, He Avaits impatiently to see his friend. The trap-door sounds, some person knock he hears ; The farmer's boy before his sight appears, With soothing voice, inquiring kind to know Hoav rested lie amidst his care and Avoe? M

title: Gilbert; or True Love rewarded: an amatory rural poem [By J. Templeman. Illustrated.]
text: 82 GILBERT. v. 9. > Book III. Gilbert is undeceived concerning Kitty. Canto v. Young Gilbert, smiling, speaks as things accord, Save of sweet Kate he mentions not a Avord ; He better thinks to let the matter rest, A secret matter in his pensive breast. Short time they stand — the morn's too good to Avaste They o'er the threshold doAvn the ladder haste ; To milk the coavs they've cross the fields to go ; Young Kitty loiters near the stile beloAv. But Avhat could equal Gilbert's new surprise, When first the damsel met his Avond 'ring eyes ! He stood convinc'd the same she could not be, Who'd in the hay-loft been so kindly free. He feels new joy — it glistens o'er his face, His friend through Kitty suffers no disgrace : . Yet who Avere she, or Avhence, that courting came, He'd gladly know, but dare not ask the same. With fodder for the cows, and pails scour'd clean, Kate and her SAveetheart walk across the green :

title: Gilbert; or True Love rewarded: an amatory rural poem [By J. Templeman. Illustrated.]
text: GILBERT. 83 v. 27 Book III. A narrow lane. The cow-house. Canto v. Poor Gilbert too ; — hoAv hard his soitoavs press ! These lovers' joys awaken his distress. Along the lane where clust'ring hazels grow, And black-thorn bushes screen the weeds below, Smooth paving-stones, laid level, keep the feet From plunging deep 'midst ruts of dirt and Avet. They singly each across the flat proceed To Avhere the coAV-barn rising tops the mead ; Down set their pails — the doors Avide open stand, Out come the coavs, a lazy lowing band. Where rails or ropes confine the spot each side, With streams of milk the vessel's well supplied. The loaded udder yields its valu'd store ; The kine, unloosen'd, seek the mead once more : Not far they stray between the verdant hills, Where grow the larches bordering the green fields ; The tender grass invites them to the plain, Till milking time, at eve, return again.

title: Gilbert; or True Love rewarded: an amatory rural poem [By J. Templeman. Illustrated.]
text: GILBERT. 84 Book III. Gilbert inquires of his night's adventure. Canto v. v. 45, Noav home the servants bend their steps with care ; High on their heads a store of milk they bear : A ready hand poor Avilling Gilbert lends, But trembling fear his slower steps attends ; He thinks enough he's cause to feel dismay 'd, A step aAvry may make him kick the glade, Dash doAvn his pail to floAv — (most piteous sight!) Banish his hopes, increase his wretched plight : Just through the lane the smoothest path he seeks ; Safe on the green arriv'd, he silence breaks, Wishing in secret guise to learn her name, Who late at night to seek a lover came : " I'd gladly have it well explain'd by you, " What kind of labour I am bound to do ; " Instruction give where I most stand in need, " And prove to me a friend sincere indeed. " The farmer's son's or daughter's temper tell : " A deal depends, I'd fain obey them well ;

title: Gilbert; or True Love rewarded: an amatory rural poem [By J. Templeman. Illustrated.]
text: GILBERT. 85 Book III. Some account of the farmer and his family. Canto v. v. 63. " Avoiding Avrong, I'd Avhat is right pursue ; " Nor servile prove, but pay attention due." His friend replies, " 'Tis meet you're told the same : " Our master has one daughter, Joyce by name ; " A comely Avench of sanguine mould is she, " And, Avhen she's pleas'd, bestOAvs her favours free: " Affront her once, nor more yourself deceive, " Tis not her nature ever to forgive ; " Her passion heated, lo ! the vixen flies " Into a rage, — dire vengeance gleams her eyes. " The sire, Avith anxious tenderness at heart, " Strives for the Avelfare of his house apart : " His duteous son becoming reverence pays, " His second wife submissively obeys. " Yet is he apt, at times, to swear them harm, " He beats the dame, drives Richard from the farm " His ano-er vented, peace he soon restores ; « Bids both return, and much Iris fault deplores.

title: Gilbert; or True Love rewarded: an amatory rural poem [By J. Templeman. Illustrated.]
text: 86 GILBERT. Book III. Gilbert's anxiety. Conto v. v. 81 This spoken, safe they measure back the ground, And in the yard the ample pails set doAvn : The milk Avarm-reeking 'mid the dairy stor'd, Yields up rich cream, fresh butter to afford. Then on the farmer next the boy attends, While pensive Gilbert to the hay-loft bends : There long he waits the grand result to know, And clouded care Avith sorrow marks his brow. Strange troubling whims his tortur'd soul assail, And o'er his reason folly Avould prevail, Vexing his mind with many a sad surmise, NeAV fears to form, and various doubts likewise : The vixen Joyce may vent her bitter rage, Persuade her sire no stranger to engage, Still to prevent her being expos'd outright, Should Kate e'er wish to bring the truth to fight, But soon his thoughts from wandering thus he stay'd ; The gentle youth at distance he survey'd,

title: Gilbert; or True Love rewarded: an amatory rural poem [By J. Templeman. Illustrated.]
text: GILBERT. 87 v. 99, Book III. The farmer is not willing to hire him. Canto v. By Avhose deportment easily he guess'd, That sanguine hope had fled his pensive breast. With falt'ring voice to speak the boy began : " Ah me ! ill luck betides our little plan ! " My master frowns — -he my endeavour foils, " Nor Avill admit you sharer in our toils. " Just now I've been the farmer's will to hear ; " His voice — O ! hoAV unusually severe ! " He says no vagrants shall his grounds infest, " Nor yet his peace or family's molest. " Refusing Avhich more clearly to explain, " Lo! I made bold to ask him o'er again : " Full angry, then, he in great passion SAVore, " He'd nail me up against the first barn-door : " A broken flail in both his hands he took, " And thrice my back with mighty force he struck " For fear of Avorse disaster swift I ran, " And met my Kitty in the narrow -lane.

title: Gilbert; or True Love rewarded: an amatory rural poem [By J. Templeman. Illustrated.]
text: GILBERT. 88 Book III. Disappointment owing to the daughter. Canto v. v. 117. " To whom the Avhole mishap I soon express'd ; " She, Avith a sigh, herself in blame confessed : " Thinking no harm, Avhen met by Joyce, the scold, " The secret things concerning you she told. " At morn the daughter Avaits upon her sire, " Betrays us both — inveterate 's her ire : " Her father sAVore, believing all she said, " Swore that no stroller o'er his doors should tread ! " Hoav things havechang'd ! now adverse thoughts succeed! " Be you refresh'd, your wav'ring journey speed ; " Here is your breakfast, good neAV milk and cake, " And here's some money, Avhich I hope you'll take : " My spying-glass I'll give to you likeAvise, " You'll think on me Avhene'er it meets your eyes. " May change of place in time your ease restore, " And Jenny's scorn create your grief no more. " Farewell, dear friend !" — Our Gilbert heav'd a sigh, Wip'd the rife tear, and thus essay 'd reply :

title: Gilbert; or True Love rewarded: an amatory rural poem [By J. Templeman. Illustrated.]
text: GILBERT. 89 135 Book III. Gilbert's answer to the farmer's boy. Canto v. v. " Alas ! alas ! your hapless cares forego, " Your master's Avrath increases not my Avoe : " Thinks he, perhaps, his prudence he'll o'errate, " And leaAe a Avandering vagrant to his fate. " His daughter's Avords full credit must obtain, " And Avhile he's vex'd, your pity comes in vain. " Strange as it is, I feel the less distress'd ; " I might have prov'd a stupid thing at best, " More giv'n to grieve, beneath some tree reclin'd, " Than, as I ought, the fanner's work to mind. " Alas ! fareAvell ! — your sp}ring-glass I'll take, " And keep the same a token for your sake; " But nothing more : your money I return ; " You're better worthy of the Avhole you earn. " FareAvell, for ever ! Heav'n your hopes befriend ! " May fortune still on all your steps attend ! " And, since to me so much regard you've shown, " My gratitude I cannot less but own." N"

title: Gilbert; or True Love rewarded: an amatory rural poem [By J. Templeman. Illustrated.]
text: GILBERT. 90 v. 153 He proceeds on his journey. Canto v. Book III. He ceas'd ; receiv'd the offer'd milk and bread ; Refresh'd by which, his way he quickly sped ; Far east the farm, Avith Avand'ring steps he Avound, The road between the cultivated ground : The stubbled field beyond a hedge appears, 'Cross the Avood-stile his lonely course he veers : DoAvn the Ioav slope, up the ridg'd hill he goes, The stubble crackling 'neath his heavy shoes. A mound he sees, — his glass he rests, — espies, O'er the Avide waste, thick clouds of smoke arise : With eagerness towards the spot he turns, Beholds a heap of braking as it burns. Tavo lab'ring boys Avith fuel feed the fire, Clear the light ashes Avhile the flames aspire ; Then water bring to knead the Avhiter clay, Form'd into balls against the market-day. Where cleanliness excites the matron's pride, To various uses are these balls applied ;

title: Gilbert; or True Love rewarded: an amatory rural poem [By J. Templeman. Illustrated.]
text: GILBERT. 91 Book III. Advantages, SsC. of cleanliness. Canto v. v. 171. The nice Avhite hearth contrasts the red-brick floor, The brighten'd hooks the mantel-piece explore. Fair Cleanliness, sweet-scented, lovely maid! Hoav blest the cottage where thou art display 'd ! Good Health delights to folloAV close thy train, And Poverty may frown at thee in vain : When thou 'midst Avant set'st out thy charms divine, Still are Ave led to fancy plenty thine ; Thy magic touch gives things more value still ; And where thou dAvefl'st, the more content we feel

title: Gilbert; or True Love rewarded: an amatory rural poem [By J. Templeman. Illustrated.]
text: CANTO VI IN O W o'er the Avaste lorn Gilbert Avalks more fast ; A narrow plank, laid on the ditch, he pass'd ; At Work sop town he Avheels his steps around, Where the pav'd street his hobnail'd shoes resound. He turns the corner to the pine-topt hills, Treads sIoav the track that leads across the fields. Behind, in sight, some ancient ruin lies ; Nigh where a church salutes the bending skies ;

title: Gilbert; or True Love rewarded: an amatory rural poem [By J. Templeman. Illustrated.]
text: GILBERT. 97 Book III. A stagnant pond. Wood scenery. Canto vi, v. 37. And, Avhere the waves reflect the azure skies, Along the marsh the skirting rushes rise. Close to a stagnant pond he bends his Avay ; The mantling cresses interpose his stay ; He picks the best, the Avorst away he throws, Then eats his cheerless dinner ere he goes. Clear from the rocks the gurgling stream issues ; He slakes his thirst : his journey he renews : On the foot-path, beyond the bar, he hastes, With quicker steps. Near the road-side he rests. Broad sturdy oaks, thick elms, Avith poplar high, Stand where the fir-tree apples scatter'd lie ; Or 'neath Avhere chesnuts ripen on each bough, The gorse, the Avilding, and the broom-flow'rs groAV ; Sharp stinging nettles, rankly run in seed, Exalt their stems o'er many a humbler Aveed. More eastward noAV the friendless Gilbert bends, Far o'er the Avaste a ling'ring look he lends ; o

text: GILBERT. 98 v. 45, Canto vi. Comes up with a gang nf gipsies. Book III. With stumbling pace he hies across the field, And seeks the path the jarring gate conceal'd. While slowly saunt'ring, careless Avhere he went, Tavo different roads to right and left present : A posted board the travelling stranger spies ; He faster Avalks, till Mansfield hail his eyes. A mile from toAvn there stood some shelt'ring trees, Beneath sat gipsies 'midst their tents at ease : The lovelorn youth approaching nigh in sight, They hear his groans, they view his AvayAvard plight, Amidst the gang tAVO ember fires appear ; O'er one, three poles the boiling pan uprear : A grateful steam in spiral clouds issued, Denotes the cooking of some mess that's good. These friendly gipsies beg he'd halt aAvhile, Step in their tent, and every care beguile. Invited kind, poor Gilbert gladly hears, Joins with the throng, and banishes his fears.

text: GILBERT. 99 63 Book III. Canto vi. v. The king makes an harangue. Along the grass a Avhiter cloth they place, Which various remnants of provision grace ; Delicious cates, fried fish, roast foAvl, abound ; Hot savoury soup in dishes smokes around : Loav on the plain the gipsies take a seat ; With one accord invite their guest to eat : The craving calls of nature better prove, How unsubstantial is mere food of love. Two taAvny girls attend the gipsy band, Fixing the goblets on a bench to stand ; Strong heady liquor from a vase one pours, The other serves ; loud mirth beguiles the hours : Full soon the master of the nightly feasts, Calls out to order, thus bespeaks his guests : " Ye friends ; SAVorn brothers ! other ties than blood ! " Hear my decrees ! let them be understood : " Tis by our sway your great resources spring ; " My various schemes luxuriant blessings bring ;

title: Gilbert; or True Love rewarded: an amatory rural poem [By J. Templeman. Illustrated.]
text: GILBERT. 100 81 Canto vi. v. Book III. Continued. " In fortunes told I sum the best events ; " Nor draAv conclusions to confound the sense : " But please the servants Avith my futile Avords, " Who, in return, give Avhat the place affords ; " Large rounds of bread, or offal, broken meat, " Or tasteful viands, fit for kings to eat : " And I, embolden'd,. seek a richer boon, " Claim my reward, a silver table-spoon. " Yet I have found some dubious Avhat to do : " Oft I'm compell'd the wiser girls to woo, " To count the cards, reneAV my empty lore, " And show how soon they may the spoon restore ; " Till rising conscience like a vision fly, " And I decamp rewarded truly high. " Noav, now's the time, the golden sun declines, " The moon, unclouded, more supremely shines ; " From yonder town the taper's amber blaze " Darts through the trees, illumes the glist'ning gaze

title: Gilbert; or True Love rewarded: an amatory rural poem [By J. Templeman. Illustrated.]
text: GILBERT. 101 Book III. Canto vi. v. 99. Continued. " Up, one and all, in secret guise to go, " Explore the rails, and Avatch the maids below. " Where creeking sign-boards, Avhistling to the gale, " Express Avhat goods poor tradesmen have on sale, " Beg hard, or steal : infest the open square, " Tempt the soft girls, and loll in plenty there ! " Hoav rich in spoil, at daAvn of day all met, " You'll add the value of Avhate'er you get ! " My ample share, by right of rule, I'll claim ; " Tis I, the king, Avho bears you on to fame. " Meantime observe, the young man I'll attend ; " A stranger quite ; but I'll his case befriend : " Our sundry laAvs I guess will set him right, " AAvake his courage, and his poAvers excite. " By grand achievements in our state he'll rise, " Till, like Careav, his fame resounds the skies : " Another king ye shall by me acquire, " Ere from the arduous office I retire.

title: Gilbert; or True Love rewarded: an amatory rural poem [By J. Templeman. Illustrated.]
text: GILBERT. 102 The king of the gipsies relates his adventures. Canto vi. v. 117. Book III. " Haste, comrades ! all, to yonder tOAvn to go ! " Look through the rails, entice the girls beloAv ; " Tell each her fortune, sum the best events, " And draAv conclusions fitting to the sense." He spoke. The gang, the better to obey, Start up in haste, the eldest lead the Avay ; A Avicked crew, let loose in every street, To beg, or steal, Avhere'er they set their feet. Where panes of glass expose the kitchen light, They crouch to beg, or fortunes they'll recite : The servant-girls neAv grievances unfold, Still pleas'd to hear their goodly fortunes told. When noAV our youth is by the king address'd : " Pray, stranger, say, Avhy throbs your lab'ring breast ? " Tis time to try your confidence to gain, " By telling how I came o'er these to reign. " Three years, or more, I left my native home, " A whimsied journey o'er the plains to roam ;

title: Gilbert; or True Love rewarded: an amatory rural poem [By J. Templeman. Illustrated.]
text: GILBERT. 103 Book III. The subject continued. Canto vi. v. 135. " I sloAvly saunter'd over hills and dales, " Through shady Avoods, o'er common-Avastes, and vales ; " Amidst a quarry doAvn I sat to rest, " Feeling Avith hunger, thirst, and grief oppress'd. " Not far, a man in tatters I beheld, " Coming towards me 'cross the neighbouring field : " He said, ' My son, some perquisite bestow ! ' Take pity on the Avretch by Avant brought Ioav ! ' Though less the gift, with thanks I still accept — ' Me, but relieve !' — " he spoke, and loud he Avept. " I ansAver'd thus : Hear now ! my Avords are true, " I've nothing left to give to such as you ; " Without a doit I travel far and Avide, " My trifling Avants are readily supplied. " Had I the means, your cares I'd soon o'erturn ; " No more, poor soul, I'd suffer you to mourn ; " But, as it is, your craving suit suspend, " Go Avhence you came, and seek a better friend."

title: Gilbert; or True Love rewarded: an amatory rural poem [By J. Templeman. Illustrated.]
text: GILBERT. 105 Book III. Continued. Canto vi. v. 171. ' His Avords observe, his voice as Avell regard, ' And sure success expect for your reAvard.' " The Avond'ring creAV to honour me agreed ; " I gave them counsel hoAV they should proceed ; " Met at a wake, or neighb'ring village fair, " To beg relief, or levy plunder there. " With diffrent Avashes, Avalnut-shells, and paint, " Sometimes the gang broAvn gipsies represent ; " They'll mark their limbs Avith angry ulcers sore ; " And, like maim'd sailors, beg from door to door. " Meamvhile our chief grew daily worse and Avorse ; " Within his tent he utter'd many a curse : " A hoary miscreant ! miserable thing ! " Not evil deeds Avill kindly comfort bring. " Late one dull morn the men abroad had sped, " He feebly calling, I ran near his bed :" * Harry,' said he, ' I feel I soon shall die ; ' But never yet were Avretch so loath as I ! — p

text: GILBERT. 106 Canto yi. v. .189. Book III. Continued. * Heard ye that voice ? — the summons I obey : ' My glass is out ! — iioav hark to Avhat I say ! ' While cold I lie, the tearful group you'll call, ' Divide -my rags, and give a share to all : ' This old surtout, where patch on patch appear, ' Keep to yourself — my riches sav'd, lie here : * Three thousand pounds, in notes and gold, you'll find ' Securely treasur'd in the seams behind. * Alas ! my son! — ah me! — -Avhat pangs of death ! ' O God ! forgive !' — " he groan'd — resigns his breath. " Compassion for the dead assails my soul ; " Fast doAvn my cheeks my tears in torrents roll. " At night the gang, Avith heavy sobs, I call, " Divide the rags, and give a share to all. " The old surtout, Avhere patch on patch appear, " I keep myself, for, sure, the treasure's here ! " Within the seams I privately have told " Three thousand pounds, bank notes, and sterling gold

text: 108 GILBERT. Canto vi. v. 225, Book III. He is treated with contempt. " Till then, I shall ray sincere passion mourn, " Plac'd on fair Jane, avIio makes me no return : " Yet may she real happiness explore, " And heights of bliss, when Gilbert is no more." To Avhom the other this reply essay 'd : " Poor silly oaf! forget the scornful maid! " Or fresh in mind her cruel scorn retain, " And let your reason meet her Avith disdain ! " Yet, hold ! — the thing Avhich I to you propose " Too hard appears — pray nourish still your Avoes, " Benumb your sense, your manly powers suspend, " Create your goddess, and devoutly bend ! " I read your thoughts — I see Avhat hurts your mind ; " There's no degree of spirit left behind : " Unnerv'd, grown useless by your foolish love ; " Unfit to liATe, unfit to die, you prove. " Go then, soft lad ! or better Avould you choose " To slumber here till morning dawn renews ?

title: Gilbert; or True Love rewarded: an amatory rural poem [By J. Templeman. Illustrated.]
text: GILBERT. 109 Book III. Gilbert sleeps under a haystack. Canto vi. v. 243. " Some disappointment in my schemes I feel ; " Yet Avhat I've said you'll never dare reveal." To Avhich the sufferer could no more reply, His bosom heaving many a far-fetch'd sigh : Derision mark'd the king's contorted face, When Gilbert hasted from the guilty place. He on the road his course benighted steer'd, And through a hedge beheld a stack late rear'd ; Beneath its welcome shelter doAvn he lay, Spent Avith fatigue, and slept till break of day.

text: CANTO VII AGAIN 'tis morn — the sparroAvs, on the spray, Proclaim their joy, and hail return of day : Young Gilbert starts, his journey to renew, And bids his airy lodging long adieu ! Soon o'er the meadoAv he attempts to pass, Where crystal dew-drops shine the Avav'ring grass ; Along the narroAV-skirted path he hies ; — A strolling gipsy near a bank he spies : Q
