text: GILBERT. 114 v. 9, Book IV. Discovery of the gipsy. Canto vii, Pensive his looks ; a loaded box he bears, Which resting doAvn, his tatter'd coat he tears : A rev'rend elm the verdant bank o'ershades ; Beneath its boughs he throAvs the ragged shreds : In the clear stream bestOAving well his pains, Washes aAvay the Avaln ut-shell's broAvn stains, Till health unfold a sweet complexion fair, And good success reAvard his steady care. Unseen stands Gilbert, peeping 'side the trees ; His Avonder rises at the sight he sees : Nor poAv'r he feels, nor Avill from thence to go ; He, loitering, Avaits the end of this to knoAv. The gentle stranger brings his little box, And o'er the stones the same he soon unlocks ; Takes out clean linen, suit of genteel clothes, A modish hat, neAv shoes, fine silken hose. Noav full he's dress'd, he quits the lonely spot ; Still seems to Avaver Avhere to shape his lot :

title: Gilbert; or True Love rewarded: an amatory rural poem [By J. Templeman. Illustrated.]
text: GILBERT. 115 27 Book TV. The young man relates his history. Canto vii. y. Along the grass his empty box he throAVS ; And, disencumber'd, o'er the meadoAv goes. SAvift Gilbert runs — the youth he overtakes, Bids him good morn ; he courteous answer makes ; His courteous answer question fresh supplies : Well pleas'd they walk, discoursing, side by side : But not on trifling subjects either dwell ; His cause for grief our lover comes to tell. Young Herbert sighs ; to pity him he deigns, And the lorn wanderer's confidence he gains. Here now in turn his story he relates ; Gilbert the more impatiently aAvaits : Strange curiosity, unfelt before, Excites the sAvain to hear th' eventful lore. " Near thirty miles, whence yonder windmills stand, " My sire's estate extends far o'er the land, " A Avealthy liquor-merchant still is he, " And traffics largely o'er the distant sea.

title: Gilbert; or True Love rewarded: an amatory rural poem [By J. Templeman. Illustrated.]
text: 116 GILBERT. v. 45. Canto vii. Book IV. Herbert and Mary-Ann. " Far round about resounds his upright fame, " While far and near the poor revere his name : " His hand's e'er open to relieve distress ; " The blind of sight, the crippled lame, to bless. " No anxious pains, no dear expense he spar'd, " To make Ave Avorthier of his best regard : " He vainly lavish'd all his kindest cares, " And hop'd by me to croAvn his latter years. " With nurse's help I'd scarcely learnt to run, " Ere I gave signs of being a headstrong son : " GroAvn dp a dunce, good counsel to despise, " And never heed my parents' groans and sighs. " Alas ! the heights of Avickedness I kneAv, " And day by day more lost to shame I greAV : " I scorn'd to folloAV Reason's golden rules, " But stood a dupe to sundry knaves and fools. " TAvas then, by chance, I Mary -Ann beheld, " Whose mental charms her outward form excell'd :

title: Gilbert; or True Love rewarded: an amatory rural poem [By J. Templeman. Illustrated.]
text: GILBERT. 117 v. 63 Book IV. The subject continued. Canto vii. " Idalia's* son, his mighty poAver to prove, " Let fly a shaft — I deeply fell in love ! " With passion Avarm'd, a suitor I became, " Reform'd my faults, cherish'd the gen'rous flame, " Bade all my old companions adieu, " And like a lamb, in gentleness, soon grew. " My father saAV this change Avith wonder great; " He blest the PoAver Avho had revers'd my fate ! " Approving thus the merit of my choice, " And by his sanction did my heart rejoice. " No cruel bar to foil my bliss I found ; " My happy lot rose enAry all around ; " My cup Avith joy seem'd ready to run o'er, " Intoxicating joy! unknoAvm before. " Our marriage-day was fix'd, alas ! in vain ; " Misfortune froAvning, left me to complain : " A dire small-pox mischievously annoy'd " Poor Mary-Ann ; — her charms were all destroy'd * Cupid.

title: Gilbert; or True Love rewarded: an amatory rural poem [By J. Templeman. Illustrated.]
text: GILBERT. 118 v. 81 Continued. Canto vii, Book IV. " Nor more of heaven in her eye appear'd ; " Nor more her finish'd excellence endear'd : " I thought her robb'd of every mental grace, " When I beheld destroy'd her lovely face. " See ! noAv, a slave of beauty all-divine, " Bend Avith devotion at her sacred shrine, " Weakly adoring outward charms, Avhich fade ; " Nor reck'd that Virtue best adorns each maid. " I cool became — the match was set aside ; " Lorn Mary- Ann took things to heart — she died ! " Her double loss — her beauty and my love, " Caus'd pining grief a Aveight of ills to prove. " Too late compassion touch'd my stubborn soul ; " Long for her sake my fruitless tears did roll. " Oh! had she liv'd but to haAre been my bride, " I'd sacrific'd in pity all my pride. " Now, now, I mourn my cruelty unkind ; " Increasing anguish settles on my mind !

title: Gilbert; or True Love rewarded: an amatory rural poem [By J. Templeman. Illustrated.]
text: GILBERT. 119 99, Gilbert and his friend arrive at Mansfield. Canto vii. v. Book IV. " Had I in time to comfort her but deign'd, " I'd sav'd her life, and happiness obtain'd. " Scarce spread the neAvs ere I from home fast fled, " Far o'er the Avilds a trackless course I sped ; " Three tedious months Avith gipsies I have liv'd, " And day and night for Mary-Ann I've griev'd. " Alas ! alas ! — sure every care is mine, " That Avrings the soul, and leaA-es us to repine ! " For thee, young man, methinks 'tis not amiss " To turn thy thoughts on future scenes of bliss : " Jane yet Avill loA'e, joy yet thy steps aAvait ; " And peace, attendant, bless thy humble state !" Concluding thus, he wipes the starting tear : Gilbert would speak; but Mansfield town is near Where the green dragon shapes a striking sign, Appears the inn for porter, ale, and Avine ! Pensive the friends conclude their fast to break, Nor further for a baiting place they'll seek :

title: Gilbert; or True Love rewarded: an amatory rural poem [By J. Templeman. Illustrated.]
text: GILBERT. 121 > Book IV. The friends enter into conversation. Canto vii. v. 135. " I'm tir'd Avith rambling, homeAvards I'll return, " Nor more my father for my sake shall mourn. " But, once to judge hoAv things are like to go, " First what he means concerning me I'll knoAV ; " If to forgive my faults he's yet inclin'd, " I'll better be, nor more afflict his mind. " Three miles this side of Loughbro' is seen " A modern building on the rising green ; " Safe Avall'd Avith brick, Avhite rails are fix'd around " The fragrant Avoodbines grace the gravell'd ground " Oblige me, Gilbert, by one favour kind ; " Carry my letter, and the merchant find : " DAvell on his action when he turns to read ; " Observe it well — there rests my fate indeed ! " With kind concern to Avhat he Avills, attend ; " Make known my grief — 'tis Avhat I now unbend ; " Do, Gilbert, say, how much your friend laments " His num'rous faults, and heartily repents." K

title: Gilbert; or True Love rewarded: an amatory rural poem [By J. Templeman. Illustrated.]
text: GILBERT. 122 Gilbert undertakes to carry a letter. Canto vii. v. 153 Book IV. The other heard, then with a smile replied : " All this I'll do, and thank you, sir, beside ; " Gratefully bound, by this convincing proof " Of your regard for a poor hapless youth ! " With Avoe oppress'd — o'erbearing, stubborn, Avoe ; " Tis all as one Avhichever Avay I go ; " From place lo place unsettled still I move ; " And, while I travel, mourn my slighted love. " Your letter safely to your sire I'll speed, " DAvell on his action Avhen he turns to read, " With due concern to Avhat he wills attend, " Make knoAvn your soitoavs, and your griefs unbend : " Nor doubt but he to ansAver kind will deign ; " He'll pardon all, receive his son again. " Thus I, for once, a little joy shall have, " Ere my misfortunes bring me to my grave." To Avhom young Herbert ansAver'd in these words : " Your kind assurance better thoughts affords :

title: Gilbert; or True Love rewarded: an amatory rural poem [By J. Templeman. Illustrated.]
text: GILBERT. 123 Canto vii. v. 171. Book IV. He is promised a farm, SfC. " O ! if my father peace to me restore, " Believe your friend — I'll let you mourn no more ! " A thriving farm on that blest day I'll buy, " Which you shall rent on terms not over high ; " Your lovely Jane your constant spouse shall be, " And trouble cease to bear its Aveight on thee. " Cheer up, dear Gilbert ! mark the words I say, " Coming from friendship, Avhich you must obey ; " A mite from my inheritance I'll give, " And thou Avith Jenny happily long live." " Thanks, gen'rous Herbert !" Gilbert quickly said, While every look his gratitude betray 'd ; " Thanks, gen'rous Herbert ! — I the gift refuse, " Which, to accept, your friendship 'twould abuse. " Had I, indeed, of Avealth a kingly store, " I still should think I'd reason to deplore ! " Had I been born estates to call my own, " Jenny had lov'd me for their sake alone !

title: Gilbert; or True Love rewarded: an amatory rural poem [By J. Templeman. Illustrated.]
text: GILBERT. 124 Book IV. They arrive at Nottingham. Canto vii. v. 189, " Here drives the thorn ! — it makes me more distress'd " It Avounds my heart — it robs me of all rest : " Were I but Avealthy, Jenny kind Avould prove ; " But humble Gilbert she disdains to love." Discoursing thus, twelve tedious miles they pass'd, And came beloAv the hollo w'd rocks at last ; Far in the distance stands a toav of mills, Along the border of the forest hills ; Where tufts of gorse, with yellow blossoms crown'd, Wide variegate the upland rising ground : Full many a sluggish jack-ass steals abroad, To crop the thistle, growing near the road. SIoav up the path, the friends their way pursue ;., The cavern'd houses strike their prying view, Till bearing doAvn to Nottingham they come, And hear the crash of many a lumb'ring loom. The higher folk in stately halls reside ; The streets are pav'd, the market well supplied :

title: Gilbert; or True Love rewarded: an amatory rural poem [By J. Templeman. Illustrated.]
text: GILBERT. 125 Book FV. Herbert writes his letter. Canto vii. v. 207. Pale manufacture bears the town a name, Its patent lace and stockings speak its fame. Industry points the certain means of Gain, While Commerce sends her labours o'er the main, Contrasting still, her riches' fair increase, With rags and filth, the fruits of idleness. Noav Avalk they fast, nor make the least delay, Aside the church Avith speed pursue their way ; The Bridge-Foot House attracts attention best, Within they go, their weary limbs to rest. On boil'd plumb-pudding, nice roast beef, they dine : The landlord call'd, he brings his choicest wine : How nice the fare ! — the lover scarce can find A will to eat — affliction rends his mind. Here Herbert Avrites, his sorrows he reveals; He folds the note, which carefully he seals : The bill discharg'd, their journey they renew, Till noble Trent extends before their view :

title: Gilbert; or True Love rewarded: an amatory rural poem [By J. Templeman. Illustrated.]
text: 126 GILBERT. Gilbert receives further instructions. Canto vii. v. 225. Book IV. Nor long the scenes their ling 'ring steps assail, The castle rock, the loAvland level vale, The far-fam'd grove of Clifton, which inspir'd Our White* to sing, Avith heavenly numbers fir'd. Across the bridge their steps they omvard bend ; And though quite Aveary, strive their pace to mend ; Or by the slope, or nigh the heavy rise, Full many a mile-stone strikes their eager eyes. Arriv'd at Bunny, Herbert thus began: " Here Avill I wait the issue of my plan : " See Avhere yon signpost meets the passing sight, " The village inn I'll make my home to-night. " Four miles from hence, the left side of the road, " You'll not mistake the merchant's fair abode : " Hear the description Avhich I gave before, " Its front is stone ; its height, a second floor ; " White rails o'ertop the walls of brick around, " And tufted trees adorn the gravell'd ground. * Henry Kirke White, of Nottingham.

title: Gilbert; or True Love rewarded: an amatory rural poem [By J. Templeman. Illustrated.]
text: GILBERT. 127 v. 243 Book IV. He proceeds on his business. Canto vii. " Soon to my father you'll my letter give — " VieAV well his look — oh ! may he it receive : " If things go Avell, inform him Avhere I Avait, " And in the morn com-ince me of my fate." He ceas'd : the letter in his hand he took, Gave it to Gilbert, who, replying, spoke : " Amidst of ills some better things remain ; " Friendship has poA\rer to banish far my pain. " Here rest at ease the while direct I go, " With heart of zeal to dissipate your woe : " I'll to your father, all your cares unfold, " Speak your repentance, speak your grief of soul " Then quick returning, Avhether Avrong or right, " I'll bring you word, your good Avill to requite." So saying, they shake hands, and silent part : Fresh hopes inspire young Herbert's grateful heart His inn he seeks, the better cheer he tries, While lovelorn Gilbert on his journey hies.

title: Gilbert; or True Love rewarded: an amatory rural poem [By J. Templeman. Illustrated.]
text: GILBERT. 128 261 Book IV. He loses himself in the fields. Canto vii. v. Hoav fast he walks ! he's on big errand sent ; Eager he feels to know the great event : No more his close attention he bestow'd On varying sights along the dusty road. Three several mile-stones Gilbert quickly pass'd : Meeting a stile to croAvn his zeal at last, This Avay to go he thinks less time Avill need ; Across he steps, his errand more to speed ; Runs up the hill, then down the valley flies, Till night's dark shadows overspread the skies. Alarm'd, he hurries o'er the dismal green ; No passage through the banded hedge is seen : The treacherous path at length, by slow degrees, Leads Avide astray ; — another road he sees : A different cut some high rails terminate ; He stands confus'd ; he mourns his folly late — Poor hapless youth ! 'twere Avrong the track to leave, A fault Avhich gave him greater cause to grieve.

title: Gilbert; or True Love rewarded: an amatory rural poem [By J. Templeman. Illustrated.]
text: GILBERT. 129 Canto vii. v. 279. Book IV. The robbers, 4"C The moon up risen, he perceives he's lost : He spies two paths, one o'er the other cross'd : Which shall he choose ? no fav'ring sprite reveals He's chosen Avrong — it leads him in the fields ! Here stands the youth unknowing Avhat to do ; No wandering rustic comes Avithin his view, Of Avhom to ask, haply to find once more The certain road he quit in evil hour. Low droops his head : his spirits 'gin to fail ! When, lo ! a cry for help, resounds the vale ; A dreadful cry — louder the noise repeats ; Poor Gilbert's breast with consternation beats. Again a shriek ! — he runs with sudden speed Towards the spot from whence the cries proceed Close to the wall four of the ruffian crew, Dragging some man to murder, come in view : A piteous scene ! it gives him mortal pain ! His feeble strength to master four, how vain ! s

title: Gilbert; or True Love rewarded: an amatory rural poem [By J. Templeman. Illustrated.]
text: GILBERT. 130 Book IV. He saves a person, whom they were about to murder. Canto vii. v. 297. Prudence his better courage will befriend ; He schemes a plan, .whate'er may be the end : Without delay takes off his upper coat ; He holds it out, then hastens to the spot : Shouts, " Here they are ! up, friends, we have them all !" The frighten'd coAvards scamper o'er the wall : Guilt strikes their conscience, feeling sore afraid, With speed they haste across the heavy glade, In fancy picturing, by the moon's pale fight, A croAvd well arm'd to intercept their flight. Meanwhile our Gilbert runs to the poor swain, Prone-lying, trembling on the skirted plain. He lifts him up, and kindly looking, said, " Take courage ! see, the Avicked rogues have fled ! " Accept the ready offer of my hand : " I'll guide you safe where'er you give command : " Happy it chanc'd, that timely here I came, " To disappoint the villains in their aim."

title: Gilbert; or True Love rewarded: an amatory rural poem [By J. Templeman. Illustrated.]
text: GILBERT. 131 Book IV. Assists the stranger in returning home. Canto vii. v. 315. To whom the stranger : " Sir, my fife you've sav'd, " And gratitude has deeply this engrav'd ; " But still I feel your offer'd help I need, " To bear my frame, enfeebled, o'er the mead. " Tis scarce one furlong from yon chalky mound, ** Where my house stands upon a rising ground ; " Whence, for the future, I'll avoid with care, " Coming alone to take the evening air." These few words spoken, their return they haste Across the meadow, field, and Avintery waste ; Nor more molested, they their course pursue, Till close at hand the king's highway they view.

text: CANTO VIII. YOUNG Gilbert blest his well reAvarded toil, And thank'd the poAver that led him o'er the stile ; He'd been the means, through Providence divine, To save from ruffian fury some poor hind. text: 9 5 Sicilian Muse, begin the strain of woe, And make the song in mournful measure flow. O ! may swift vengeance seize the traitor's soul More dreadful vengeance than the deadly bowl : My hand is feeble to avenge thy wrong ; Accept, 'tis all I have, the pitying song. Could I, like Orpheus or Alcides, go, Or wise Ulysses, to the shades below, To hear thy song, even thither I'd attend Thy fleeting steps, thou dear, departed friend. O ! pour to Proserpine thy magic strain ! For once she sported on Sicilia's plain ; The Doric song she lov'd, and sung by thee, Sweet as the sounds that freed Euridice, A like effect thy music shall obtain, And give thee back to life and love again. As Spring to the fields, or as dew to the flow'r, To the Earth parch'd with heat as the soft dropping show'r, As health to the wretch who lies languid and wan, Or as rest to the weary — is Freedom to man. Where Freedom the light of her countenance gives, There only he revels, there only he lives. Seize then the glad moment, and hail the decree That bids millions rejoice, and a Nation be free. 3. France ! we share in the rapture thy bosom that fills, Whilst the spirit of Liberty bounds o'er thine hills ; Redundant henceforth may thy purple juice flow, Prouder wave thy green woods, and thine olive tree- grow. For thy brows may the hand of Philosophy twine, Blest emblems, the Myrtle, the Olive and Vine ; And Heav'n, thro' all ages, confirm the decree, That tears off thy chains, and bids millions be free !

text: 32 ODE TO THE POPPY. Not for the promise of the labour'd field, Not for the good the yellow harvests yield, I bend at Ceres' shrine ; For dull to humid eyes appear The golden glories of the year ; Alas ! a melancholy worship's mine ! I hail the goddess for her scarlet flow'r. Despairing I rove by this still running stream ; While Corin's sad fate is for ever my theme, For 'twas Here we oft wander'd the long summer days, And each vale, then harmonious, re-echoed his lays : The woods with delight bow'd their tops to his song, While the streamlet responsive ran murm'ring along, The songsters were mute when he tun'd his soft reed, And fays danced around on the green-chequer'd mead. As it has long been the language of the populace, local usage has thrown such irregularity upon its verbs, that gram marians conceived them to be governed by no rule, till Gene ral Vallancey demonstrated the error of that opinion, in Ireland, and Mr. Shaw, in Scotland. The poets have been long in the habit of substituting E for /, or / for E, and of using A O or U indifferently, in composition, and sometimes in simple primitives. This habit, which rather savours of the Eastern school, is evi dently injurious. In opposition to the general usage of ancient languages, the Irish fall into a compendious method, of making but one syllable, and frequently but one sound, out of as many vowels as come together in a single word. Several of the consonants, in composition, are either silenced by a point, or an H, or so changed and softened in the mode of oral delivery, that one's ear is no longer able to judge of the component parts, in a multitude of compound words. In this abuse, the neighbouring Scotch imitate the Irish, because they have been generally in the habit of using Irish books, and masters. It is evident, that such customs did not prevail anciently,

WE have hitherto traced only the general principle, upon which the symbols of Druidism were constructed, and the application of that principle, to the formation of an alphabet. We have seen, however, nothing, as yet, of the number, the powers, or the characters, of their letters; nor discriminated the individual kind of sprig, or symbol, by which either of the elementary sounds was represented. These particulars are as open to investigation, a3 those, which have been just explained ; but our intelligence respecting them, must be obtained from different sources. In the allegorical poem, quoted above, Taliesin has, in deed, given us curious hints, upon this topic. At pre sent, I shall defer enlarging upon them, as they are not clear enough to elucidate the whole plan. Druidical teachers, of the sixth century, guarded their secret with too much caution, to divulge their whole mys teries in the ears of the uninitiated. But this great arcanum, as far as relates to that subject, has been laid open by their successors, and by their neighbours. As the mysterious doc trines of Druidism, were held, by degrees, in less idola trous veneration, the disclosure of their secrets began, by the same degrees, to be regarded as less profane : and there was an order of men still, who could have imparted much information respecting them.

text: JACOBINISM. 2 Or paced with truant foot the sweet domain,* Where polish'd Braybroke holds his gentle reign. Lone, as I muse, in this auspicious hour, Thou, goddess, Memory, wake thy magick power ! O lead my willing steps to yonder grove, Where my young heart first felt the throb of love, Felt the strange rapture of an amorous sigh, And drank the witching glance of Celia's eye I O hours of painful bliss, of hope, of dread, Of maddening transport — whither are ye fled ? As o'er her hand's harmonious skill I hung, And heard the liquid musick of her tongue ; To whom my earliest secret vows were given, Whose look was rapture, and whose smile was heaven ! Dear, conscious forest ! thy embowering maze Along, once more, thy fond enthusiast strays Oft have I wept, thy noon-tide shades among, My hopeless passion, my unheeded song ; Oft in thy bosom pour'd the frantick strain, And taught thy midnight echoes to complain. text: JACOBINISM. 5 When June's hot suns with envious rage look down On the long lingering winter of the town ; When Bond-street's promenade invites no more, And the vain contest of the rout is o'er ; Where shall the peer display his close-cropp'd hairs, And high-born misses sport their mannish airs ? From pastoral scenes, from Flora's fragrant reign, The world of fashion rushes to the main ; Forsakes the breathing mead, the silent shade, For squabbling raffles, and the throng'd parade; And pleased prefers to Thames' translucent flood, The sweets of sea- weed, and sublime of mud.f The enervate mind by dissipation charm'd, By pleasure heated, and by sloth disarm'd, Hails the new dawn on Gaul's polluted shore, And drinks with fatal thirst its poisonous lore. * Of such preposterous and pliant materials is the fashionable world com posed, that it can stoop occasionally to imitate the customs and manners even of those whom it affects to despise. Till very lately, our watering-places were visited, almost exclusively, by genuine unsophisticated cits ; who, incapable of relishing the elegant pleasures of retirement, cannot exist out of a crowd -, and therefore wherever they go, carry London along with them; that is, their divi sion of it, its vulgar manners and dissipations. But, at present, our nobility and gentry, instead of enjoying the little time they can afford to deduct from the routs, the exhibitions, and promenades of the metropolis, at their own terrestrial paradises, repair in shoals to Brighton, Margate, &c. and waste the finest season of the year, which was once devoted to the admiration and improve ment of rural scenery, the accommodation of their tenants, and the comfort of their dependants, in the frivolous and childish amusements of these modern Bethesdas.

title: Jacobinism: a poem [By J. C. Hubbard; with an appendix.]
text: JACOBINISM. 9 The day's bright planet sickens to behold, And shrouds, in deepest gloom, his beams of gold ; Earth shrinks his eye's detested glare beneath, And life recoiling withers in his breath ! Roused by his roar, and new to human kind, Demoniack phrensy fastens on the mind ; — Unheeded, starting from his cave profound, With cautious step, Sedition prowls around ; In every ear he pours the insidious tale, In every land the glozing lies prevail ; In every breeze that wakes the orient day, The subtle hell-hound snuffs his destined prey. High o'er the Cross see atheist banners wave ! See Desperation triumph o'er the grave ! See man renounce his title to the skies, And join the brute, that labours, feeds, and dies ! How long, O France, on thy devoted shore, The dogs of havock howl'd for human gore ! As o'er thy throne their murderous glance they threw, All comfort died, and the last hope withdrew All worldly comfort— that, which Virtue gives, Unhurt, on wheels, and free in prisons, lives ; The tyrant's malice, and his axe defies, Spurns the low earth, and mounting claims the skies. To fiends, exulting o'er the atrocious deed, More horrid deeds, and blacker fiends succeed : The parent's deep and agonizing sigh, The virgin's shrieks, and infant's trembling cry, C

Her secret hand more fatal weapons wields Than those of slaughter, in embattled fields ; With cautious skill her sophist crew she arms, And pours o'er every land their locust-swarms ; Discord, dire fiend, their murderous rout pursues, And, as they prompt, her harpy screams renews ; Fell Havock hears, and, ravenous for blood, Exulting bathes him in the reeking flood ; Revenge unshackled, Rapine raging near, And Desolation, close the dreadful rear. Again Britannia rushes to the field, Again she rears her adamantine shield ; — Above the human tempest's madd'ning clime, Still rising in her might, she soars sublime ; Bids the dire vengeance of her thunders roll, And shakes the prostrate world from pole to pole. 'Tis hers, alike to vanquish, or relieve, Provoked, to punish, or implored, forgive : Whose guardian arm the drooping exile rears, Whose bounty feeds him, as her pity cheers ; Gives him to range her hills, and catch the gales That wake the verdure of her happy vales. No more her ports display their boasted stores, While Commerce dozes on her desert shores :— Once the proud rival-mistress of the waves, • The scourge of tyrants, and the dread of slaves,

text: JACOBINISM. What envious demon, ranging to destroy, Has marr'd your sports, and closed your songs of joy ? What horrid yells the affrighted ear assail ! What screams of terror load the passing gale ! See ruffian hordes with tiger-rage advance, The shame of manhood, and the boast of France ! See trampled, crush'd, and torn, in lustful strife, The loathing virgin, and indignant wife ! While wanton carnage sweeps each crowded wood, And all the mountain torrents swell with blood ! Lo ! where yon cliff projects its length of shade O'er fields of death, some wounded chief is laid ! Around the desolated scene he throws A look, that speaks insufferable woes ; Then starting from his trance of dumb despair, Thus vents his anguish to the fleeting air : — ** Dear native hills, amidst whose woodland maze I pass'd the tranquil morning of my days, On whose green tops malignant planets scowl, Where hell-hounds ravage, and the furies howl ; Though changed, deform'd, still, still ye meet my view, Ye still are left to hear my last adieu ! My friends, my children ! gored with many a wound, Whose mangled bodies strew the ensanguined ground, To parch and stiffen in the blaze of day, Consign'd to vultures and to wolves a prey, Your toils are past ; no more ye wake to feel Lust's savage gripe, or Rapine's reeking steel ! 16

But the joint by Avhich the hand is connected with the arm, is the wrist. And the ex ternal part of the hand is nervous, and Avithout a name. With respect to the legs, hoAvever, they are inflected toAvards the anterior part, tOAvards Avhich part also they are moved ; and the more motive part of the foot and its flexure, are also anterior. But the heel has a posterior position. And each of the ankles has the same position in the tibia, as the ears have in the head. The arms hang from the right and left side of the body, and have their flexure inward ; and are so inflected, especially in man, that the incur vation of the legs and the arms have a position opposite to each other. With respect to the senses, however, and the sensoria, viz. the eyes, the nostrils, and the tongue, man has them situated in the same, i. e. in the anterior part ; but he has the hearing, and its sensorium, the ear, in a lateral position indeed, but in the same circumference Avith the eyes. Man likewise has his eyes proportionally less distant than other ani mals. But of the senses, the most accurate in him is the touch, the next to this in accuracy is the taste, but in the other senses he is ex celled by many animals. CHAPTER XVI. The brain there- fore occupies the first situation in the head, and is posited in the an- terior part of it ; and this similarly takes place in other animals that have this part. But all sanguineous animals have it, and besides these the mollia. Man, hoAvever, in proportion to the magnitude of his body, has the largest and the moistest brain. Two membranes like- Avise contain it ; one about the bone, Avhich is the stronger of the two ; but the other about, the brain itself, Avhich is less strong. The brain how- ever in all animals is twofold, and to the posteriorpart of it, that which is called the cerebellum, is joined, Avhich has a different form * from the brain, both according to the touch and the sight. But the posterior part of the head in all animals is [partially at least] empty and holloAv, according as the head is larger or smaller. For in some animals that have a larger head, the part of the face Avhich is subjected to the head is small ; as is the case Avith those animals that have a round face. Other animals, on the contrary, have a small head but long cheeks, such as all the genus of labouring cattle, or animals that have a tuft of hair on the forehead. The brain however in all animals is exangui- ous, has no veins, and is naturally cold to the touch ; and in the middle of it, in most animals, there is a small cavity ; but the membrane Avhich surrounds it is veiny, and of the nature of skin. Above the brain also, there is a bone which is the thinnest and weakest of all the bones of the head, and is called the sinciput. But their avenues, or ducts, tend from the eyes to the brain ; the largest indeed, and the mid- dle, tend to the cerebellum ; but the smallest tends to the brain itself. And the smallest of these ducts, is that which especially verges to the nose. The greatest ducts, therefore, are parallel to each other, and never coincide; but the middle ducts coalesce. Within the neck are what is called the oesophagus, which has its de- nomination from its narrowness and length, and the aspera arteria. The aspera arteria, however, is prior in position to the oesophagus in all animals that possess it ; and all animals have it that have lungs. But this artery is indeed naturally cartilaginous, has but little blood, and is surrounded by many thin veins. It is also placed in the supe- rior part towards the mouth, opposite to the ducts Avhich extend from the nostrils to the mouth. Hence it happens, that if Avhen we are drinking, the liquor enters into the aspera arteria, and is throAvn upAvard, it departs through the nostrils. The head of the aspera arteria, in the superior part in Avhich it extends to the mouth, has, Avhat is called the epiglottis, which is in the middle of the tAvo avenues that reach from the nostrils to the mouth. The aspera arteria, therefore, in the superior part is conjoined Avith the tongue, but Avith the other extremity it descends into the middle of the lungs ; aftenvards from this it is divided into each part of the lungs. For the lungs are bipar- tite in all the animals that have them. In viviparous animals, however, the separation is not similarly apparent, and it is in the smallest degree apparent in man. But the lungs of man are not multifidious, as they are in some viviparous animals, nor are they smooth, but anomalous. In oviparous animals, however, as in birds, and such quadrupeds as are oviparous, the two parts of the lungs are very much separated from, each other, so that they seem to have two lungs. Since the lungs therefore are bipartite, the aspera arteria which is one, Avhen it arrives at the lungs is divided into two canals, as it were, and insinuates itself into each part of the lungs ; it is also connected Avith the great vein, [or vena cava] and Avith another vein which is called the aorta. When in respiring, however, we inflate the aspera arteria, then the breath enters into the hollow parts of the lungs. The heart also is conjoined Avith the aspera arteria by fat, cartilaginous, and fibrous bonds, and in that part in which it depends from the aspera arteria, it is holloAv [and sinuous]. But though in some smaller animals it is not manifest, whether Avhen in respiring they inflate the aspera arteria, the breath not only enters the lungs, but likeAvise the heart, yet in larger animals it is evident that the breath insinuates itself through the aspera arteria into the heart likewise. The aspera arteria therefore subsists after this manner, and its office consists in alone receiving and emitting the breath, but it does not receive any dry or liquid nutriment. Indeed, if food, either liquid or dry, happens to fall into the aspera arteria, the animal is in pain till it is ejected. The stomach however, [or oesophagus] depends in the superior part of it from the mouth, adheres to the artery, and is conjoined both with the spine and the artery by membranaceous ligaments. But it passes through the transverse septum, [by which the breast is divided from the belly] and ends in the ventricle. It has also a fleshy nature, and is adapted to be extended both according to length and according to breadth. The human, however, is similar to the canine ventricle; for it is not much larger than the intestine, but resembles, as it Avere, a broader intestine. Under the ventricle the intestines are situated, one of which is simple and winding, but the other is broad; and the Ioav er cavity, [or the alvus, which contains the intestines] is similar to that of a soav ; for it is broad, and the part under the alvus, Avhichis extend ed to the seat, is short and thick. From the middle of the alvus the omentum depends ; Avhich is naturally a fat membrane, in the same manner as in all other animals which have only one ventricle, and teeth on each side of the mouth. Above the intestines is the mesentery, which is membranaceous, broad and fat. But from the great vein and the aorta many veins are deduced, Avhich are diffused through the me sentery in that part by Avhich it is connected Avith the intestines, and beginning from the summit of the mesentery, they are diffused as far as to its lowest parts. Both the liver and the spleen, however, are in the loAver belly, near to the omentum [by which the intestines are covered.] The spleen hoAvever of a man is narrow and long, and resembles that of a hog. WITH respect, hoAvever, to the parts of other animals, some are com mon to all animals, as Ave have before observed, but others are peculiar to certain genera. But they are the same with or different from each other, in the way we have frequently mentioned. For nearly all ani mals Avhich are of a different genus, have most of their parts specifically different. And some indeed have their parts only analogously the same, but generically different ; but others have them generically the same, and specifically different ; and there are many parts Avhich some animals have, but others have not. Viviparous quadrupeds therefore [accord with man, and Avith each other, in this, that they] have a head and neck, and all the parts in the head. But the several parts differ from each other in their form. And the neck of the lion indeed, consists of one bone, but has no verte brae. The left legs, hoAvever, of quadrupeds, except those of the elephant, are less agile and expedite than the left hands of men. But the elephant has the division of the five toes in the foot, indistinct, and has the fore much larger than the hind legs. In his hind legs also, he has small mallets. He has hoAvever a nose of such a kind and so large, that it serves him instead of hands. For he both eats and drinks extending his nose [or proboscis] to his mouth. He also ex tends this to his keeper Avhen riding on his back, tears up trees Avith it, and respires by its assistance when he Avalks through the Avater. The extremity likeAvise of the proboscis may be bent, but cannot be fold ed; for it is cartilaginous, [though the other parts of it may also be folded.] Man hoAvever is the only animal that is ambidexter, or has the use of both his hands. With respect to the breast, hoAvever, all animals have this part ana logous, but not similar to the breast of man ; for the human breast is broad, but that of other animals narroAV. But no other animal besides man has mammæ in the anterior part; for the elephant has two mam mæ indeed, yet they are not in the breast, but near [i. e. a little below] the breast. The legs hoAvever of other animals, as well the fore as the hind legs, have flexions contrary to each other, and to the flexions of the legs and arms of man, the elephant being excepted. For viviparous quadrupeds have their fore legs bent towards the fore part, but their hind legs bent towards the hind part, and they have the cavity of one flexion opposite to the cavity of the other. What is asserted of the elephant, hoAvever, by some, is not true [i. e. that he cannot bend his legs, nor sit] for he can do both, except that he cannot on account of his weight at one and the same time bend each fore leg, and recline on each side, but he can alone bend one leg, either the right or the left, and alone recline on one side, and in this manner he sleeps, [leaning against some, wall :>r tree.] But he bends his hind legs in the same manner as men. But man has contrary flexions of his arms and legs. For he bends his- arms so as that they are hollow in the anterior part, the cavity a little inclining to the oblique ; but he bends his legs so as to form a ca vity in the posterior part. Birds also have inflexions similar to those of quadrupeds. For, being bipeds, they bend their legs towards the posterior part ; but instead of arms and fore legs, they have Avings, the flexion of which is toAvards the anterior part. ■ The sea-calf however is, as it were, a mutilated quadruped ; for im mediately after the shoulder-blade it has [two fore] feet similar to hands, such as are the [fore] feet of bears. For the [fore] feet of the sea-calf have five toes, each of Avhich has three flexions, and a nail which is not large. But the [two] hind feet, have indeed five toes, and flexions and nails similar to the fore feet, but in their form they resemble the tails of fishes. The motions however both of quadrupeds, and animals that have many feet, are according to a diameter, and in this manner also they stand. But the principle of motion in all animals is from the right hand parts. The lion also, and both the Bactrian and Arabian camel, Avalk foot by foot.

The horns hoAvever of the hippe laphi are similar to those of a roe-buck. But the elephant is the least hairy of all quadrupeds. The tails also of quadrupeds, Avhen they have any magnitude, follow the condition of the body, Avith respect to abounding with or being deprived of hairs ; for some have so little hair that it can scarcely be perceived. Camels, however, differ from other quadrupeds in this, that they have what is called a tuber or swelling on the back. But the Bactrian differ from the Arabian camels. For the Bactrian camel has two swel lings on the back, but the Arabian has only one. Each camel also has another swelling in the inferior similar to that in the superior part, by which the rest of the body is supported when they bend their knees. The camel likewise has four mamillæ, in the same manner as coavs, a tail similar to that of an ass, and the pudendum behind. It also has but one knee in each leg, and not many flexions as some say ; but through the form of the belly [which is very small and drawn up] it ap pears to have many knees or flexions. And it has indeed an ankle bone similar to that of an ox, but a small thigh in proportion to the magnitude of its body. It is also bisulcous, and has no teeth in the up per jaw. But it is bisulcous in such a Avay, that in the inferior part of the foot it is bipartite, as far as to the second flexion of the toes, but in the superior part it is quadripartite, as far as to the first joints of the toes. The intervals of the fissures also are covered with a certain membrane, similar, as it Avere, to that Avith Avhich the intervals of the fissures in geese are covered. All quadrupeds, hoAvever, have bony, nervous and fleshless legs ; and, in short, this is the case Avith all other animals that have feet, except man. They are also Avithout hips, and especially birds. On the con trary, man has hips that are very fleshy Avith respect to the other parts of his body, and his thighs and tibiæ are very fleshy ; for that part of the tibia Avhich is called sura, is very fleshy. But of sanguineous and viviparous quadrupeds, some are multifidous, as the hands and feet of man ; for some have feet with many fissures, as the lion, the dog, and the panther ; but others have bifidated feet, and instead of nails have hoofs, as sheep, goats, stags, and the hippo potamus. Others have their feet without fissures, such as those that have solid hoofs, as the horse and the mule. The genus of swine, hoAV ever, is ambiguous ; for in Illyria, Pœonia, and other places, the swine have solid hoofs. Bisulcous animals, therefore, have tAvo fissures behind and before ; but animals that have solid hoofs -have feet Avith out fissures. Some animals likewise have horns, but others are Avithout horns. Most of those therefore that have horns are naturally bisulcous, as the ox, the stag, and the goat ; but Ave have seen no animal that has solid hoofs, and is bicornous. There are hoAvever a few animals that have one horn and solid hoofs, as the Indian ass. But the oryx • has one horn, and is bisulcous. The Indian ass also is the only animal that has an astragalus3 {xrpayxAos) of those that have solid hoofs. For the hog, as we before observed, is ambiguous. Hence its astragalus is not Avell formed. But of bisulcous animals, men have an astragalus. THE HISTORY OF ANIMALS. 41 galus, and man also is Avithout it ; but the lynx indeed has that which is similar to a semi-astragalus, and the lion in the place of the astraga lus has a certain Avinding bone like a labyrinth. All animals, however, that have the astragalus, have it in their hind legs, so that it is erect in the flexure by which the foot, is conjoined to the leg. The astragalus also in its prone part [which because it is a little convex is called the back] is external; but in its supine part [which because it is holloAV is called the belly] is external. The parts likeAvise of the astragalus Avhich are called veneres, are inAvardly turned toAvards each other ; but the parts of it Avhich are called calus, have an external direction; and that part of the astragalus Avhich is turned upAvard, is called antenna. The position, therefore, of the astragalus in all animals that have it, subsists after this manner. There are however some animals that are bisulcous, have manes, and are bicornous, as the bonasus, Avhich is produced in Pœonia and Media. But all such animals as are horned are quadrupeds, unless some animal should be metaphorically said to have a horn, as the Egyptians assert of the Theban serpents, as if something resembling a horn projected from their head. Of animals hoAvever that have horns, the stag alone has a horn wholly solid ; but the horns of other animals are to a certain extent hollow, and at the extremity are solid. The interior and concave part of the horn there fore seems to be naturally formed from skin ; but the exterior and solid part is formed from bone, and appropriately surrounds the interior part ; and such are the horns of oxen. But the stag is the only animal that casts off its horns annually, beginning to do so at the age of tAvo years ; and other horns groAv in their stead. Other animals, hoAvever, never lose their horns unless they are deprived of them by violence. Farther still, quadrupeds differ from each other, and also from man, both in the mammæ, and in the organs subservient to generation. For some animals have the niammæ in the anterior part of the body, i. e. in the breast, or a little under the breast; and they have also two mam mæ and two papillæ or nipples, as man, and the elephant, as Ave have before observed. For the elephant has tAvo mammæ under the shoul ders; but the female elephant has perfectly small mammæ, and not in G proportion

text: THE HISTORY OF ANIMALS. BOOK II. 42 proportion to the magnitude of the body, so that obliquely they can scarcely be seen. The male also, as Avell as the female elephant, has very small mammæ. The bear hoAvever has four mammæ. Again, other animals have two mammæ, and two papillae betAveen their thighs, as the sheep ; but others have four papillae, as trie cow. Others again have the mammæ, neither in the breast, nor betAveen the thighs, but in the belly, as the dog, and the swine, yet they are not all equal. Other animals, therefore, [as the dog, the SAvine, and many other quadrupeds,] have more than four mammæ in the belly ; but the pan ther has four, and the lioness has two, in the belly. The camel also has tAvo mammæ, and four papillæ, in the same manner as the coav. The males, however, of those animals that have solid hoofs are Avith out mammæ, except such offspring of these as resemble their mother, Avhich sometimes happens to be the case in horses. . But Avith respect to the pudenda of males, some of them have this member externally, as man and horse, and many other animals ; but others have it internally, as the dolphin. And of those that have it externally, some indeed have it in the anterior part of the body, as the above-mentioned animals. Of these again, some have both the penis and the testes hanging loose, as man; but others have them ad hering to the belly ; and in some animals they are more, but in others less loose ; for this part is not similarly detached in a boar and a horse. The elephant also has a penis similar indeed to that of a horse, but small, and not in proportion to the magnitude of his . body ; but his testicles are not externally apparent, but are inward and near the reinr Hence in coition he is rapidly liberated. The female elephant, how ever, has the pudenda in the place in which the mammæ of sheep are situated ; but Avhen she ardently desires coition, she draws this part upAvard, and turns it externally, so that copulation may be easy to the male. The opening also is proportionally very large. In most ani mals, therefore, the pudenda subsist after this manner. But some of them discharge the urine backward, as the lynx, the lion, the ca mel, and the hare. The males, therefore, of these animals differ from each other in the manner Ave have shown, but all the females discharge the

text: THE HISTORY OF ANIMALS. BOOK II. 43 the urine backAvard ; for the female elephant has the pudenda in the same manner as other animals, between the thighs. There is, hoAv ever, a great difference in the pudenda of animals. For some have the penis cartilaginous and fleshy, as man ; the fleshy part of which cannot be inflated, but the cartilaginous part admits of increase ; other animals have it nervous, as the camel and the elephant > and in others it is bony, as in the fox, the Avolf, the pole-cat, and the weasel ; for the Aveasel also has a bony penis. In addition to this also, man when he has acquired his proper mag nitude, has his superior less than his inferior parts ; but in other san guineous animals, the contrary takes place. We call hoAvever the supe rior part that which extends from the head as far as to the part in which there is an egress of the excrements-, and Ave denominate the inferior part, that which remains of the body from the places through Avhich the excrements are emitted. In those animals, therefore, that have feet, the hind legs determine the magnitude of the inferior part ; but in those that have no feet, the magnitude of the inferior part is deter mined by the tail, and whatever is instead of a tail. Such, therefore, are animals when they have arrived at perfection. For man in his in fancy has the superior larger than the inferior parts ; but the contrary takes place as he increases through age. Hence man alone has not the same progressive motion when he is an infant, and Avhen he has ar rived at perfection ; but at first he creeps on the ground with his hands and feet, like a quadruped. Some animals also have an analogous in crease of the superior and inferior parts, as the dog. But in others, the superior parts are at first less, and the inferior larger, but as they advance to perfection, the superior parts become larger, as animals which have a tuft of hair on their forehead. For these receive no in crease in the inferior part Avhich extends from the hoof to the hip. There is however much difference in the teeth of other animals, both with respect to each other, and those of man. For all such qua drupeds as are sanguineous and viviparous have teeth ; but in the first place, some have teeth on both sides, and others have not.' For such animals as horses have not teeth on both sides ; since they have g 2 not*

title: The History of Animals of Aristotle, and his Treatise on Physiognomy, translated from the Greek. By Thomas Taylor
text: THE HISTORY OF ANIMALS. BOOK II. 44 not the fore teeth of the upper jaw. But there are some animals which neither have teeth on both sides, nor horns, as the camel. And some animals indeed have teeth projecting beyond the mouth, as male swine, but in others they do not project. Again, some animals have serrated teeth, as the lion, the panther, and the dog ; but others have them in a continued series, as the horse and the ox. For those animals have serrated teeth, Avhich have at the same time the order of the sharp teeth changed, [so that the space intercepted betAveen the tAvo inferior teeth is occupied by the superior tooth, and the space intercepted between the two superior teeth is occupied by the inferior tooth.] No animal, however, has at one and the same time projecting teeth and a horn ; nor is there any animal Avhich has serrated teeth, and is horned, or has projecting teeth. But most animals have the fore teeth sharp, and the inward teeth broad. The sea-calf, hoAvever, has all its teeth serrated, as being an animal allied to fishes; for nearly all fishes have serrated teeth. None also of these genera of animals have double rows of teeth ; though if we may believe Ctesias, there is a certain animal which has. For he says, that in India there is a savage animal, the name of which is Martichora, that has a triple row of teeth in each jaAv. He adds, that this animal is equal in magnitude to a lion, that it is similarly hairy with, and has feet resembling those of a lion, but that its face and ears are like those of a man, and that its eyes are azure, and its colour resembling that of cinnabar. It has also a tail armed with a sting, and resembling the tail of the land scorpion- It is likewise furnished with certain native darts, which it hurls forth ; and it utters a sound resembling that of a pipe and a trumpet. But it runs with no less swiftness than the stag, and is savage and feeds on human flesh. Man, therefore, sheds his teeth, and also other animals, such as the horse, the mule, and the ass. Man, however, sheds his fore teeth, but no animal sheds the maxillares or grinders. And the swine, in short, does not shed any of its teeth. CHAP.

text: BOOK n. THE HISTORY OF ANIMALS. 45 CHAPTER II. It is dubious, hoAvever, Avith respect to dogs whether thev shed their teeth or not. And some indeed are of opinion that they do not shed any of their teeth ; others assert that they only shed their canine teeth ; and others think that they shed their teeth in the same manner as men, g but that this is latent, because they do not shed them, before other teeth equal to them grow inwardly in their stead. It is reasonable also to suppose that the like takes place in other savage animals, since they are said to shed only their canine teeth. The age of dogs, hoAvever, is known from their teeth; for those that are young have white and sharp teeth; but those that are elderly have black and obtuse teeth. CHAPTER III. The contrary, however, takes place Avith respect to teeth in other animals and in horses ; for other animals as they advance in age have blacker teeth, but the horse as he grows old has whiter teeth. But the teeth Avhich are called canine separate the sharp from the broad teeth, participating of the form of both ; for beneath indeed they are broad, but above they are sharp. The males also have more teeth than the females,

title: The History of Animals of Aristotle, and his Treatise on Physiognomy, translated from the Greek. By Thomas Taylor
text: THE HISTORY OF ANIMALS. 46 BOOK II. females, in men, in sheep, in goats, and in swine ; but in other ani mals this has not yet been seen. For the most part, however, those animals that have more teeth live longer ; but those that have fewer and thinner teeth are for the most part shorter lived. CHAPTER IV. In the human species, however, the last maxillary teeth, which they call genuini, [or the innermost cheek teeth] grow about the twentieth year, both in men and Avomen. But in some women, and also in some men, the maxillary teeth have groAvn when they have been only eighteen years of age, but in rising have been attended with pain. This, however, has happened to such as have not had the innermost cheek teeth in their youth. CHAPTERS V. and VI. But the elephant has indeed four teeth on each side, by which he elaborates his food, and grinds it into the appearance of flower. Be sides these also, he has two other large teeth. The male elephant, therefore, has these large, and turned upward ; but the female has them small, and in a position contrary to the males ; for the teeth of these are

title: The History of Animals of Aristotle, and his Treatise on Physiognomy, translated from the Greek. By Thomas Taylor
text: BOOK II. THE HISTORY OF ANIMALS. 47 are turned downward. The elephant also has teeth as soon as he is born, those however that are large, being at first immanifest. But he has a tongue very small, and so inward that it is difficult to see it. CHAPTER VII. Animals also differ in the magnitude of the mouth. For the open ing of the mouth of some is very wide, as in the dog and the lion, and all those that have serrated teeth. But other animals have a small mouth, as men ; and others have a mouth of a moderate size, as the genus of swine. The Egyptian hippopotams, however, has a mane, in the same manner as a horse ; but is bisulcous, in the same manner as an ox ; and is flat-nosed to the view. He has also the astragalus, in the same manner as bisulcous animals ; teeth someAvhat prominent, a tail resembling the tail of a hog, and a voice like that of a horse. But the magnitude of his body is that of the ass. His skin likewise is so thick that hunting shields are formed from it ; but his imvard parts resemble those of a horse and an ass. CHAPTERS VIII. and IX. Some animals hoAvever have an ambiguous nature, because they partly imitate man and partly quadrupeds, such as apes, the coebi [a kind of apes] and the cynocephali. But the cœbus has the tail of an ape ; and the

text: THE HISTORY OF ANIMALS. BOOK II. 48 the cynocephali have the same form with apes, except that they are laro-er and stronger, and have a more canine face. Their manners also are more savage, and they have teeth more canine and strong. Apes, hoAvever, as being quadrupeds, are hairy in the prone part of their body ; and in a similar manner, in their supine parts, as having in these the human form. For hairiness, as we have before observed, subsists contrarily in men and quadrupeds ; except that apes have very thick and dense hairs, both in the prone and in the supine part. But the face of the ape has many similitudes to that of man ; for it has si milar nostrils and ears; and both its fore and maxillary teeth resemble those of man. And farther still, since other animals have not hairs on both eye-lids, the ape has, though they are very thin, especially on the inferior eye-lid, and very small ; for other quadrupeds are deprived of these. The ape also has tAvo papillæ of small mammæ in the breast. It has likeAvise arms in the same manner as man, except that they are hairy : and they bend these and their legs in the same way as man, viz. so that the curvatures of the arms are contrary to the curvatures of the legs. Besides this also, apes have hands, fingers and nails, similar to those of the human species, except that all these are of a more brutal form. They have however feet peculiar to themselves ; for they are as it were large hands; and Avith respect to their toes, in the same manner as in the fingers of the hand, the middle is longer than the rest; and the sole of the foot resembles the palm of the hand, except that it extends itself as far as to the extremity, or heel. But the last part of their foot is callous, and rudely and obscurely imitates the heel of the human foot. They likeAvise use their feet, both as hands and feet, and bend their [fore] feet in the same manner as hands. The cubit how ever and thigh of apes are short in proportion to the other part of the arm and the tibia. They likewise have not a prominent navel, but a certain hard substance in the place of the navel. The superior part of the body also of these animals is much larger than the inferior part, in the same manner as in quadrupeds ; for in quadrupeds the length of the superior is to the length of the inferior part, nearly as five to three. They

text: BOOK II. THE HISTORY OF ANIMALS. 49 They degenerate therefore from men on this account, and also because they have feet similar to hands, and Avhich are as it Avere composed from the foot and the hand ; from the foot indeed, according to the ex tremity of the heel; but from .the hand according to the other parts : since the toes have what is called the palm of the hand. They likewise live for a longer time prone after the manner of quadrupeds, than erect [after the manner of men]. And they neither have hips, as being quadrupeds, nor a tail as being a biped ; for Avhat they have as a tail is very small, as if it were designed merely as a mark. But the private parts of the female ape are similar to those of a woman ; and those of the male more resemble the privities of a dog than of a man The cœbi also, as Ave have before observed, have a tail. The whole genus of apes, however, in their interior parts resemble men. The external parts there fore of viviparous animals subsist after this manner. CHAPTER X. All quadrupeds however Avhich are oviparous and sanguineous, (and no terrestrial and sanguineous animal is oviparous, Avhich is not a qua druped or without feet) have a head, neck, back, and the prone and su pine parts of the body. They have also fore and hind legs, and that which is analogous to a breast, in the same manner as viviparous qua drupeds; and most of them have a long tail, but a few [as tortoises] have a short tail. All of them however have feet, consisting of many toes, and divided into many parts. Besides this likewise, all of them have sensoria and a tongue, except the Egyptian crocodile. But this ani mal resembles certain fishes. For, in short, as fishes have a thorny tongue, and which adheres to the jaAv bone, thus crocodiles have the place destined to the tongue so smooth, that no vestige of a tongue is ap- u parent
name: Aristotle

title: The History of Animals of Aristotle, and his Treatise on Physiognomy, translated from the Greek. By Thomas Taylor
text: THE HISTORY OF ANIMALS. BOOK II. 50 parent in them, unless the lips are very much drawn up. All oviparous quadrupeds likeAvise have no ears, but have only a certain avenue sub servient to hearing; nor have they either mammæ, or a penis, or testi cles, externally apparent, but they are imvardly latent. They are also without hairs, but all of them are covered with scales. All of them like- Avise have serrated teeth. River crocodiles, however, have eyes similar to those of swine, but their teeth are large and prominent, their nails are strong, and their skin consists of impenetrable scales. They also do not see well in the water, but out of it they see most acutely. For the most part of the day, therefore, they live on the land, but at night in the water: for the water is then warmer than the air x. CHAPTER XI. The chamæleon has the whole figure of its body resembling a lizard, but its sides tend downward, and are conjoined under the belly, in the same manner as in fishes, and the back bone rises above the other parts in a manner similar to that of fishes. The face also of the chamæleon is most similar to that kind of ape which has the face of a SAvine, but it has a very long tail which ends in a point, and is convolved like a thong of leather. It is more erect hoAvever from the earth than the lizard : but the flexions of its legs subsist in the same manner as in the lizard. Each of its feet too is bipartite, and the two parts into which each is divided have a position with respect to each other, similar to that which the 1 The air in the day is hotter than the water; but in Egypt the water at night is warmer than the serene air, because the water preserves longer than the air the heat produced from the sun in the day. thumb

text: BOOK II. THE HISTORY OF ANIMALS. 51 thumb has to the rest of the hand. Each of these parts of the foot of the chamæleon also is divided as it Avere into certain fingers. The first part of the foot therefore corresponds to a thumb, but the second part, to the rest of the hand, and is therefore divided into many other fingers. The second part hoAvever of the forefeet, is not divided in the same Avay as the second part of the hind feet, but the second part of the fore feet is divided imvardly, i. e. toAvards the sole, into three parts, and as it were fingers, but outwardly it is divided into two parts only. But the second part of the hind feet, is divided towards the sole into two fin- gers as it Avere, and outAvardly, i. e. in the superior part, it is divided into three parts resembling fingers. These parts also are covered Avith crooked nails. The Avhole body however of the chamæleon is rough, in the same manner as that of the crocodile. But its eyes are situated in a cavity, are very large and round, and are covered with a skin si- milar to that of the rest of the body ; and in the middle of the skin that covers the eye there is a small avenue, through which it sees, which avenue is never covered with any skin. The motion also of its eye is circular, and it transfers its sight to all places, and thus sees Avhat it Avishes to see. But the mutation of its colour takes place when it is inflated. It has also a black colour, not very remote from that of the crocodile, and a pale colour like lizards, variegated with black spots like the panther. A mutation likeAvise of this kind takes place through the Avhole of its body ; for its eyes and its tail are changed in a manner similar to the rest of the body. But its motion is very slow like that of the tortise. When it is dying also it is of a pale colour, and it has a colour of this kind Avhen it is dead. But the parts about the stomach, and the aspera arteria, are situated similarly to those in the lizard. It has, however, no flesh, except in the head, the jaws, and the extremity of the tail, and these parts have a little flesh. It like wise has blood only about the heart, the eyes, the parts Avhich are above the heart, and such veins as extend from these parts. But in these there is very little blood. Its brain also is placed a little above the eyes, but in continuation with them. And if the skin which covers the eyes is taken away, the eyes will be found to contain a shining h 2 substance
name: Aristotle

title: The History of Animals of Aristotle, and his Treatise on Physiognomy, translated from the Greek. By Thomas Taylor
text: THE HISTORY OF ANIMALS. BOOK II. 52 substance resembling a thin brazen ring. Many strong membranes likewise are extended nearly through the whole of its body, and which are much superior in strength to those which cover the rest of its body. And when it is Avholly dissected, it breathes for a long time, a small motion strenuously yet remaining in it about the heart. It is likewise capable of contracting all the parts of the body, and especially the parts about the sides. It has not however any Avhere the spleen ap parent ; and it conceals itself in caves in the same manner as lizards. CHAPTER XII. In like manner birds also have certain parts in common Avith the above-mentioned animals. For all of them have a head, neck, back, the supine parts of the body, and that which is analogous to the breast. They differ likewise from other animals in this, that they are bipeds in the same manner as man, except that their legs are bent like those of quadrupeds, in a way contrary to those of man, as we have before ob served. They have, hoAvever, neither hands nor fore-feet, but [instead of them] they have Avings, Avhich are peculiar to birds. Farther still, they have a hip similar to a thigh, Avhich hip is long, and extends as far as to the middle of the belly, to which it is affixed, so as to appear when divulsed to be a thigh. But the thigh in the other part is joined to the tibia. Birds, however, that have crooked nails have the largest thighs, and their breast is more robust than that of other birds. But all birds have feet armed with many nails, and all of them are after a manner multifidous ; for the feet of the greater part of birds have toes. Those birds also which seek their food by sAvimming, though they have broad feet, and which are covered with a skin, yet they have perfect and distinct toes. All such birds, however, as fly high have four
name: Aristotle

title: The History of Animals of Aristotle, and his Treatise on Physiognomy, translated from the Greek. By Thomas Taylor
text: THE HISTORY OF ANIMALS. 53 BOOK II. four toes ; for they have three for the most part in the anterior part of the foot, and one in the posterior part, in the place of the heel. But some few have tAvo toes indeed in the anterior part, and tAvo in the posterior part, as is the case with the bird called jynx. This bird, how ever, is a little larger than the chaffinch, and its plumage is various. But it has something peculiar in the disposition of its toes, and its tongue is similar to that of serpents ; for it can extend this to the length of four fingers out of the mouth, and again draAv it Avithin its, beak. Farther still, it can also turn its neck round to the hind part of it, the rest of the body being quiescent, in the same manner as ser pents. It has also large nails, and Avhich are naturally similar to those of a jack-daAV ; and it emits a shrill voice. Birds, however, have indeed a mouth, but one peculiar to them selves ; for they have neither lips nor teeth, but a beak ; nor have they cars or nostrils, but they have the avenues of these senses ; of the nos trils indeed, they have the avenue in the beak, but of the hearing in the head. All of them, however, have tAvo eyes, in the same manner as other animals, but Avithout eye- lids. Heavy birds also [i. e. those which do not fly high] wink, that is, shut and open the eyes Avith the inferior eye-lid ; and they likewise cover the eyes Avith a certain mem brane emitted from the corner of the eye. Nocturnal birds, however, wink with the superior eye-lid. Animals also that are covered Avith scales do the very same thing, such as lizards, and others that are of a kindred nature to these animals. For all of them wink with the in ferior eye-lid, though all of them do not cover the eyes with a mem brane emitted from the corner of the eye. Again, birds have neither scales, nor hairs, but feathers. But all feathers have a quill. And they have not indeed a tail like that of quadrupeds, but their tail consists of feathers. Those birds also which have long legs and broad feet, have a short tail, but those which have short legs and not a broad foot have a longer tail. Those birds too, which have a longer tail, when they fly have their legs contracted to their belly ; but those that have a short tail, when they fly have their iegs extended to their tail. All birds likewise have a tongue, but this is
name: Aristotle

title: The History of Animals of Aristotle, and his Treatise on Physiognomy, translated from the Greek. By Thomas Taylor
text: THE HISTORY OF ANIMALS. BOOK II 54 is dissimilar; for some have a long, others a short, others a broad, and others a narrow tongue. Some genera of birds also, beyond all ani mals after man, utter the sound of our letters; and this is especially the case with those birds whose tongue is broad. No oviparous ani mal, hoAvever, has the epiglottis on the aspera arteria, but they are able to contract and dilate the avenue of the aspera arteria, so as to prevent any weight from falling on the lungs. Some genera of birds also have a spur ; but there is no bird Avhich has at the same time crooked nails and a spur. Some birds, however, that are armed with crooked nails fly high ; but those birds that have spurs are heavy [and fly near the earth]. Again, some birds have a comb, or crest, consist ing of raised feathers j but the cock alone has a peculiar crest, which is neither flesh, nor very remote from the nature of flesh. CHAPTER XIII. Among aquatic animals, however, the genus of fishes alone is di- vided into many species. For they have a head, and the prone ' and supine parts ; and in the supine part of the body their belly and in- testines are contained. In the last part of the body also they have a tail, which is in continuity Avith, and is not divided from, the rest of the body ; and this tail is not similar in all fishes. But no fish has a neck, or hands, or feet, or in short testicles, either internally, or externally ; nor have they any mammæ. To be deprived of mammæ, however, is not peculiar to fishes, but is common to them Avith many other ani mals, since all animals that are not viviparous are Avithout mammæ, 1 The prone parts in fishes have a direction towards the heavens, and the supine parts to wards the earth. and
name: Aristotle

title: The History of Animals of Aristotle, and his Treatise on Physiognomy, translated from the Greek. By Thomas Taylor
text: THE HISTORY OF ANIMALS. BOOK II. 55 and of viviparous animals, those only have them which do not first conceive an egg in themselves, but an animal. For the dolphin is vi viparous ; and hence it has two mammæ, yet not in the superior, but in the inferior part, and near the organs of generation. It has not, however, like quadrupeds, apparent papillae, but in the place of these it has as it were two orifices, one on the right, and the other on the left side, from which the milk flows. From these it is sucked by its young that follow it ; and this by certain persons has been evidently seen. Fishes, therefore, as we have said, have neither mammæ, nor any exterior and apparent genital member. They have, however, certain peculiar members, viz. gills and fins, by Avhich they return the water which they receive through the mouth. Most fishes likewise are furnished with four fins, yet there are some that have only tAvo ; for certain long fishes, such as eels, ha\*e only tAvo, near the gills. In a si milar manner also, the mullets have only tAvo fins, Avhich are produced in the lake in Siphæ [in Tuscany] ; and this is likewise the case with the fish called tœnia. But some of the long fishes, such as lampreys, have neither fins nor gills entire and perfect like other fishes. Of those, however, that have gills, some have them concealed and others ap parent; but all the cartilaginous kind have them apparent. And all those, indeed, that have their gills concealed, have them obliquely situated. But of cartilaginous fishes, those that are broad, as the torpedo and the ray, have their gills in the inferior and supine part ; but those that are long have them in their side, as is the case Avith all the genera of lampreys. The frog fish, however, has them obliquely and concealed, yet not with a thorny covering, like those fishes that are not cartilaginous, but with a skinny covering. Farther still, of some fishes the gills are single, but of others two-fold ; but that part of the tAvo-fold gills Avhich is turned towards the body of the fish is not tAvo-told but single. And some fishes indeed have feAv gills, but others many. In either case, hoAvever, they have as many on one side as on the other. But those that have the fewest gills, have one on each side ; and this is tAvo-fold, as in the fish called the boar. Others again, have

Others have four gills indeed, but they are in a tAvo-fold order, except the last, as the sea-thrush, the perch, the glanis, and the carp. All those, however, that are of the nature of lampreys have two-fold gills, and five on each side ; but the sword-fish has eight tAvo fold gills. And thus much concerning the multitude of gills in fishes. Farther still, fishes differ from other animals, not only in their gills, but also in the covering of their body. For they neither have hairs in the same manner as terrestrial viviparous animals ; nor have they scales l like some oviparous quadrupeds ; nor are they covered with feathers, as the genus of birds ; but most of them, indeed, have thin scales, a feAv of them are rough, and a very few of them are smooth. Of the cartilaginous kind, therefore, some are rough, but others are smooth ; but the conger, the eel, and the tunny, are among the num ber of the smooth. All fishes, likewise, have serrated teeth, except the scarus. All of them too have their teeth sharp, and some of them have many rows of teeth, and inserted in the tongue. They have also a hard and thorny tongue, and so adherent and fixed, that sometimes they seem not to have a tongue. With respect to the mouth, in some fishes it is very open, in the same manner as in some viviparous quadrupeds. But with respect to the sensoria or organs of sensation, they neither have the sensoria of hearing or smelling, nor the avenues of these apparent ; but all of them have eyes without eye-lids, though their eyes are not hard. The Avhole genus of fishes, therefore, is sanguineous ; but some of them are oviparous, and some of them are viviparous. All those indeed that are covered with thin scales are oviparous ; but all the cartilaginous kind are viviparous, except the frog-fish. * i. e. Scales resembling those of a serpent. CHAP.

text: BOOK II. THE HISTORY OF ANIMALS. 57 CHAPTER XIV. Of sanguineous animals, however, there remains the genus of ser pents. But they partake of the nature both of terrestrial and aquatic animals. There are also marine ser pents similar in form to the terrestrial genus, except that their head more resembles that of the conger. There are, however, many genera of marine serpents, and they have an all-various colour; but they are not generated in very deep places. Serpents, also, are Avithout feet, in the same manner as the genus of fishes. There are, likewise, marine scolopendra, resembling the terrestrial in their form ; but their magnitude is someAvhat less. These marine sco lopendra are generated in rocky places [of the sea] ; but their colour is more red, they have a greater number of feet, and their legs are thin ner, than those of terrestrial scolopendra. These, likewise, are not ge nerated, as neither are serpents, in very deep places of the sea. There is, also, a certain little fish found on rocks, which some call echeneida, or the sea lamprey, and some use it as a philter, and for the purpose of obtaining victory in judicial processes ; but it is useless for food. Some also say that it has feet, but it has not. It appears, how ever, to have them, because it has fins resembling feet. text: BOOK II. THE HISTORY OF ANIMALS. 58 CHAPTER XV. In the first place, therefore, avc must [next] shoAv how the internal parts subsist in sanguineous animals. For the greatest genera of ani mals differ from the rest in this, that the one are sanguineous, but the other exanguious. Sanguineous animals, hoAvever, are man and vivi parous quadrupeds ; and besides these, oviparous quadrupeds, birds, fish, cetaceous animals, and others Avhich are not contained in these greatest genera, but are signified by the name of species, as serpent and crocodile. All such animals, therefore, as are quadrupeds and viviparous, have a stomach and aspera arteria, and these are situated in the same man ner as in men. This is also the case Avith such quadrupeds as are ovi parous, and Avith birds ; but they differ in the form of these parts. In short, all such animals as by receiving the air respire and expire have lungs, the aspera arteria, a stomach ; and the position of the stomach and aspera arteria is similar, though these parts differ in species from those of other animals. On the contrary, the lungs are not only spe cifically different in different animals, but have also a different posi tion. Farther still, all sanguineous animals have a heart, and a transverse septum or diaphragm ; but in small animals, the blood is not similarly apparent, on account of its tenuity and paucity, except in the heart. It is also peculiar to a certain genus of oxen, but not to all oxen, to have a bone in the heart ; and the heart of horses, likewise, has a bone. All sanguineous animals, however, have not lungs.
