But the bird called Ægocephalus, [i. e. having the head of a goat] is entirely Avithout a spleen, she like also takes place in oviparous quadrupeds ; for these have a very small spleen, as is evi dent in the tortoise, the rubeta or land toad, the lizard, the crocodile, and the frog. Again, of those animals that have a liver, some have the gall annexed to the liver, but others have not. Of viviparous quadrupeds, indeed, neither the stag, nor the fallow-deer, nor the mule, nor the ass, nor the sea-calf, has the gall ; and this is also the case with some rats. With respect to stags, however, those which are called achaini, seem to have the gall in their tail ; but they have, indeed, a colour in their tail resembling gall, yet it is not fluid like gall, and in the interior part is similar to the spleen. All these stags, too, have in their head living, Avorms ; and these are generated under the concavity of the tongue, about the vertebra, by Avhich the head is connected with the neck. They are also not less in magnitude than the largest Avorms. But they are generated at once, and in continuity, and they are about twenty in number. Stags, therefore, as avc have said, are Avithout a gall, but their intestine is so bitter, that the dogs are not willing to eat it, un less the stag himself is very fat. The liver of the elephant also is with out a gall, yet if it is cut in that part to Avhich the gall usually adheres, a liquor Aoavs from it which is more or less bilious. But of animals which receive the sea water, and have lungs, the dolphin alone has no gall. All birds, and other fishes, however, have a gall, and all oviparous quadrupeds, in short, have it more or less ; but some fishes have the gall in the liver, as the sea-dog, the glanis, the skate, the smooth ray, and the torpedo ; and among long fishes, the eel, the acus or needle fish, and the zagœna or libella. It frequently happens, how ever, that the same genus of fishes is seen to have the gall in both situations, as the conger ; and some indeed have it at the liver, but others at the intestines. The like also takes place in birds. For some of these have the gall joined to the belly, but others to the intestines; as the dove, the croAv, the quail, the swalloAv, and the sparrow. Some birds, likewise, have the gall at the same time, both at the liver and at the belly, as the ægocephalus; but others have it, at the same time, at the liver .and the intestines, as the haAvk and the kite. The aspera arteria also in all animals extends to the lungs, but in what manner we shall afterwards explain. But the stomach, in such animals as have it, extends to the belly, through the diaphragm ; for fishes, for the most part, as we have already observed, have no sto mach, but the belly in these animals is immediately connected Avith the mouth. Hence it frequently happens, that Avhile some of the larger fishes pursue the less the belly falls into the mouth. All the above-mentioned animals, hoAvever, have a belly, and simi larly situated. They have, however, bellies of a various form. For, in the first place, such viviparous and horned qua drupeds as have not teeth in both jaAvs, have four such avenues, or ducts ; and these quadrupeds are said to ruminate. For the stomach, beginning from the mouth, extends dowmvard to the lungs, from the diaphragm, and ends in the [first, Avhich is called] the great belly, the internal parts of which are rough and wrinkled. To this first belly, in that part in Avhich it is joined to the stomach, a second cavity and belly are united, Avhich form a similitude to the fillets of Avomen they call reticula ; for this fillet is externally similar to the first belly, but internally resembles folded fillets. This reticulum also is much less than the first belly. After the second sinus, or belly, folloAvs the third, which is called omasum ; which in the interior part is rough, and dis tinguished by certain cells after the manner of a sponge, and is similar in magnitude to the second belly, or reticulum. After this follows the fourth belly, which is called abomasum ; which is of a more ample mag nitude than the omasum, but its figure is more oblong; and inwardly it contains many large and smooth cells. For serpents are covered with scales, and have both the prone and supine parts similar to those of the lizard ; except that they have no testicles : instead of Avhich they have tAvo avenues in the same .manner as fishes, Avhich con cur in one place, and a small and bifidated vulva. text: THE HISTORY OF ANIMALS. BOOK III. 76 CHAPTER III. Such, then, are the assertions of Syennesis and Diogenes. But Poly bus thus Avrites, [concerning the origin and propagation of the veins.] " There are four conjugations of the veins. The first conjugation, in deed, contains two veins, which originate from the posterior part of the head, and passing through the exterior part of the neck, and the sides of the spine, descend to the hip and legs, and afterwards arrive through the tibia, and exterior ankle bones, at the feet. These veins are called jugular, and de scending inAvardly through the back, near the spine, arrive at the tes ticles, and afterwards through the loins, the hind part of the knee, and the tibia, tend to the interior ankle bones, and the soles of the feet. Hence, in pains of the loins and testicles, physicians bleed those Avho are so afflicted from such veins of the hind part of the knee and ankles. Afterwards through the arm, cubit, and elboAV, they descend to the palm of the hand and the fingers. From such veins under the arm-pit a branch originates, which passes through the ribs, till one of the veins arrives at the spleen, but the other at the liver; and aftenvards each, through the superficies of the belly, terminates in the genital parts." Such nearly are the assertions of others, [concerning the origin and progress of the veins.] There are, also, certain physiologists, Avho, though they have not written on the veins with so much accuracy as physicians, yet all of them similarly ascribe the origin of the veins to the head and the brain ; Avhich, nevertheless, is false. Since, hoAvever, as we have said, the survey of the veins is difficult, they can alone be sufficiently inspected by those who pay attention to things of this kind, in animals which have first Avasted aAvay by leanness, and are afterwards strangled. The nature of the veins, however, subsists in the following manner. There are two veins in the thorax, situated near the spine, of Avhich the greater is in the anterior part, but the less is in the posterior part. And the greater, indeed, declines more to the right side, but the less to the left side. Some, likeAvise, call the less vein the aorta, because the nervous part of it is also seen in dead bodies. These veins, however, originate from the heart. For the whole of them extend through the other A'iscera, preserving their own nature as veins ; but the heart is, as it were, a part of them, and is more manifestly the principle of the larger vein, which is in the anterior part ; so that one of the two prin cipal veins is above, but the other beneath, and the heart is in the middle of them. All hearts, however, contain in themselves a [triple] cavity ; but in very small animals, the greatest cavity of the heart can scarcely he seen. But in animals of a moderate size, the first cavity of the heart, Avhich is the greatest, is not only visible, but also the second ; and in the largest animals all the three are visible. The point, however, of the heart is directed to the anterior part, as we have before observed ; the greatest

But the other two are much less than the greatest. All these cavities, likewise, are connected by perforations Avith the lungs ; but, except one, they are immanifest through the smallness of the cavities. The great vein, therefore, originates from the greatest cavity of the heart, Avhich is constituted in the highest and right part of the heart. Aftenvards passing through the middle cavity, it again receives in it the form of a vein, since the middle cavity of the heart is a part of the greater vein in Avhich the blood stagnates. But the aorta originates from the middle cavity, yet not after the same manner as the great vein originates from the greatest cavity, but it communicates with it by a much narroAver canal. And the great vein, indeed, extends through the heart, but the aorta from the heart. The great vein, also, consists of membrane and skin ; but the aorta is narroAver than this vein, and is very nervous. Being far extended, also, from the heart to the head, and the inferior members, [i. e. to the feet,] it becomes more narroAV, and perfectly nervous. One part, therefore, of the great vein extends in the first place to the lungs, and in that place, in which it is conjoined Avith the aorta, is divided into tAvo branches, one of which proceeds to the lungs, but the other to the spine of the back, and the last vertebræ of the neck. The vein, therefore, Avhich extends to the lungs, because the lungs are bipartite, is also first divided into tAvo branches, corresponding to the two parts of the lungs, and aftenvards is divided into many other branches, through Avhich it enters the several pipes and avenues of the lungs; the larger, indeed, through more ample veins, but the less through narrower veins, and in such a manner that there is no part of the lungs in which there is not an avenue and a little vein. For the last avenues and parts of the small veins are immanifest, on account of their smallness. But the other nerves, which are about the flexion of the bones, are anonymous. For all the bones, whether they touch each other, or so subsist that the one is inserted in the other, are bound together by nerves; and there is a multitude of nerves about all the bones, except the bone of the head, in v/hich there is no nerve, but the head is connected by the sutures of its bones. The nature of nerve, however, is divisible according to length, but is indivisible according to breadth, and possesses much tension. A mucous moisture, likewise, white and glutinous, is pro- duced about the nerves, by which they are nourished, and from which they appear to be generated. A vein, therefore, may be burnt [with- out being destroyed] ; but every nerve is destroyed when burnt ; and if it is cut off it will not be reproduced ; nor does any part of the body experience a numbness where there is no nerve. Most of the nerves, likewise, are about the feet and the hands, the shoulders, neck, and arms. All sanguineous animals, too, have nerves ; but those animals that are without flexions or curvatures of the members, and are de prived of feet and hands, have thin and immanifest nerves. Hence, in fishes, the nerves near the fins are especially conspicuous. CHAPTER VI. The fibres, however, have a nature between nerve and vein ; but some of them have the moisture of lymph, and tend from the nerves to the veins, and from them to the nerves x. Fibres, therefore, are inherent in the blood of most animals ; but there are no fibres in the blood of the stag, the deer, the buffalo, and certain other animals. Hence, their blood is not congealed in a manner similar to that of other animals ; but the blood of stags is congealed similar to that of hates. The congelation, however, of the blood of both these is not of a firm consistence, like that of other animals, but is fluid, so as to resemble milk without the coagulum. But the blood of the buffalo is congealed in a greater degree ; for it is similar, or not much less congealed than the blood of sheep. After this manner, therefore, vein, nerve, and fibre, subsist. CHAPTER VII. All the bones, likewise, in animals, depend from one bone, and are in continuity with each other, in the same manner as the veins ; but there is no bone which subsists itself by itself. The spine of the back, however, is the principal in all animals that have bones. But the spine is composed from vertebrae, and extends from the head as far as to the hips. All the vertebrae, therefore, are perforated. But the bone of the head, which is called the cranium, is in continuity with the last vertebrae ; and the place in which one part of the cranium is inserted in the other is called the suture. The cranium, however, does not subsist similarly in all animals ; for in some, as in the dog, the cranium consists of only one bone [without any sutures] ; but in others, as in man,

text: THE HISTORY OF ANIMALS. BOOK III. 87 The dolphin, also, has bones, but not a spine. But other sanguineous animals either have bones not very different from those of the animals hitherto enumerated, as birds; or, though they are without bones, they have something analagous to them, as fishes. For, of fishes, such as are viviparous have a cartilaginous spine, as is the case with the fishes called selache, or of the cartilaginous kind ; but such of them as are oviparous have a thorn, which subsists in them in the same manner as the bone of the back in quadrupeds. It is, however, the peculiarity of certain fishes, that within the flesh they have separate thorns. Ser pents, also, accord with fishes in this, that in the place of bones they have the spine of the back. With respect, however, to oviparous qua drupeds, the larger among them [as the crocodile] have in the back something which is more similar to bone than a thorn, but the less [as the lizard] have in the back something which more resembles a thorn than bone. But all animals that are sanguineous have a spine, which is either bony or thorny ; and the other bones that have been enumerated are inherent in some animals, and in others not, just as they have certain members, or are deprived of them. For such animals as have not legs and arms, are also deprived of the bones of the legs and arms ; but those which have these parts, or what are ana logous to them, have also bones corresponding to such parts, which differ in the more and the less, or in the analogous. The particulars, therefore, respecting the bones, subsist after this manner in animals. CHAPTER VIII. Cartilage, however, is of the same nature with the bones, but differs from them in the more and the less ; and as a bone when cut off is not increased, this is also the case with a cartilage. But the cartilages in sanguineous

text: THE HISTORY OF ANIMALS. BOOK III. 88 sanguineous animals that are terrestrial and viviparous are not hollow, nor have they marrow within them, in the same manner as there is in bones. In cartilaginous aquatic animals, however, the cartilage which is under the back, in the place of the spine, is hollow, and full of a certain moisture which is analogous to marrow. But in viviparous and pedestrious animals there are cartilages about the ears and the nostrils, and about certain extremities of the bones. CHAPTER IX. Again, there are other genera of parts, which have neither the same nature with these, nor are remote from them ; such, for instance, as nails, the horn of the foot, whether the foot is one entire hoof, or is cloven, the horns of the head ; and, besides these, the beaks of birds. For these are flexible and fissile, but no bone is either of these, but is alone frangible. The colours, likewise, of horns, nails, and hoofs, follow the colour of the skin and the hair. For the horns and hoofs of animals that have a black skin are black, but of those that have a white skin are white ; and the like takes place in the intermediate co lours. The nails, also, subsist after the same manner. But the teeth are of the nature of the bones ; and hence in black men, such as Ethio pians, and the like, the teeth and the bones are white; but the nails are black, in the same manner as the whole of the skin. Of horns, however, the greater part is hollow from the root, which is at the mouth, and inwardly proceeds from the head; but the extre mity of the horn is solid and simple. And the horns of stags alone are solid throughout, and multifidous. Other horned animals, likewise, do not change their horns ; but the stag alone changes them every year, unless he is castrated. text: THE, HISTORY OF ANIMALS. BOOK Til. 90 CHAPTER XL The nature of the hairs, however, is fissile. But hairs differ from each other, in the more and the less ; and some are so gradually in durated, that they no longer resemble hairs, but thorns, such as the hairs of the land hedge-hog. The like, also, takes place in nails ; for the genus of nails in some animals is so hard, that it does not in any respect differ from bones. Man, however, has the thinnest skin of all animals, in proportion to the magnitude of his body. But in all skin there is a mucous vis cosity ; in some, indeed, less, but in others more. Thus, for instance, in the skin of oxen there is a mucous moisture, from which they make glue ; and in some places, glue is made from fishes. The skin, also, when cut off, is of itself deprived of sense ; and this is especially the case with the skin of the head, because, between this and the bone, [or cranium,] nothing of flesh intervenes. But, whenever the skin is by itself, if it is cut, it does not coalesce ; as in the thin parts of the cheek, prepuce, and the eye-lids. In all animals, likewise, the skin is continued through the whole of the body, so that its continuity is not interrupted, except where there is a natural evaporation through the pores, and where the mouth and nails are situated. All san guineous animais, therefore, have skin, but all have not hairs, but those only of whom mention has been already made. The hair, however, changes its colour in old age, and in men be comes whiter ; but in other animals it becomes whiter indeed, yet not very apparently so, except in the horse. Hair, also, becomes white at the extremity, [which is the most distant from the skin ;] but most hair that is hoary becomes white immediately ; from which it is evi- dent.

text: THE HISTORY OF ANIMALS. BOOK III. 92 and those, also, are impotent who are without hairs on the private parts. Other hairs, therefore, are increased by a certain law of nature, either more or less, especially those in the head ; in the next place, those in the beard, and particularly those that are more thin. In some persons, likewise, the eyebrows are so thick with hair, when they be come old, that they ought to be shaved ; and this is because the mois ture, from which the eyebrows are produced, proceeds from the com missures of the bones, which commissures in old age are loosened, and, therefore, a greater quantity of moisture pervades through them. But the hairs of the eyelids are not increased ; and they fall off Avhen ve nery begins to takes place, and are more abundant in those that are more addicted to venery. They also become hoary very slowly. While we are growing, also, the hairs, if they are plucked out, are re-produced, but when we no longer grow, they are no longer re-pro duced. All hair, too, has a viscous moisture at the root, and there fore, if the hair, as soon as it is plucked out, touches any thing light by its root, it adheres to, and draws it. But animals, which are covered with hairs of many colours, have also a variety of colour in their skin, and in the skin of their tongue. With respect to the beard, however, it happens that some have the chin and upper lip hairy, but others have these parts smooth, and have the cheeks covered with thick hair ; and those that have a bipartite chin and lip, are less accustomed to become hoary. The hair, likewise, is increased in certain diseases, and especially in those of the consumptive kind, in old age, and in dead bodies, and instead of being soft becomes harder. The very same things, also, happen with respect to the nails. In the libidinous, how ever, the connascent hairs more rapidly fall off, but those of posterior origin are more swiftly produced. Those, likewise, whose veins are more tumid than is proper, are less subject to baldness; and some when afflicted with this disease have abundance of hair. Hair, how ever, when cut off, is not by this mean increased, but growing from the root becomes longer. The scales, also, of fishes become harder and thicker ; and in those that are slender and old, they become more hard.

Other animals, therefore, have hair alone in the prone part, [i. e. in the back,] but they have not any in the supine part, [i. e. in the breast and belly,] and they have also hairs externally, and not internally; but the hare alone has hairs within the mouth, in the cheek, and under the feet. Farther still, the fish called mysticetus has no teeth in its mouth, but has hairs similar to those of a swine, in the place of teeth. Hairs, therefore, when they are cut, grow from the root, and not from the place where they are cut ; but feathers if they are cut? neither grow from the root, nor from the part where they are cut, but fall off. Those animals, also, that have continued wings, and not com posed from many feathers, as bees, and the like, have not their wings re-produced if they are plucked out ; nor is the sting of the bee re produced when it is ejected ; but bees when they loose their sting shortly after die. CHAPTER XIII. There are, likewise, membranes in all sanguineous animals. But a membrane is similar to a strong and thin skin; and it is also of a dif ferent genus from skin, since it is neither fissile, nor capable of being stretched. About each of the bones, however, and each of the vis cera, there is a membrane, both in larger and smaller animals; but the membranes are immanifest in smaller animals, because in these they are very thin and small. The largest, however, of the mem branes are the two which are about the brain; of which the superior, and

But a mem brane when cut does not coalesce and become reunited ; and bones when deprived of their membranes mortify. CHAPTERS XIV. and XV. The epiploon, or caul, is also a membrane. And all sanguineous animals have an epiploon ; but in some, indeed, it is fat, and in others lean. In animals, likewise, that are viviparous, and have teeth on both sides, the epiploon originates, and depends from the middle belly, where a certain suture, as it were, exists of the epiploon with the belly ; and in animals which have only teeth on one side, the epiploon in a similar manner depends from the greater belly. The bladder, likewise, is indeed membranous, but it is a membrane of a different genus, since it can be extended. All animals, however, have not a bladder, but all viviparous animals have it; and of ovi parous animals the tortoise alone. The bladder, likewise, when cut, does not coalesce, except in that part which is called the neck of the bladder, unless very rarely ; for a thing of this kind has happened. In the dead, indeed, no moisture pervades to the bladder; but in living animals, not only moisture, but also dry substances, descend into the bladder, from which the disease called the stone is produced. text: THE HISTORY OF ANIMALS. BOOK III. 98 With respect to the viscera, likewise, animals are especially fat aboufe the kidneys. But the left kidney is always more fat than the right ; and though the kidneys should be very fat, yet there is always some part in the middle of them which is not fat. The kidneys, however, of animals which have suet, are more fat than the kidneys of those that have fat, and this is especially the case with the kidneys of sheep ; for when the kidneys are entirely covered with fat this animal dies. Sheep, however, become fat about the kidneys through feeding abun dantly, as is the case with the sheep in Sicily, about Leontium; and, on this account, the shepherds in that country lead the sheep to pasture late in the day, in order that they may take less nutriment. CHAPTERS XVIII. and XIX. The part, however, about the pupil of the eye is common to all ani mals; for all such as have the pupil in the eyes, and have not hard eyes, have it composed from suet, and not from fat. Fat animals, also, both male and female, are less prolific ; and they become more fat when they are elderly than when they are young, but this is especially the case when the body, having obtained its proper length and breadth, begins to be increased in depth. With respect to the blood, also, it subsists as follows ; for this is most necessary, and most common to all sanguineous animals, and is not adventitious, but is inherent in all animals whose body is not in a cor rupted state. All the blood, however, is contained in what are called the veins, as in a vessel, but in nothing else, except in the heart alone. In some men, also, after puberty, a small quantity of milk is induced, and from some by sucking a great quantity has been produced. A fatness, likewise, is inherent in milk, which in coagulation becomes of an oily nature, [and is called butter.] In Sicily, however, and other regions, where there are a great quantity of she-goats, they mingle the milk of goats with that of sheep, [for the purpose of making cheese.] But milk is espe cially coagulated, not only that which contains the greatest quantity of cheese, but also that which contains the driest cheese. Some ani mals, therefore, have more milk than is sufficient to nourish their off spring. The milk, also, of sheep and goats is most useful for the purpose of making cheese and reserving ; and next to this, the milk of the cow. But the milk of the mare and the ass are mingled in order to make Phrygian cheese. There is, however, more cheese in the milk of the cow than in the milk of the she-goat. For shepherds say, that from an amphora of goat's milk twenty cheeses wanting one are made, for an obolus a piece; but that thirty were made from an amphora of cow's milk. The milk, however, of those animals which have as much as is sufficient to nourish their offspring is useless for the pur pose of making cheese ; and of this kind are all those animals that have more than two mammæ ; for the milk of none of these is either abundant or adapted to make cheese. But the juice and coagulum of the fig coagulate milk. Wool, therefore, imbued with the juice of the fig is washed with a little milk; for this milk, being mingled with a greater quantity of milk, coagulates the whole. CHAP.

There is, also, another genus, which is as small indeed as crabs, biit in form resembles lobsters. All these, therefore, as we have before observed, have externally that which is solid and testa ceous in the place of skin ; but internally that which is fleshy. They have the supine part of the body, however, [i. e. the belly] distin guished by certain tablets, into which the females deposit their eggs. With respect to feet, indeed, locusts have five on each side, together with their ultimate claws ; and, in a similar manner, crabs have ten feet, together with their claws. But of squills, those that are crooked have five feet on each side, which verge to the head, and are acute. They have, also, five others on each side, at the belly, the extremities of which are broad. They have not, however, tablets in the supine parts ; but in the prone parts [i. e. in the back] they resemble locusts. But the contrary takes place in the crangones ; for they have on each side four feet, near the head, and three other thin feet consequent to these, and the rest of the body, which in the greater part is without feet. The feet, likewise, of all the above-mentioned animals, are bent obliquely [i. e. towards the body of the animals ;] in the same man ner as the feet of insects ; and those which have claws bend them in wardly, [so that the cavity is towards the body.] The locust, also5 has a tail, and five fins on each side ; but the squills which are called crooked, have a tail, and four fins on each side. The crangones, like wise, have a tail, and fins on each side of it. But the middle fins of the squills of each genus are thorny ; except that the middle fins of the cr6bked squills are broad, but those of the crangones acute. The crab, however, alone, of animals of this kind, is without a tail ; and the body, indeed, of locusts and squillæ is long, but that of crabs is round. The male locust, however, differs from the female [in many re spects.] For the first foot of the female is bipartite, but that of the male is simple. With respect to the sins, also, in the supine part 01 the body, the female locust has large fins, but they diminish as they q approach

text: THE HISTORY OF ANIMALS. BOOK IV. 116 ferences of crustaceous animals. Locusts, therefore, as we have be- fore observed, have two large and hollow teeth, in which there is a juice similar to the moisture called mytis; and between the teeth there is a small piece of flesh, which is a species of tongue. After the mouth, also, there is a short oesophagus, and a membranous belly, adhering to this ; and in the mouth of this belly there are three teeth, two of which are opposite to each other ; but the third is below the other two. But the intestine, beginning and proceeding from the side of the belly, is simple, and of an equal thickness throughout, as far as to the egress of the excrement. Locusts, squills, and crabs, therefore, have these parts. Farther still, locusts have, also, an ave nue, which depending from the breast is extended, as far as to the egress of the excrement. But this, indeed, is the matrix of the female locust, and in the male is the receptacle of the genital seed. This avenue, however, is situated near the cavity of the flesh, so that the flesh is between this cavity and the intestine. For the intestine is constituted in the convex part, but the avenue is near the cavity; just as they subsist in quadrupeds. Indeed, this avenue in the male differs in no respect from that of the female ; for both are thin and white, and contain in themselves a pallid moisture, and both, also, are suspended from the breast. But after this manner squills have eggs, and certain spirals. The male, however, differs from the female in having in the flesh of the breast two white parts, which in colour and figure resemble the proboscis of the cuttle-fish. But these white parts are contorted in the same manner as the trumpet called mecon, and they derive their origin from the acetabula or joints, which are under the last feet. The breast, however, contains, also, red flesh, and is of of a sanguineous colour; but it is viscous to the touch, and does not resemble flesh [in general.] Near those two white parts, also, which are contorted like a trumpet, there is another spiral of the thickness of a string, under which there are two sandy substances, adhering to the intestine, and destined to the reception of the genital seed. These parts, therefore, the male possesses ; but the female squill lays eggs of a red

text: BOOK IV. THE HISTORY OF ANIMALS. 117 red colour, which are involved in a thin membrane, and are annexed to the belly, and each side of the intestine, as far as to the fleshy parts. These, therefore, are the parts as well internal as external of crustaceous animals. CHAPTER III. It happens, however, that the internal and external parts of sangui neous animals have [appropriate] appellations, [but the genus of exanguious animals wants many of those parts with which sanguine ous animals are indued.] For all sanguineous animals have viscera, but this is not the case with any exanguious animal. A belly, however, mouth, and intestine, are common both to exanguious and sanguine ous animals. With respect to the claws and feet of crabs, indeed, we have already shown the manner in which they subsist. For the most part, however, all of them have the right claAV larger and stronger than the left. We have, also, before spoken about the eyes of crabs, and shown that most of them look obliquely. But with respect to the mass of the body, the head, and the other parts of the trunk, are one indistinct whole. The eyes, however, are not in all of them in the same position ; but some of them have the eyes obliquely situated under the prone part of the back, and very much distant from each other; and others, as the he racleotic crabs, and those called maiœ, have the eyes in the middle, and near to each other. Under the eyes is the mouth, and in it there are two teeth, in the same manner as in locusts, except that the teeth of the crab are not round, but long. The teeth, also, of crabs are co vered with two valves, as it were, between which there is a certain fleshy part

text: THE HISTORY OF ANIMALS. 118 BOOK IV part, which is used by them instead of a tongue, in the same manner as in locusts. They receive water, therefore, in the mouth by removing those valves, and return it by the superior avenues of the mouth, shut ting the valves through which it entered. These avenues, however, are immediately under the eyes; and when the water is received, they shut their mouth with both the valves, and thus afterwards eject the water they had received. After the teeth a stomach follows, so very small that the belly seems immediately to succeed after the mouth. But from the middle of the belly an intestine originates, which is simple and slender; and the intestine is terminated under the external part of the covering, as was before observed [in Chap. 2.] Within the cavity, also, or alvus of the crab, there is a pale [excrementitious] liquor, and toge ther with this certain small, oblong, white substances, and other red substances, variegated with spots. The male, however, differs from the female crab in magnitude, thickness, and covering. For the fe male has a covering [at the avenue of the intestine] larger, more dis tant, and more hairy, as is, also, the case in female locusts. After this manner, therefore, the parts of crustaceous animals subsist. CHAPTER IV. With respect to testaceous animals, however, snails, whether of the land or the sea, and all such as are called shell-fish, and besides these, the genus of sea hedge-hogs, if they have a fleshy substance have it similarly to crustaceous animals, for they have it inwardly ; but they have the shell externally, and inwardly they contain nothing hard [and analogous to bones.] They have, however, many differ ences with respect to themselves, both as to their shells, and the inter- nal

text: BOOK IV. THE HISTORY OF ANIMALS. 121 and hard. And as ox-flies, and horse-flies, pierce with their proboscis the skin of quadrupeds, in like manner these testaceous animals perfor ate the shells of others on which they feed. After the mouth immediately follows the belly, which resembles the craw of a bird, and is similar to the belly of the sea-snail. But in the inferior part they have two white and firm substances, similar to mam mæ ; such as are, also, found in the cuttle-fish, except that these are of a firmer consistence. After the belly, however, there is a long twofold stomach, which is extended as far as to the mecon [i. e. to the mem brane containing the excrements;] which membrane is in the bottom [of the navel.] These things, therefore, are manifest in the purple, and buccina, in the spiral of the shell. But the intestine follows the stomach, the whole of which is simple as far as to its egress. The be ginning, however, of the intestine is about the spiral of the mecony than which it is broader. For the mecon is as it were, for the most part, in all testaceous animals, full of an excrementitious matter. But after wards, the intestine being inflected upward, tends again to the fleshy parts, and terminates near the head ; from which place all turbinated testaceous animals, as well terrestrial as marine, eject their excrements. In large sea-snails, however, under the belly, a membrane is annexed to the stomach, from which a long and white avenue extends, and which is similar in colour to those fleshy parts which have the form ol mammæ. This avenue, also, has incisures similar to those which are in the egg of the locust, except that the colour of this avenue is white. but the egg of the locust is red. This avenue, however, has no egress, but is contained in the narrow cavity of a thin membrane. From the intestine, also, certain black and rough parts extend downward in a continued series, such as are in the tortoise, except that they are less black. Other snails, however, have these parts white, except that they are less in smaller snails. The univalves, also, and bivalves, are partly similar to snails, and partly dissimilar. For they have a head, horns, and a mouth, and a certain part which has the form of a tongue ; yet in less animals of this kind these parts, on account of their smallness, are immanifest ; and in 11 such

Thevhave, also, two slender red horns, and two small eyes under these, which do not recede inwardly, nor incline, like the eyes of crabs, but are direct. Under the eyes, like- wise, is the mouth, which is surrounded, as it were, with numerous capil- laments. And consequent to these are two bifurcated feet, by which they convey food to their mouth. There are, also, two other feet on each side, and a third small foot. The inferior part, however, of the thorax, is wholly soft, and within it a certain matter of a pale colour is contain- ed. One avenue, likewise, extends from the mouth to the belly ; but the avenue by which the excrementis emitted is not apparent; and the feet and the thorax are hard, indeed, but less so than in crabs. They do not, how- ever, adhere to the shell in the same manner as the purple and the buc- cina, but they easily liberate themselves from it. Those small crabs, also, that dwell in turbinated shells are longer than the neritæ, i.e. than those that dwell in sea-shells (ev roa vngnatf.) Though, however, the small crabs called neritæ are different from the turbinated kind, and, also, differ from them in length, yet in other respects they are not dissimilar to them. For in the neritæ, of the bifurcated feet which are under the mouth, the right foot is small, but the left is large ; and, therefore, in walking they more frequently use the left than the right foot. Among the shell-fish, however, which after the manner of testaceous animals adhere to the shell, there is one which they call the little lame fish. But the neritæ have a smooth, large, and round shell, and a form simi- lar to the buccina, except that they have not the mecon black, like the buccina, but red- They, also, firmly adhere to the middle of the shell. In fair weather, therefore, they leave their shell, and search for food ; but when the wind blows [violently] the small crabs betake themselves to rocks, and there quietly remain. But the neritæ adhere to rocks after the manner of the lepas, and the aporrhais, and others of the like kind. AU these, however, adhere to rocks, by removing the shell which serves them for a covering. For what both shells are to the bivalves that one shell is to those of the turbinated kind. Within the shell, however, there is a fleshy substance, and in this there is a mouth. The like, also, takes place in the aporrhais, in the purple, and all such r 2 like

THE HISTORY OF ANIMALS. 125 however, there are a great number of black parts, which are extended as far as to the external avenue, [or excretory duct], but are uncon joined with each other, and are separated by certain limits. Those sea hedge-hogs, likewise, that are esculent, are moved more frequently, and more rapidly, which is always indicated by their bristles, [to which some extraneous matter constantly adheres.] All of them, therefore, have eggs, but some are very small, and not sit to be eaten. It happens, however, that what are called the head and mouth in the hedge-hog are in the bottom part; but the part through which the excrement is emitted is upward ; and the very same thing happens in all testaceous animals of the turbinated kind, and in the lepas. For these animals search for their food in the ground, so that their mouth is towards the earth, where their nutriment is ; but the excrement is in the upward part, and in the prone parts of the shell, [i. e. in the parts directed towards the heavens.] The hedge-hog, also, has five teeth, which are inwardly hollow ; and in the middle of these there is a fleshy substance, which performs the office of a tongue. After this follows the stomach, and then the belly, which is divided into five parts, and is full of excrement. All the cavities of the belly, likewise, unite in one at the egress of the excrement, i. e. at the avenue where the shell of the hedge-hog is perforated. What are called eggs, how ever, are contained under the belly in another membrane, and these are equal in number in all of them; for they are five, and are, there fore, an odd number. But above the eggs are those black parts, which depend from the root of the teeth, and ape bitter, and not fit to be eaten. In many animals, however, a thing of this kind, or that which is analogous to it, happens ; for it happens in tortoises, in the hedge frog, in the common frog, in turbinated shell-fish, and in the mollia. But eggs of this kind differ in colour, and are either entirely unfit to be eaten, or more so than others. The body of the hedge-hog, therefore, is continued from the beginning to the end, but resembles a lamp, which is without a circular covering.. The hedge-hog, also, uses his prickles instead of feet for supporting himself, and being moved on these, he clianges his place. CHAP.

Those animals, however, which are called tethya, [and in Latin are by some denominated vertibula, or calli, and which, by following the etymology of the Greek word, may be called mammillae,] have a cer- tain most peculiar nature ; for the whole body of these animals alone is concealed in a shell ; but the shell is of a substance between skin and shell, and on this account may be cut like a hard hide. This ani- mal, therefore, adheres by its shell to rocks. But it has two avenues, distant from each other, very small, and not easily seen, through which it emits and receives moisture ; for it has no apparent excrement, like other testaceous animals, such as that which is in the hedge^hog, or in that animal which is called mecon. When, however, they are opened, in the first place, they are found to have a nervous membrane about the shelly part, and in this the fleshy substance of this animal is con- tained, but it does not resemble the flesh of other animals. This flesh however, is similar in all the tethya. This flesh, also, adheres in two places to the membrane and the skin obliquely ; and where it adheres, it is in each place narrower. In these places, likewise, there are two avenues, through which these animals receive and eject nutriment and moisture, just as if one of these avenues was a mouth, but the other the passage through which the excrement is emitted. And one of these avenues, indeed, is thicker, but the other thinner, but within these is a cavity on each side, between which a certain small conti- nued substance intervenes, and in one of the cavities moisture is pro duced. They have not, however, any other part, either organic, or destined

text: THE HISTORY OF ANIMALS. BOOK IV. 127 destined to sensation, nor is any excrement found in them, as it is in other testaceous animals, as we have before observed. The colour, also, of this animal is partly pallid, and partly red. The sea-nettle, also, constitutes a peculiar genus of animals. It ad heres, however, to rocks in the same manner as some testaceous ani mals, but is sometimes liberated from them. It, likewise, has no shell, but the whole of its body is fleshy. But it is sensitive, and seizes the hand, to which also it adheres, [of any one that touches it,] in the same manner as the polypus with its arms, so as to cause the flesh of the hand to swell. It has, also, a mouth in the middle of its body, and lives in a rock just as testaceous animals live in a shell. It, likewise, takes, as if it were a hand, any little fish that may fall in its way; and if it meets with any thing esculent it eats it. A certain genus, also, cf the sea-nettle is liberated from rocks, and eats the hedge-hogs and cockles that may fall in its way. These animals, however, do not appear to have any excrement, but in this respect they resemble plants. There are, also, two genera of sea-nettles ; one of which, indeed, is less, and more eatable; but the other is large and hard, such as are those which are produced about Chalcis. In winter, therefore, their flesh is firm, and on this account they are then sought after, and are eatable ; but in summer they are dissolved. For then they become fluid, are rapidly dispersed by the touch, and in short cannot be pluck ed. But when they suffer very much from the heat, they betake themselves into the more interior parts of rocks. And thus much con cerning the parts, as well exterior as interior, of the mollia, and of crustaceous and testaceous animals. CHAP.

text: THE HISTORY OF ANIMALS. BOOK IV. 130 the intestine, which in most insects is straight and simple, as far as to its exit; but in some few it has convolutions. No insect, however, has either viscera, or fat, as neither has any other exanguious animal. But some, of them have a belly, and from this the remaining intestine is either simple, or convolved, as in the locust. The grasshopper, also, is the only insect, and, indeed, is the only animal, that has not a mouth; but, instead of a mouth, has along, compact, and undivided part, simi lar to that tongue-like substance which is in animals that have a sting behind. Through this part the grasshopper is alone nourished with dew ; but it has no excrement in the belly. There are, however, many species of these insects, and they differ in magnitude and parvitudc. The grasshoppers, also, which are called canorous, are divided under the transverse septum, in which they have a visible membrane, which small grasshoppers have not. There are, however, certain peculiar animals in the sea which, be cause they are rare, cannot be referred to any certain genus. For now some experienced fishermen say, that they have seen in the sea ani mals resembling black and round pieces of wood, of an equal thick ness; and also other animals resembling shields, of a red colour, and furnished with numerous wings. They, likewise, report that they Jhave seen some animals similar in form and magnitude to the puden dum of a man, except that, instead of testicles, they have two wings ; and that such an animal was once caught by the top of the instru ment [used by fishermen,] which consists ,of many hooks. After this manner therefore, the external and internal parts of all animals in each genus, as well peculiar as common, subsist. chap.

text: THE HISTORY OF ANIMALS. BOOK IV. 134 sense of smelling. For the greater part of them is only to be caught with a recent bait ; and all fishes are not caught with the same baits, but with particular baits, which they know by the smell. Some, indeed, are caught by fetid baits; as, for instance, the stock-fish by dung. Again, many fishes live in caverns ; and fishermen when they wish to catch them anoint the mouth of the cave with briny odours, by which the fishes are soon allured [and taken]. After this manner, also, eels are caught. For fishermen, in order to catch them, use a certain vessel con- taining brine, in the mouth of which they place the collar of a bow-net. In short, all fishes are allured by the smell of roasted flesh ; and hence fishermen roasting the flesh of the cuttle-fish, use the smell of it as a bait -, for fishes are thus more easily caught. They also say that fishermen put into their nets roasted polypi, on no other account than for the sake of the smell. Farther still, the fishes called ruades, when the lotion or the filth of fishes is discharged, fly from it, in consequence of smelling the fetid odour. They, likewise, say that fishes quickly smell the blood of those of their own species. This, indeed, is evident by their flying to distant places when the blood of fishes is poured forth. And, in short, if putrid baits are put into the nets, fishes will neither be will ing to enter into nor approach the nets; but if the bait consists of fresh roasted meat, they will immediately tend to it, though at a dis tance, and enter into the nets. What has been said, however, is especi ally evident in dolphins. For these have no apparent sensorium of hearing, but they are caught in consequence of being oppressed with a heaviness in the head from sound, as was before observed. Neither, likewise, have they any apparent sensorium of smelling ; and yet they smell acutely. That these animals, therefore, have all the senses is evident ; but the remaining genera of animals have a fourfold division, which compre hends the mollia, crustaceous and testaceous animals, and besides these insects. Of these, however, the mollia, crustaceous animals, and insects, have all the senses ; for they have sight, the smell, and the taste. For insects, as well those that have as those that are without wings, perceive at a distance. Thus, for instance, bees, and the cnipes [a kind of gnats have

text: BOOK IV. THE HISTORY OF ANIMALS. 135 have a sensible perception of honey ; for they perceive it at a distance, as knowing it by the smell ; and many insects perish from the smell of sulphur. Farther still, if the powder of sulphur and wild marjoram is sprinkled over the habitation of ants, they leave their holes ; and the greater part of such kind of insects fly from the odour of the burnt horn of a stag ; but they especially avoid the fume of storax. The cuttle-fish, likewise, the polypi, and the lobster, are caught by baits ; and the polypus so pertinaciously adheres to a bait, as to suffer himself to be cut in pieces rather than be divulsed from it. If, however, any one presents to him the herb flea-bane, it is said, that as soon as he smells it, he will drop the bait. The like, also, takes place with respect to the taste. For sometimes insects pursue a different food, and all of them are not delighted with the same sapours. Thus, for instance, bees do not approach to any thing fetid, but to what is sweet ; and the conops, or gnat, does not fly to any thing sweet, but to what is acid. To have a sensible perception, nowever, by the touch is, as we have before observed, common to all animals. But testaceous animals have, indeed, the smell and the taste ; and this is evident from the baits by which they are caught ; as, for instance, in the purple fish. For this animal is allured by putrid substances, and approaches to a bait of this kind, as having a sensible perception of it at a distance. That testaceous animals, also, have a sensation of sapours is evident from the same arguments ; for each of them is de lighted with the sapour of those substances to which it is allured by the smell. And again, such as have a mouth receive either pleasure or pain from the contact of sapours. With respect, however, to the sight and hearing of testaceous ani mals, nothing stable nor very apparent can be asserted. But the so lenes are seen to withdraw themselves, and to subside lower, when they perceive the iron instrument by which they are caught ; for a small part of their body only is seen, but the rest is as if it were in a place of retreat. And with respect to cockles, if any one presents his finger to them they open and shut themselves, as having the sense of sight. Aad

text: BOOK IV. THE HISTORY OF ANIMALS. 137 likewise, the case with flies, bees, and all the rest, in consequence of raising and depressing that membrane when they fly. For [such] sound is produced by the attrition of the internal air. But crickets pro duce a sound through the attrition of the legs by which they leap. Neither any one of the mollia, however, nor any crustaceous animal has a voice, or produces any natural sound. Fishes, also, are without voice, since they have neither the trachea nor the pharynx. Those, however, that are said to be vocal emit certain sounds and noises, as the fish called the lyre and the chromis; for they emit as it were a certain grunting ; and this is, also, the case with that fish, in the river Achelous, called the wild-boar ; and with the chalcis and cuckow. For the first of these fishes produces a kind of whistling ; but the second emits a sound similar to that of the bird called a cuckow ; whence, also, it derives its name. All these fishes, however, that appear to utter a voice, pro duce it either by the attrition of the more rigid gills which they possess, or of the air which they contain in the cavity of their belly. For in each of these there is a hot air, the attrition and motion of which pro duce sounds. Those cartilaginous fishes, also, called the selache ap pear to produce a stridulous sound. These, however, cannot be properly said to have a voice, but to produce a sound. For cockles Avhen they are seen floating on the surface of the water, which they call flying, make a crashing noise ; and this is, also, the case with the swallows of the sea: For these fly high, and do not touch the sea, their wings be ing broad and long. As, therefore, the sound produced by the wings of flying birds is not voice, so neither is the sound produced by any thing of the above-mentioned kind. The dolphin, likewise, produces a stri dulous sound, and murmurs when he comes into the air, yet not in a manner similar to the before-mentioned fishes. For the sound emitted by the dolphin is voice ; since he has lungs and a trachea, but his tongue is not loose, and he has no lips, so that he cannot produce articulate voice. But of those animals which have a tongue and lungs, such as are oviparous and quadrupeds, emit a voice, which is, however, feeble. And some, indeed, produce a hissing sound, as serpents ; but others a slender and feeble voice ; and others a small hissing, as tortoises. The t frog,

text: BOOK IV. THE HISTORY OF ANIMALS. 139 tongue. The tongue, also, at first is imperfect, and it is some time before it is detached ; so that children, for the most part, lisp and stutter. Voice and speech, also, differ according to places. Voice, there- fore, is, indeed, especially manifest by acuteness, and gravity ; nor is there any specific difference in [inarticulate] voices of the same genera. But the difference in articulate voice, which may be called as it were speech, differs according to places in different animals, and, also, in animals belonging to the same genus. Thus, with respect to partridges, the voice of some of them repeats the syllables cac, cac, but of others tri, tri. And some small birds, if they are taken from their parents, so that they cannot be educated by them, do not emit the same voice as their parents, but become accustomed to the manners and singing of other birds. A nightingale, also, has been seen instructing her young in singing ; so that speech and voice are not similarly natural, but the former may be acquired by instruction. Men, likewise, have, indeed, the same voice, but not the same speech. The elephant, how ver, is vocal, not through the nose [or proboscis], but emits a windy voice through the mouth, such as men emit when they breathe, and at the same time speak ; but with his proboscis he emits a hoarse sound, which resembles the sound of a trumpet. With respect, however, to the sleep and wakefulness of animals, it is obvious to sense that all such as are pedestrious, and sanguineous sleep, and are wakeful ; for all such as have eyelids sleep by closing them. Again, not only men are seen to dream, but, also, horses, dogs, T 2 and

text: THE HISTORY OF ANIMALS. BOOK IV. 141 conceal themselves while they sleep in the sand. They are detected, however, by the figure of the sand, and are caught by striking them with a trident. With this instrument, likewise, the sea-wolf, the gold fish, the mullet, and others of the same kind, are caught in the day, in consequence of being asleep ; but it does not appear that any of these are caught with the trident, unless they are asleep. But those cartilaginous fishes called selache sometimes sleep so profoundly as to be caught by the hand. The dolphin, however, the whale, and such fishes as have a pipe [through which they eject the water], sleep, ele vating this pipe, through which they respire, above the sea, and gently moving their fins. Some, also, assert that they have heard the dolphin snore. The mollia, likewise, sleep after the same manner as fishes ; and similarly with these, crustaceous animals. That insects, also, sleep, is evident from such indications as the fol lowing : For they are sometimes manifestly quiet and without motion, and this is especially evident in bees ; for by night they are still, and cease to hum. And this is manifest in those insects with which we are especially conversant, [viz. in flies.] For they are quiet by night, not only because they do not then acutely see, for all animals that have hard eyes see obscurely, but when near the light of a lamp they are nevertheless seen to be quiet. Man, however, dreams the most of all animals. And infants, in deed, and very young children do not dream ; but, for the most part, children begin to dream about the fourth or fifth year of their age. There are, also, some men and women that have never known a dream. Some of these, however, as they have advanced in years have begun to dream, after which a change has taken place in their body ; in some, indeed, the change terminating in death, but in others in disease. Ajid thus much concerning sense, and sleep, and wakefulness. CHAP

text: THE HISTORY OF ANIMALS. BOOK V. CHAPTER I. IN the preceding books, therefore, we have spoken concerning the in ternal and external parts of animals ; and farther still, concerning their senses, voice, and sleep, and the difference between the males and the females. Hence it remains, that we should now direct our attention to their generation, and in the first place discuss such particulars as are first. The generations, however, of animals are many, and possess much variety ; being, indeed, in one respect dissimilar, but in another similar, to each other. Since, also, the genera of animals was first di vided by us, we must now endeavour that the speculation shall be formed after the same manner ; except that, then, in speculating about the parts, we made the beginning from man, but now we shall speak u about
name: Aristotle

title: The History of Animals of Aristotle, and his Treatise on Physiognomy, translated from the Greek. By Thomas Taylor
text: THE HISTORY OF ANIMALS. BOOK V 146 about man in the last place, because the generation of man requires the most ample discussion. But we shall first begin from testaceous animals ; afterwards speak of such as are crustaceous ; and then dis cuss the rest after this manner, in an orderly series. And these are the mollia and insects. After these, we shall direct our attention to the genus of fishes, both the viviparous and the oviparous ; and then con sider the genus of birds. And, in the next place, we shall speak con cerning the generation of pedestrious animals, as well viviparous as oviparous. But some quadrupeds are viviparous, and man is the only biped that is viviparous. A common circumstance, therefore, happens in the generation of ani mals, as well as in the generation of plants. For of plants some are generated from the seed of other plants, but others are generated spon taneously from analogous causes. And of these some receive their nutriment from the earth, but others are ingenerated in other plants, as we have shown in the speculation concerning plants. Thus, also, with respect to animals, some indeed are generated from animals, ac cording to an alliance of form ; but others have a spontaneous origin, and not from kindred natures. And of these some are generated from putrid earth and plants, as happens to be the case with many insects ; but others are generated in animals themselves, and from the excre ments in the parts of animals. Animals, however, which are generated from kindred animals, if there is the distinction in them of male and female, are generated from coition. But in the genus of fishes, some are generated neither male nor female, and though they accord in genus yet differ in spe cies from other fishes, and some are entirely peculiar. There are, also, some fishes, among Avhich there are females without males, and from which, in the same manner as in birds, windy eggs are produced. All such eggs of birds, however, are unprolific, but the nature of these birds is able to accomplish the generation of an egg, unless some other mode of communication with the males happens to them ; which particulars, however, will be more acurately discussed hereafter. But it happens to certain fishes, when they generate spontaneous eggs, that animals

text: THE HISTORY OF ANIMALS. BOOK V. 148 ward, as lions, hares, and lynxes, copulate backward*; and with re spect to hares, the female frequently gets on the back of the male. The mode of copulation, likewise, is the same in the greater part of other animals. For the usual mode of copulation with most quadru peds is for the male to get on the female ; and this mode is adopted by the whole tribe of birds. There are, however, certain differences with respect to birds. For with some, while the female sits on the oround, the male gets upon her, and this is the case with the bustard, and the cock ; but with others, as with cranes, the female does not sit on the ground, during the act of coition ; for among these the male leaping is conjoined with the female, and the copulation is rapidly ac complished, in the same manner as with sparrows. Of quadrupeds, however, bears lying on the ground copulate in the same manner as other animals who rest on their feet during the act, the supine parts of the male being in contact with the prone parts of the female ; but land hedge-hogs copulate erect, having the supine parts in contact with each other. Among large viviparous animals, however, the female stags do not suffer the males to have connexion with them, unless rarely, nor the cow the bull, on account of the stiff ness of the penis, but as they withdraw themselves from the male they receive the genital seed ; for this has been seen to happen in tame stags. But wolves copulate after the same manner as dogs ; and cats do not copulate backward, but the male is erect, and the female places herself under him. Females, however, are naturally libidin ous, incite the males to copulation, and cry out during the act of coi tion. But camels copulate the female sitting, and the male covers her, not having his buttocks in an opposite direction, but in the same manner as other quadrupeds. They continue, likewise, in the act for a whole day ; but when they copulate withdraw into solitude, and it is not then safe for any one but the herdsman to approach them. The penis also of the camel is so nervous that the string of a bow may be made from it. Elephants, likewise, copulate in solitary places, and i. e. The buttocks of the one being in an opposite direction to the buttocks of the other. especially

text: BOOK V. THE HISTORY OF ANIMALS. 149 especially near rivers, and where they are accustomed to dwell. But the female elephant copulates lowering her body, and removing her legs ; and the male gets upon her back. The sea-calf, also, copulates after the same manner as animals that discharge the urine backward, and, as well as dogs, are a long time in the act of coition. The males, likewise, have a large penis. CHAPTER III. Among pedestrious animals, also, oviparous quadrupeds copulate after the same manner. For, just as with viviparous animals, the males of some of these get on the back of the female, and this is the case with the land and sea tortoise. But the avenues have something with which they are conjoined, and to which they approximate in coition, as is evident in the turtle-dove, the frog, and every such like genus of animals. CHAPTER IV. But animals without feet, and which have a long body, as the ser pent and the lamprey, copulate by enfolding the supine parts with the supine, [i. e. the belly with the belly.] And serpents are so closely en- folded

title: The History of Animals of Aristotle, and his Treatise on Physiognomy, translated from the Greek. By Thomas Taylor
text: THE HISTORY OF ANIMALS. BOOK V. 151 some of the selache differ from the females, because in the males two appendices hang from the orifice through which the excrements are discharged, and of which the females are deprived ; as may be seen in the sea-dog. Neither fishes, therefore, nor any other animal without feet, have testicles, But serpents and male fishes have two avenues, which be come full of genital seed about the season of coition, and all of them emit a milky moisture. These two avenues, however, unite in one, in the same manner as in birds. For birds have testicles internally, and every thing, also, which is possessed by oviparous animals that have feet. This, therefore, is inclosed, and extends to the place and recep tacle of the female. But the same avenue of the seed and of the moist ex crement exists externally in viviparous and pedestrious animals ; and in ternally there is another avenue, as we before observed in explaining the difference of the parts of animals. In those animals, however, that have no bladder the same avenue of the dry excrement exists externally, and internally there is another avenue, both which are near to each other. These, also, subsist similarly both in the males and females of this genus of animals. For, except the tortoise, these animals are without a bladder ; and the female tortoise has one avenue, though she has a bladder. But with respect to tortoises, they rank among oviparous animals. The copulation, however, of oviparous fishes is less manifest, and on this account many are of opinion that the females become prolific by swallowing the genital seed of the males; since they are frequently seen to do this. For about the season of copulation, the females, fol lowing the males, do this, and strike their belly with their mouths ; but the males in consequence of this emit their seed, and in greater abun dance. At the time of delivery, however, the males follow the females, and devour the eggs which they lay ; and from those that are left fishes are generated. But about Phœnicia fishes are caught through the assistance of each other. For the fishermen take the male and present them to the female mullets, and the females to the males. In consequence?
name: Aristotle

title: The History of Animals of Aristotle, and his Treatise on Physiognomy, translated from the Greek. By Thomas Taylor
text: THE HISTORY OF ANIMALS. BOOK V. 152 consequence, therefore, of this being frequently seen, an opinion has been formed that the females become pregnant from swallowing the seed of the males. This very same thing is, also, done by quadrupeds. For about the season of copulation, both males and females dis charge a seminal moisture, and smell the private parts of each other. But with respect to partridges, if the females stand opposite .to the males when the wind blows, they become pregnant ; and they frequently become pregnant even from the voice of the male, if they happen to be enflamed with the desire of coition. The same effect is also pro duced from the male flying above the female, in consequence of her inbibing the odour which then proceeds from the male. Both the male and female, likewise, during the act of coition have their mouths open, and their tongues hanging out. The true copulation, however, of oviparous fishes is seldom seen, because they do not continue long in the act ; since their copulation has been seen to be effected after this manner. CHAPTER VI. The mollia, also, the polypus, the cuttle-fish, and the calamary, after the same manner copulate with each other ; for they are con nected with each other by the mouth, at the same time adapting their arms to each other. The polypus, therefore, when it has fixed what is called its head against the earth, and has unfolded its arms, another polypus adapts itself to the extension of the arms, and they make the acetabula to be in continuity with each other. Some, also, say that the male

text: BOOK V. THE HISTORY OF ANIMALS. 153 male has a kind of penis in one of its arms, in which there are two of the largest acetabula ; that a thing of this kind is as it were nervous, and is extended as far as to the middle arm ; and that the whole of it enters into the nose of the female. But the cuttle-fish and the cala mary swim at the same time that they are connected with each other; and coadapting their mouths and arms, they swim in a direction oppo site to each other. The nose, likewise, as it is called, of the one adheres to the nose of the other. And with respect to the swimming, that of the one is in a backward direction, but that of the other is towards the mouth. But they bring forth in that part of the body which is called the fistula, by which part, also, it is said by some that they copulate. CHAPTER VII. Crustaceous animals, however, such as locusts, lobsters, squills, and others of the same kind, copulate after the manner of quadrupeds that discharge the urine backward, the female causing her tail to be supine, and the male placing his tail upon it. They copulate, also, near the land, at the beginning of the spring ; for the copulation of all such animals has been detected. Sometimes, also, they copulate when figs begin to be ripe. After the same manner, likewise, lobsters and squills copulate. But crabs copulate by their anterior parts, adjusting to each other their envelopments, which consist of many folds. In the first place, therefore, the less gets on the larger crab from behind, and afterwards the larger crab turns himself obliquely. Hence the female differs in nothing else from the male, except that the envelop ment of the female is more ample, detached, and hairy, in which she x brings

text: THE HISTORY OF ANIMALS. BOOK -*, 160 cuttle-fish is more variegated than the female, and his back is blacker. The polypus, however, copulates in winter, but brings forth in the spring, and is concealed for about two months. The egg, also, which it lays is as it were a tuft of hair, and resembles the fruit of the white poplar. This animal, however, is very politic ; for from the egg of the polypus an infinite multitude of pelypi are produced. But the male differs from the female, both in having a longer head, and because it contains that white substance in its arm which fishermen call the puden dum. The female, also, incubates the eggs which she brings forth ; and hence the polypi at that time are in an ill condition of body, because they do not then take any nutriment. The purples, likewise, are generated about the spring, and the buc cina at the end of the winter ; and, in short, testaceous animals appear in the spring and autumn to have what are called eggs, except those sea hedge-hogs that are fit to eat ; for these though they have eggs especially in spring and autumn, yet they are at no time without eggs, and they particularly abound with them during the full moon, and in warm days. Those hedge-hogs, however, must be excepted, that live in the Pyrrhæan straits ; for these are better in winter. And they are, indeed, small, yet full of eggs. In a similar manner, likewise, all snails are seen to be pregnant in the same season of the year [the spring]. csiaf

text: BOOK V. THE HISTORY OF ANIMALS. 162 CHAPTER XIV. Animals, also, differ with respect to copulation, according to age. In the first place, therefore, most animals do not at one and the same time begin to emit their seed, and possess a generative power, but the latter of these is posterior to the former. For the young of all ani mals are at first unprolific ; and if they happen to be prolific, their offspring are smaller and more infirm. This, however, is especially evident in men, quadrupeds, and birds. For the two former, when they are young, produce smaller children, and young birds lay smaller eggs. In the next place, animals of the same species are, for the most part, adapted to copulation at the same age, unless some premature circumstance prevents them, either arising from something prodigious and monstrous, or from their nature having sustained some injury. In the human species, therefore, the aptitude to copulation is indicated by the mutation of the voice, and the pudenda, not only in magnitude, but also in form, and in a similar manner in the mutation of the mammæ, and especially by the hairs of the private parts. But man begins to have seed about the fourteenth year of his age, and possesses a [perfect] generative power about the age of twenty-one. Other animals, however, have no hairs in the private parts. For some, in short, have no hair, but others have no hair in the supine parts, or have less than in the prone parts. The change of the voice, also, is in some animals manifest ; but in others, other parts of the body in dicate the commencement of the seed and prolific power. With respect to voice, also, that of the female in most animals is more
name: Aristotle

title: The History of Animals of Aristotle, and his Treatise on Physiognomy, translated from the Greek. By Thomas Taylor
text: BOOK V. THE HISTORY OF ANIMALS. 163 more acute, and of the younger than that of the older. For among stags, the males have a graver voice than the females ; and the males, indeed, are vocal at the season of copulation, but the females when they are terrified. The voice of the female, however, is short, but that of the male is long. The voice, likewise, of dogs is more grave when they become old. The voices, also, of horses differ. For as soon as they are born, in deed, the females emit a slender and small voice, but the males a small voice, yet louder and graver than that of the female ; and in progress of time they have a still louder voice. But when they become two years old, and begin to copulate, the male, indeed, emits a loud and grave voice, but the female a louder and clearer voice than she emit ted before, and this is the case, for the most part, till the twentieth year of their age. After this period, however, the voice both of males and females is weaker. For the most part, however, as we have said, the voice of males dif fers from that of females, as being more grave, in such animals as have an extension of voice. Yet this is not the case in all animals ; but in some, as in oxen, the contrary takes place. For in these the voice of the female is graver than that of the male, and the voice of calves than that of perfect oxen. Hence, bulls when they are castrated change their voice into that of the female, since through this their voice becomes more acute. The times, however, of copulation, according to age, subsist in ani mals as follows: Female sheep and goats, therefore, eopulate and are pregnant at the age of one year ; but this is more especially the case with goats. And the males, also, copulate at the same age. But the offspring of sheep and goats differ in these and other respects; since the males are better when they are produced in the second year, or when they are produced by a male and female of an advanced age. Both the male and female swine, however, begin to copulate in the eighth month of their age ; but the female brings forth at the age of one year ; for thus the time of her pregnancy happens to take place. The male, also, generates in the eighth month of his age, but Y 2 the

As we have observed, however, the ages of the copulation of animals are not every where similar. Fc-r in some places, both male and female swine copulate when they are four months old ; so as to produce and nurture offspring in the sixth month. But in other places, boars begin to copulate in the tenth month of their age, and for three years retain a perfect generative power. Dogs, however, both male and female copulate, for the most part, when they are one year old ; but it sometimes happens that they co pulate in the eighth month of their age ; though this rather takes place with the females than with the males. The females, also, are preg nant during sixty-one, or two, or three days at farthest ; but they are not pregnant for a less time than sixty days. And if they happen to be delivered prior to this period, the progeny never arrive at perfec tion. After they are delivered, likewise, they copulate again in the sixth month, and not before. With respect to horses, also, both the male and female begin to co pulate when they are two years old, and at this period are able to ge nerate ; yet the offspring which at that time they produce is small and feeble. For the most part, however, they copulate when they are three years old, and every succeeding continues to be more excellent than the preceding offspring, till they are twenty years old. But the male copulates till he is thirty three years old ; and the female till she is forty ; so that horses copulate nearly during the whole of their life. For the male, for the most part, lives thirty-five years, and the female more than forty years. A horse, also, has been known to live seventy five years. With respect to the ass, however, both the male and female copu late in the thirtieth month of their age ; yet they do not for the most part generate at this period, but when they are three years old, or three years and six months. There has, however, been an instance of an ass which has conceived when but a year old, and has reared her progeny. This has, also, been the case with a cow, the progeny of which has been reared, and arrived at its proper magnitude. The

text: BOOK V. THE HISTORY OF ANIMALS. 166 and night ; but if he is not well fed, he principally possesses the power of copulating in the spring. And when old, as we have before observed, he is always less able to copulate. Frequently, however, such of them as are unable to copulate rapidly, through age or imbecility, approach ing to each other, copulate reclining, through the infirmity of the fe male. The sow, however, then, especially becomes pregnant, when, being furiously eager for copulation, she hangs her ears ; for if this is not the case, she does not become pregnant, but the seed is ejected by the womb. Dogs, however, do not copulate through the whole of life, but only as far as to a certain acme of their age ; but, for the most part, their copulations and pregnancies continue till they are twelve years of age. Some dogs, however, have been known to possess the power of gener ating, and some bitches of being pregnant, even at the ages of eighteen and twenty ; though these, as well as other animals, are deprived by old age of the ability of generating and bringing forth. But the camel discharges its urine backward, and copulates in the manner before explained. The time, however, of its copulation, in Arabia, is in the month of September. This animal, also, is preg nant during the space of twelve months, and only brings forth one at a birth ; for it is uniparous. Both the male and female, likewise, be gin to copulate when they are three years old ; and the female again copulates in one year after her delivery, f The female elephant, however, begins *o copulate at the earliest pe riod, indeed, in the tenth year of her age, and at the latest period, when she is fifteen ; but the male copulates, when he is five or six years of age. The time, also, of their copulation is the spring. The male, likewise, again copulates after an interval of three years, but is never a second time connected with a female that he has made pregnant. The time, however, of the gestation of the female is two years, and she brings forth only one offspring ; for she is uniparous. The em bryo, also, of this animal is about the size of a calf of the age of two or three months. And such are the particulars concerning the copu lation of animals. CHAP.
