text: BOOK V. THE HISTORY OF ANIMALS, 167 CHAPTER XV. We must now, however, discuss the generation both of animals that are produced by copulation, and of those that are produced without it, and in the first place the generation of testaceous animals ; for the whole of this genus is, as I may say, produced without copulation. The purples, therefore, in the spring, collecting together in one place, make what is called their wax. But this is, as it were, the honey-comb of bees, except that it is not such an elegant production, but resem bles a multitude of the shells of white peas collected in one heap. No one of these shells, however, has any avenue ; nor are the purples gener ated from these, but both the purples and other testaceous animals are generated from putrefaction and mud. This wax, therefore, or honey-comb is, as it were, a certain purgation both of the purples and buccina ; for the buccina, also, make wax. Hence those testaceous animals that make wax are generated after the same manner as other testaceous animals, and, indeed, they are more easily generated this way, when homogeneous substances pre-exist [in the putrid matter.] When the purples, therefore, make their wax they emit a certain mu cous viscosity, from the concretion of which those substances resem bling the shells of white peas are formed. But these shells, being analyzed by putrefaction, the putrid mucus contained in the shells is diffused into the earth, and in the place into which it flows small pur ples are formed, which are found when they are caught adhering to larger purples, and some of them which thus adhere are not yet per fectly formed. If, however, the larger purples are caught before they have
name: Aristotle

title: The History of Animals of Aristotle, and his Treatise on Physiognomy, translated from the Greek. By Thomas Taylor
text: THE HISTORY OF ANIMALS. BOOK V 168 have produced that mucus from which the small purples originate, they do not bring forth in any casual place, but in mats and hurdles, in the same manner as they bring forth in the sea, and from the narrowness of the hurdle in which they are delivered, their foetus resembles a grape. There are, however, many genera of purples ; and some of them indeed, are large, a those aobut Sigeum and Lectum; but others are small, as those in the Euripus, and about Caria. And those, indeed, which are found in gulfs are large and rough, and most of them have a black flower, but some of them have a red and small flower. Some of them, likewise, are large, and weigh twelve ounces and a half. The small purples, however, are found in shores, and about coasts, and have a red flower. Again, in the northern parts, they are for the most part black, but in the southern parts red. They are, likewise, caught in the spring, when they make their wax; but during the dog-days they are not caught, for then they are not fed, because they retire and con- ceal themselves. But that part of them which is called the flower, [and with which wool is dyed] is between the neck and the mecon, [or papaver ] That, likewise, which unites these two parts is compact, and the colour of it resembles a white membrane, which is taken off. When the flower, also, is pressed it tinges and dyes the hand, and extends through it like a vein. This, however, appears to be the flower ; but the remainder of that which unites the neck and the mecon resembles alum, 'she flower, likewise, of the purples is then in the worst condition when they make their wax. But [in order to collect the flower of the purple] they bruise the small purples together with their shells ; for it is not easy to collect the flower in any other way. They divest, however, the larger purples of their shells, and then take away the flower, on which account the neck and the mecon are, also, separated ; for the flower is between these, above that part which is called the belly. The flower, therefore, being taken away, the neck and mecon are necessarily divided. But those that collect the flower of the purples endeavour to bruise them while they are alive, for if they should die before they are bruised, they cast out the flower together with their life ; on which account they are preserved in bow-nets, till

title: The History of Animals of Aristotle, and his Treatise on Physiognomy, translated from the Greek. By Thomas Taylor
text: BOOK V. THE HISTORY OF ANIMALS. 171 CHAPTER XVI. Animals, also, that have no shell, such as the sea-nettle, and the sponge, are generated after the same manner as testaceous animals, in the caverns of rocks. There are, however, two genera of sea-nettles ; for some of them adhere to the cavities of rocks, so that they cannot be liberated from them ; but others adhere to smooth and broad places, so that they can be liberated from them, and change their habita tion. In the second place, sponges have certain cavities. And in these cavities certain animalcula are generated, which have the same analogy to the sponges as the guardians of the pinnæ [above-mention ed] to the pinnæ, from which guardians deriving their appellation they are called pinnophylaces. But these animalcula dwell in the cavities of the sponges, just as small spiders dwell in their cavities. They, likewise, cause the sponge to open when small fishes are about to enter into it, and to shut when they have entered, these little fishes being their prey. There are, however, three genera of sponges ; one of which is thin, the second dense, and the third, which is called Achillœan, is most thin, dense, and strong. Sponges, also, of the last kind are put under the helmets and greaves of soldiers, and cause a blow to produce a less sound ; but they are very rare. Of sponges, however, those that are very hard and rough are called goats. All sponges, likewise, are either produced near rocks or shores ; but they are nourished in mud, of which this is an indication, that when they are taken they are found to be full of mud. For other animals that adhere to any substance derive their nutriment from that to which they adhere. The dense, z 2 however,
name: Aristotle

title: The History of Animals of Aristotle, and his Treatise on Physiognomy, translated from the Greek. By Thomas Taylor
text: THE HISTORY OF ANIMALS. BOOK V. 172 however, are more imbecil than the thin sponges, because the adherence of the former is not so tenacious as that of the latter. The sponge, also, as they say, is sensitive; of which this is an indi cation, that it contracts itself at the approach of the person who plucks it, so that the divulsion of it is difficult. It, likewise, does the very same thing when there is much wind, and the weather is tempestuous, in order that it may not be removed from its situation. There are, however, some who are dubious with respect to this circumstance, as for instance, the inhabitants of Torona. For they say that the sponge nourishes certain animals within itself, such as worms and the like ; which, when the sponges are divulsed, are devoured by the fishes that live in rocks, together with the remaining roots of the sponges, but that if the sponges are not radically extirpated, they grow again from what remain, and are again filled. The largest sponges, therefore, are those that are thin, and of which there are a great number about Lycia; but the dense sponges are most soft ; for the Achillœan sponges are more compact than these. In short, the sponges which are found in places where the water is deep, and of a mild temperature, are most soft, for wind and cold harden them, in the same manner as other productions of the earth, and pre vent their increase ; on which account, the sponges in the Hellespont are dense and rough, and, in short, those which are beyond and within the promontory of Malea differ in softness and hardness. Sponges, however, will not bear immoderate heat, for they become putrid through it in the same manner as plants. Hence the sponges which are found near shores where the sea is deep are the best ; for they acquire a proper temperament, on account of the depth of the water. But while they are unwashed and alive they are black. They adhere, how ever, to rocks, neither by one part only, nor by all their parts ; for between the parts which adhere there are certain void spaces, and a membrane, as it were, is extended about the roots ; but they adhere by many of their parts. But the other void spaces in the upper part are closed. Four or five of them are, however, apparent ; on which account some assert that these are the avenues by which they receive their food. There
name: Aristotle

title: The History of Animals of Aristotle, and his Treatise on Physiognomy, translated from the Greek. By Thomas Taylor
text: BOOK V. THE HISTORY OF ANIMALS. 173 There is, also, another genus of sponges which they call aplysia, because it is incapable of being washed. These sponges have, indeed, large avenues, but all the rest of their body is dense. And when they are dissected they are found to be more dense and viscous than other sponges, and the whole of their substance resembles the lungs. It is, however, universally acknowledged that this genus of sponges is sensi tive and lives for a long time. They are, likewise, easily distinguished in the sea from other sponges, because others are found to be white when the mud subsides, but these are always black. And thus much concerning sponges, and the generation of testaceous animals. CHAPTER XVII. Of crustaceous animals, however, locusts are pregnant after copula tion, and carry their eggs during the three months of May, June, and July ; after which they deposit them in the folds under their belly, and in these the eggs increase in the same manner as worms increase. The same thing, also, takes place in the mollia, and in such fishes as are oviparous ; for the eggs of all these are increased. The egg, therefore, of locusts is friable, and is divided into eight parts. For to each of the covers which exist at the side of the locust a certain cartilaginous sub stance is united, to which the eggs adhere, and the whole resembles a grape; for each of these cartilaginous substances is divided into many branches. And these, indeed, when divided are apparent; but when they are beheld undivided, they seem to form one mass. The largest eggs, however, of the locusts are not those which are near to the avenue of their egress, but those which are situated in the middle ; and the least
name: Aristotle

title: The History of Animals of Aristotle, and his Treatise on Physiognomy, translated from the Greek. By Thomas Taylor
text: THE HISTORY OF ANIMALS. BOOK V. 176 is so connected by one certain substance, that the eggs cannot easily be separated. For the male pours on the eggs a certain mucous mois- ture, by the viscosity of which they adhere to each other, and in- crease. And these eggs, indeed, as soon as they are emitted are white, but when the cuttle-fish sprinkles them with her ink, they be- come larger and black. But when a little cuttle-fish is generated, it is wholly formed within the egg from the white of it, and the mem- brane of the egg bursting, it comes forth. When, however, the female has sprinkled the egg with her ink, the interior white part of the egg be- comes like a drop of hail ; and from this the little cuttle-fish is produced, the head being first formed, in the same manner as birds, and the belly being connected with the head. The mode, however, in which the navel of the cuttle-fish is connected with that part of the egg from which the little cuttle-fish originates has not yet been discovered, except that as the little cuttle-fish increases the white of the egg always becomes less; and at length, in the same manner as the yellow in the eggs of birds, this white entirely disappears. But, as inother animals, so likewise in these, the eyes at first are seen to be large. As for instance, let A be the egg, B C the eyes, and D the little cuttle-fish1. The cuttle-fish, also, is pregnant in the spring; but she brings forth in fifteen days [after conception]. And when she is delivered of her eggs, in the space of another fifteen days they become like the small stones of a grape ; on the bursting of which little cuttle-fish come forth. If, however, any one cuts the mem- brane of the eggs before they spontaneously burst, the little cuttle-fish, being not yet completely formed, emit dung, and change their colour through fear, so that from being white they become red. Crustaceous animals, therefore, differ from the mollia in this, that the former hatch their eggs conjoined to themselves ; but the polypus, the cuttle-fish, and other animals of the like kind, hatch their eggs separated from themselves, wherever they may be, and this is especially the case with the cuttle-fish, whose belly during her incubation is frequently seen near the ground. But the female polypus at one time hatches her eggs-by incubation, and at another time, placing herself at 1 See the figure in Scaliger's edition of this work. the

text: THE HISTORY OF ANIMALS. 177 BOOK V. the entrance of her hole, she extends her arm over the eggs, and thus hatches them. The cuttle-fish, however, brings forth near the earth, among weeds, branches of trees, reeds, heaps of stones, or any other accumulation of this kind. Hence fishermen deposit, in opportune places, bundles of twigs, [in order that they may allure the cuttle-fish to bring forth in them] ; for the cuttle-fish in these bundles lays that long series of eggs, adhering to each other, which resembles a lock of hair. The cuttle-fish, also, when she lays her eggs, after some respite, sprinkles them with her ink, because the act of bringing them forth is painful. But the calamaries bring forth in the deep sea; and their eggs are in a connected series, like those of the cuttle-fish. Neither the calamary, however, nor the cuttle-fish live long ; for except some few of them, they do not live the space of two years. This is, also, the case with the polypi. But from one egg one small cuttle-fish is produced ; and the like, also, takes place with the calamaries. The male calamary, however, differs from the female ; for if the belly of the female is dissected, it will be seen that she contains in it two red substances, which resemble small mammæ, and which the male has not. The * cuttle-fish, also, has this difference ; and besides this, the male is more variegated than the female, as was before observed. CHAPTER XIX. With respect to insects, also, we have before shown that the males are less than the females ; that in copulation the male gets on the back of the female, and that they are a long time before they are separated. Most, however, of those insects that generate from coition bring forth 2 a very
name: Aristotle

title: The History of Animals of Aristotle, and his Treatise on Physiognomy, translated from the Greek. By Thomas Taylor
text: THE HISTORY OF ANIMALS. BOOK V. 178 very soon after copulation. All insects, likewise, bring forth worms, except a certain genus of butterflies, and these bring forth a hard sub stance resembling a grain of bastard saffron, but which internally is liquid. An animal, however, is not generated from a certain part of worms, in the same manner as it is from a certain part of eggs ; but the whole is increased, and becomes a distinctly formed animal. Some insects, also, are generated from kindred animals. Thus, for instance, the spiders called phalangia, and other spiders, are generated from phalangia and spiders, and the attelabi(a. species of locusts), crickets, and grasshoppers. But other insects are not generated from animals, but are produced spontaneously. And some, indeed, are generated from the dew which falls on leaves ; and these insects are naturally gener ated in the spring, but they are likewise frequently produced in winter, when for a long time the weather has been mild, and the wind southern. Others, again, are generated in putrid mud and dung, but others in wood ; some, indeed, in the wood of plants, and some in dry wood. Some, likewise, are generated in the hairs, but others in the flesh, and others in the excrements, of animals. And of these, some are generated when the excrements are ejected, but others, as what are called lumbrici, or belly-worms, while the excrements are yet in the animal. There are, however, three genera of these ; those which are denominated broad, and the round, and the third kind, what are called ascarides. From the round, therefore, and the ascarides, nothing else is generated ; but the broad kind, which alone adhere to the intestines, produce something similar to the seed of a cucumber ; by the emis sion of which, physicians conjecture that this broad worm is latent in the intestines. What are called butterflies, however, are generated from caterpillars; but caterpillars are generated from green leaves, and especially from raphanos, which some call cabbage. And at first, indeed, something less than a grain of millet is produced ; afterwards small worms origin ate from this ; and these increasing, in the space of three days are formed into small caterpillars. Such caterpillars, also, when increased, cease from motion, change their form, and are called chrysalides, or aureliæ.
name: Aristotle

title: The History of Animals of Aristotle, and his Treatise on Physiognomy, translated from the Greek. By Thomas Taylor
text: THE HISTORY OF ANIMALS. BOOK V. 182 instance, worms are produced in old snow. But old snow is of a redder colour ; and hence the worms that are formed in it are red and hairy. The worms, however, that are generated in the snow in Media are large and white ; but all of them move with difficulty. But in Cyprus, where the stone chalcitis [a stone of a brazen colour] is calcined, after the calcination has continued for many days, winged animals are generated in the fire, in a small degree greater than large flies, which walk through the fire, and leap. These animals, however, and the worms which are produced in snow, die ; the former when separated from the fire, and the latter when separated from the snow. But that it is possible for the bodies of certain animals to remain in fire without being burnt is rendered evident by the salamander. For this animal, as they say, while it walks through the fire extinguishes it. About the river Hypanis, however, which is near to the Cimmerian Bosphorus, at the time of the summer solstice, a kind of shells are found in the river, larger than grape-stones, from the bursting of which a winged quadruped comes forth. This animal lives, and flies, till the afternoon; but when the sun declines it wastes away, and dies when he sets, its life not being extended beyond one day; on which account, also, it is called ephemeron. Most animals, however, that originate from caterpillars and worms are at first enclosed in certain substances which resemble the webs of spiders. Such, therefore, is the generation of these animals. CHAP.
name: Aristotle

title: The History of Animals of Aristotle, and his Treatise on Physiognomy, translated from the Greek. By Thomas Taylor
text: BOOK V. THE HISTORY OF ANIMALS. 184 CHAPTER XXI. With respect to the generation of bees, however, there are various opinions. For some say that bees neither bring forth nor copulate, but bring their offspring, some, indeed, from the flower of the honey suckle but others from the flower of the calamus; and others assert that they bring it from the olive-tree, of which they say this is an indication, that when there is an abundance of olive-trees, then, also, the swarms of bees are most numerous. Others, again, assert, that the drones bring their offspring from some one of the above-mentioned flowers, but that the honey-bees derive their origin from the leaders, [i. e. from the kings1.] Of the leaders, however, there are two genera, one of which is red, but the other is black, and more variegated. The magnitude, also, of the leaders is double that of the labouring bees, and in these, the inferior part, after the transverse septum, is to the superior part in the ratio of three to two. By some, likewise, they are called mothers, because they are thought to produce the honey-bees ; of which they say this is an indication, that the drones are produced without the leaders, but the progeny of the honey-bees are not. But others assert that bees are generated from copulation, and that the drones are the males, and the honey-bees the females. The generation, however, of the ordinary bees is in the cavities of the honey-comb, but the leaders are generated under the honey-comb, and remain 1 For, with respect to bees, what the moderns call the queen is called by Aristotle the king bee, as may be seen in his Treatise on the Generation of Animals. suspended,
name: Aristotle

title: The History of Animals of Aristotle, and his Treatise on Physiognomy, translated from the Greek. By Thomas Taylor
text: BOOK V. THE HISTORY OF ANIMALS. 185 suspended, separately, six or seven in number. The honey-bees, also, have a sting, but the drones have not ; and the kings or leaders have, indeed, a sting, but they do not use it; on which account some are of opinion that they are without a sting. CHAPTER XXII. There are, however, many genera of bees; and the best kind, indeed, is small, round, and variegated; the second is lono-, and resembles a wasp; but the third is called a thief, and this kind is black, and has a broad belly. In the fourth class, also, are the drones, which in magnitude, indeed, are the largest of all, but are without a sting, and are spurious; on which account certain persons intwine something at the bottom of the hive, so as to leave room for the honey-bees to enter into it, but prevent the drones, because they are larger. As we have before observed, however, there are two genera of the leaders. But in each hive there are many leaders, and not one only; and the hive perishes if it does not contain a sufficient number of leaders ; not because it would then be without rulers, but, as it is said, because the leaders contribute to the generation of the honey-bees. The hive, also, perishes if the leaders are very numerous, for they divulse it. When, therefore, the spring is late, the season is dry, and blights are prevalent, then bees are produced in less abundance. In dry seasons, however, they produce more honey ; but in rainy seasons they are more prolific; and on this account it happens that at one and the same time there is a fertilitv of olives and of bees. But B
name: Aristotle

title: The History of Animals of Aristotle, and his Treatise on Physiognomy, translated from the Greek. By Thomas Taylor
text: THE HISTORY OF ANIMALS. BOOK V. 188 their honey. White and very thick honey, also, is brought to Amisum from mountainous places; and this honey is made by bees, without hives, in the cavities of trees. Honey, likewise, of this kind is made in Pontus. There are, also, bees that construct triple hives, [i. e. dis tinguished by a triple order of cells,] in the cavities of the earth ; and these hives, indeed, contain honey, but have no worms [from which bees are produced]. Neither, however, are all hives such as these, nor do all bees make such hives. CHAPTER XXIII. But hornets and wasps make hives for their offspring, when they are without a leader, and when they wander and cannot find one. The hornets, indeed, construct their hives in some elevated place, but wasps in a hole. But when hornets and wasps have a leader, they build their hives under the earth. All the hives, therefore, of these, in the same manner as those of bees, are hexagonal ; but they are not composed from wax, but from a matter which is of the nature of bark and sand. The hive, also, of hornets is much more elegant than that of wasps. But they deposit their fœtus or seed, which is of the size of a drop of liquor, in the same manner as bees, in one side of their cells, to the wall of which it adheres. The fœtus, however, is not of the same size in all the cells, but in some it is so large as to be able to fly ; in some, also, there are nymphæ, [i. e. fœtus enclosed in mem branes] ; and in others there are worms. Among the fœtus, also, of hornets and wasps, the worms alone emit excrement, in the same manner as among bees; and as long as the fœtus are nymphs, so long they
name: Aristotle

title: The History of Animals of Aristotle, and his Treatise on Physiognomy, translated from the Greek. By Thomas Taylor
text: THE HISTORY OF ANIMALS. BOOK V. 189 they remain immoveable and enveloped in membranes. Opposite, likewise, to the cell of the fœtus, as much honey as is equal in size to a drop of liquor is produced in the hives of hornets. The offspring, however, of hornets and wasps are not generated in the spring, but in the autumn, and they especially receive an apparent increase during the full moon. The fœtus, also, and the worms of these insects do not lie at the bottom of the cell, but adhere to the side of it. CHAPTER XXIV. Some silk-worms, also, in a stone, or something of this kind, con struct nests of mud or clay, which terminate in an acute angle, and which they cover with plaster, so as to give them the appearance of salt. And these nests are so thick and hard, that they can scarcely be perforated with a lance. In these, likewise, they bring forth white worms, involved in a black membrane. But, separate from the mem brane, wax is produced in the clay. And this wax is much paler than the wax of bees. CHAP
name: Aristotle

title: The History of Animals of Aristotle, and his Treatise on Physiognomy, translated from the Greek. By Thomas Taylor
text: BOOK V. THE HISTORY OF ANIMALS. 192 the female. From one of these spiders, likewise, a hundred small phalangia are produced. But spiders, from being small, become per fect in about the space of four weeks. CHAPTER XXVIII. Crickets, also, copulate after the same manner as other insects, the less getting upon the larger, for the male is less than the female. But the female brings forth on the ground, fixing in it the tube which she has at her tail, and which the males have not. A multitude of crickets, likewise, assembling together, bring forth at once, in the same place ; so that there is, as it were, a hive of them. Afterwards, when they have brought forth, worms in the form of eggs are produced in the place of their delivery, which are enveloped in a certain thin earth, as in a membrane ; and from this, when it bursts, they come forth, and fly. The fœtus, however, of the cricket is so soft that it is crushed even if it is touched. But they do not deposit their offspring on the surface of the earth, but a little below it. And when the offspring have arrived at maturity, small and black crickets come forth from that terrene substance in which they are enclosed ; and afterwards, the skin burst ing, they immediately become larger. They, likewise, bring forth at the end of the summer ; and when they have brought forth, die. For, at the time of their delivery, worms are produced about their neck [which strangle them ;] and the males die about the same time. But they come forth from the earth in the spring. Crickets, however, are not generated in mountainous places, nor in barren ground, but in plains,
name: Aristotle

title: The History of Animals of Aristotle, and his Treatise on Physiognomy, translated from the Greek. By Thomas Taylor
text: BOOK V. THE HISTORY OF ANIMALS. 193 plains, and crevices of the earth ; for they bring forth their offspring in crevices. Their eggs, also, remain during the winter in the earth ; but, together with the summer, crickets are produced from the fœtus of the former year. CHAPTER XXIX. In a similar manner, also, the attelabi [grass- worms, or a kind of locusts] bring forth, and having brought forth, die. But their eggs are destroyed by the autumnal rains, when they are abundant ; though, if it happens to be a dry autumn, a greater number of attelabi are gener ated, because they are not similarly destroyed. For the destruction of these insects appears to be without order, and their generation to be casual. CHAPTER XXX. Of grasshoppers, however, there are two genera; some, indeed, being small, which are the first that are seen, and the last that perish ; but others are large, which also sing, and these are produced last, and are 2 c the

title: The History of Animals of Aristotle, and his Treatise on Physiognomy, translated from the Greek. By Thomas Taylor
text: THE HISTORY OF ANIMALS. BOOK V. 194 the first that perish. The grasshoppers, however, that sing, whether they are small or large, have similarly an incision at the transverse septum ; but those that do not sing have not this incision. Some, also, call the large and singing grasshoppers achetæ, but those that are small cicadulæ. Some of these small grasshoppers, also, that have an incision at the transverse septum sing a little. Grasshoppers, however, are not produced where there are no trees, on which account they are not generated in the plains of Cyrene, but there are many of them in the environs of the city ; and they are especially numerous where there are olives, because these trees are not the occasion of much shadow. For grasshoppers are not produced in cold places, and hence neither are they produced in shady thickets. The large and small grasshoppers, also, similarly copulate with each other, in a supine position. And the male inserts a part of himself into the female, in the same manner as other insects ; but the private parts of the female have a fissure. Grasshoppers, likewise, bring forth in uncultivated land, excavating it with the sharp point which they have behind, in the same manner as the species of locusts called at telabi; for the attelabi, also, bring forth in uncultivated ground ; and, on this account, they abound in Cyrene. Grasshoppers, likewise, bring forth in the reeds with which they support vines, for this purpose per forating the reeds ; and, also, in the stalks of the squill. These fœtus, however, fall to the ground. But they are numerous in rainy seasons. When, also, the worm of the grasshopper increases in the earth, it is called tettigometra, or the matrix of the grasshopper, and then the grass hoppers are most pleasant to the taste, before they burst through the bark or matrix in which they are enclosed. But about the time of the summer solstice they come forth by night, the matrix then immedi ately bursting, and grasshoppers are produced from the tettigometra. They immediately, however, become black, more hard and large, and begin to sing. But in both genera of grasshoppers, [i. e. both in the larger and less kind] the males sing, and not the females. And at first, indeed, the males are sweeter food, but after copulation, the females ; for they have white eggs. When grasshoppers, however, at the
name: Aristotle

title: The History of Animals of Aristotle, and his Treatise on Physiognomy, translated from the Greek. By Thomas Taylor
text: BOOK V. THE HISTORY OF ANIMALS. 195 the approach of any one, fly away, they emit a liquid like water, which husbandmen say is their urine ; and they also assert, that, as they are fed with dew, they emit excrement analogous to dew. If any one, however, bending and unbending his finger, gradually approaches to grasshoppers, they will remain where they are sooner than if he imme diately extends his finger. They will, also, get upon his finger ; for, in consequence of seeing obscurely, they conceive the finger to be a leaf agitated by the wind. CHAPTER XXXI. All such insects, however, as are not carnivorous, but feed on the juice of living flesh, such as fleas, lice, and bugs, generate from coition what are called lendes, from which nothing else is again produced. But of these insects, fleas, indeed, arc generated from the least putridity ; for they are formed where there is dry dung ; bugs are generated from the vapour which arises from the skin of animals; and lice are gener ated from flesh. For when lice are nearly generated, certain pustules without pus are formed, and if these are opened with a needle lice come forth. Some men, also, are aflicted with disease when there is an abundance of humidity in the body, and some have after this man ner perished, as they say was the case with the poet Alcman, and Phe recydes of Syria. And in certain diseases great quantities of lice are produced. There is, likewise, a kind of lice which are called fierce. These are harder than the common sort, and are with difficulty separ ated from the body. Lice, therefore, are produced in the heads of children ; but in a less 2 c 2 quantity
name: Aristotle

title: The History of Animals of Aristotle, and his Treatise on Physiognomy, translated from the Greek. By Thomas Taylor
text: igg THE HISTORY OF ANIMALS. BOOK V. quantity in the heads of men. Women, also, are more subject to lice than men ; but those that have lice in the head are less afflicted with a pain in the head. Lice, likewise, are generated in many other ani mals. For birds have them, and what are called pheasants are destroy ed by them, unless they roll themselves in the dust ; and other birds whose wings have a quill have lice. Other animals, also, that are hairy have lice, except the ass, who has neither lice, nor ticks ; but oxen have both. Sheep, however, and goats have ticks, but not lice ; and swine have large and hard lice ; but in dogs, what are called cynoræstæ, or dog-flails, are generated. All lice, however, are generated from those animals that have them. But animals that wash themselves, and produce lice, then generate a greater quantity of them when they change the water in which they wash. In the sea, also, lice are ge nerated in fishes ; not, however, from the fishes themselves, but from the mud. These lice too, in their form resemble wood-lice, except that they have abroad tail. There is one form, however, of marine lice, and they are generated every where, but especially in caverns. But all these animals have many feet, are exanguious, and insects. About the fins, however, of some of the tunny a horse-flie is produced, which resembles a scorpion, and is as large as a spider. But in the sea which lies between Cyrene and Egypt, there is a certain fish about the dol phin which they call a louse; and this fish is the fattest of all lice, in consequence of its being furnished with abundance of nutriment from the hunting of the dolphin. CHAP.
name: Aristotle

title: The History of Animals of Aristotle, and his Treatise on Physiognomy, translated from the Greek. By Thomas Taylor
text: BOOK V. THE HISTORY OF ANIMALS. 197 CHAPTER XXXII. Other small animals, likewise, are generated, as we have before observed, some, indeed, in wool, and in such substaaces as are formed from wool; as, for instance, moth-worms, which are principally produced in dusty woollen substances, but especially if a spider is enclosed in them ; for if there is any moisture in the wool, the spider absorbs it, and renders the wool dry, [which in this state is adapted to the genera- tion of moth-worms.] This worm, also, is produced in garments. In lod wax, also, in the same manner as in old wood, an animal is gener- ated, which appears to be the smallest of all animals, is white, and is called acari. In books, likewise, other animals are generated ; some of which, indeed, are similar to those in garments, but others to very little scorpions, without a tail. And, in short, in all dry substances when they become moist, and in all moist substances when they become dry. little animals are generated [on account of the change of the tempera ment, from which corruption follows.] There is, likewise, a small worm, which is called xylopthorum, or the wood-destroyer, which is no less singular than any of the before-men tioned insects. For a variegated head comes forth from the shell in which it is enclosed, and its feet are at one extremity of its body [i. e. near the head], like those of other worms. But the rest of its body is enclosed in a garment of the nature of a spider's web, which is surrounded with sprigs, so that it seems to adhere to this garment when it walks. These sprigs, however, are connascent with the garment, in the same manner as the shell in which snails are enclosed naturally adheres to the snails ; nor
name: Aristotle

title: The History of Animals of Aristotle, and his Treatise on Physiognomy, translated from the Greek. By Thomas Taylor
text: BOOK V. THE HISTORY OF ANIMALS. " 198 nor do they fall off, but, as being connascent, can only be separated by divulsion; and if any one takes away the garment of this insect it becomes useless and dies, in the same manner as a snail when divested of its shell. In the course of time, also, this worm becomes a chrysalis, in the same manner as caterpillars, and lives without any [visible] motion. But the winged animal which is generated from it has not yet been seen. The wild fig-tree, also, produces an insect which is called psen. This insect is at first a small worm; but, afterwards, the skin in which it is enclosed bursting, the psen leaving it flies away, enters into the fruit of the wild fig-tree, and opening it, is the cause that the fruit does not' fall off. Hence, husbandmen append branches laden with wild figs near to those that are fit to eat, and plant the wild in the neighbour hood of domestic figs. CHAPTER XXXIII. With respect, however, to sanguineous and oviparous quadrupeds, their generations, indeed, are in the spring ; yet they do not all co pulate at the same season ; but some in the spring, others in the sum mer, and others in autumn, according as each finds the following sea son is adapted to the generation of its offspring. The tortoise, there fore, brings forth eggs enclosed in a hard shell, and distinguished by a twofold colour, in the same manner as the eggs of birds ; but, having brought them forth, she digs a hole in the earth, in which she buries them, and having made the surface of the ground smooth, she then incubates her eggs, and in the following year discloses them. But the water
name: Aristotle

title: The History of Animals of Aristotle, and his Treatise on Physiognomy, translated from the Greek. By Thomas Taylor
text: BOOK V. THE HISTORY OF ANIMALS. 199 water- tortoise, coming out of the water, excavates in the earth a ditch in the form of a tub, in which she brings forth, and leaves her eggs. After thirty days, however, have elapsed, she again digs up the earth, rapidly discloses her eggs, and immediately brings her young into the water. The marine tortoises, also, bring forth in the earth eggs si milar to those of tame birds ; and, burying them in the ground, incubate them at night. But they bring forth a great multitude of eggs ; for they bring forth a hundred. Lizards, also, and both land and river crocodiles, bring forth in the earth. But the eggs of the lizard are spontaneously disclosed in the earth. For the lizard does not live the space of a year ; since the pe riod of its existence is said to be six months. The river crocodile, however, brings forth many eggs, at most about sixty, and of a white colour; she also incubates them for sixty days ; for the life of this animal is long. But from the very small eggs of the crocodile a very large animal is produced ; for the egg is not larger than that of a goose, and the little crocodile which is born from it is in proportion to the size of this egg. It increases, however, to the magnitude of seventeen cubits. Some, likewise, say that it increases as long as it lives. CHAPTER XXXIV. Of serpents, however, the viper produces an animal external to her self, having first produced an egg within herself. But the egg, in the same manner as that of fishes, is of one colour, and the shell of it is soft. The young viper, also, which is not enclosed in a hard shell, as
name: Aristotle

title: The History of Animals of Aristotle, and his Treatise on Physiognomy, translated from the Greek. By Thomas Taylor
text: THE HISTORY OF ANIMALS. BOOK V. 200 as neither are the young of fishes, is contained in the superior part of the womb. But the viper brings forth small vipers, which are enve loped in membranes, which burst on the third day, [and the young vipers come forth.] Sometimes, however, it happens that the little vipers eat through the mother, and come forth. The viper, likewise, brings forth one at a time in one day ; but she brings forth more than twenty little vipers. Other serpents, however, produce their eggs ex ternally, and these eggs are connected with each other, like the neck laces of women. But when they bring forth, they deposit their eggs in the earth, and there incubate them. These eggs, also, they disclose in the following year. THE
name: Aristotle

title: The History of Animals of Aristotle, and his Treatise on Physiognomy, translated from the Greek. By Thomas Taylor
text: THE HISTORY OF ANIMALS. BOOK VI. CHAPTER I. AFTER this manner, therefore, the generations of serpents and insects, and besides these of oviparous quadrupeds, subsist. With respect to birds, however, all of them are oviparous, but the season of their copu lation and bringing forth their young is not the same in all. For some, as I may say, copulate and bring forth at all times, such as the hen and the pigeon. The hen, indeed, during the whole year, except two months in the winter solstice, [i. e. in December and January]. But some hens, that are of a generous breed, are so prolific, that they lay sixty eggs before they begin to incubate them ; though hens of a gener ous breed are less prolific than those of a common breed. The hens, however, which are called Adrinnic, are, indeed, of a small size, but 2 d they
name: Aristotle

title: The History of Animals of Aristotle, and his Treatise on Physiognomy, translated from the Greek. By Thomas Taylor
text: THE HISTORY OF ANIMALS. BOOK VI. 202 they bring forth every day ; but they are choleric, and frequently de stroy their young. They have, likewise, all various colours. Domestic hens, also, bring forth twice in the same day. And some of them on account of their very great fecundity soon die. Hens, therefore, bring forth, as I have said, continually ; but the ring-dove, the turtle dove, and the vinous pigeon [or stock-dove], bring forth twice every year, and not ten times, like domestic pigeons. Most birds, however, bring forth in the spring, and some of them, indeed, are multiparous. But they are multiparous in a twofold re spect; some, indeed, because they bring forth frequently, as pigeons; but others because they bring forth many at a time, as hens. All birds, however, with crooked claws are pauciparous, except the kes trel. And this bird is the most prolific of all those that have crooked claws ; for she has been seen to lay four eggs, and she has brought forth more than four. Other birds, indeed, bring forth in nests ; but those which do not fly much, as partridges and quails, do not bring forth in nests, but in the earth, collecting together twigs in which they deposit their eggs. This is, likewise, the case with the lark, and the tetrix, [which, according to some, is a species of larks.] These birds, therefore, build their nests in the open air; but the bird which the Bœotians call merops is the only bird that builds its nest in caverns of the earth. Thrushes, how ever, form their nests from mud, in the same manner as swallows, in lofty trees, and they frame them in such successive connexion Avith each other, as to resemble from their continuity a chain of nests. But the lapwing is the only bird of its kind which does not build a nest ; but entering into the hollow trunks of trees, it there brings forth with out any preparation. And the cuckoo builds its nest both in edifices and in rocks. But the tetrix, which the Athenians call ourax, neither builds its nest in the earth, nor in trees, but in low plants. CHAF.
name: Aristotle

title: The History of Animals of Aristotle, and his Treatise on Physiognomy, translated from the Greek. By Thomas Taylor
text: THE HISTORY OF ANIMALS. BOOK VI. 204 The genital seed, therefore, of all birds is white, in the same manner as the seed of other animals. But the female having by copulation received the seed in the superior part of the womb, which is near the transverse septum, conceives an egg, which at first appears to be small and white, but afterwards is red and sanguineous ; and when in the course of time it is increased, the whole becomes red and yellow. When, also, it becomes more thick it is distinguished by two colours ; and the yellow is inward, but the white externally surrounds it. But when it becomes perfect, it is liberated from the womb [to which it was fixed], and comes forth into the light. At that time, likewise, the shell from being soft becomes hard ; so that the egg in proceeding from the womb has not a firm consistence, but when it has proceeded from it, it imediately becomes firm and hard, unless it is diseased. An egg, also, has been seen to come forth entirely yellow, so as to resemble the young bird which is afterwards produced from it. Such eggs, likewise, are found in a hen, when she is dissected, under the transverse septum ; for in that place, to which the eggs usually adhere, eggs are seen having the magnitude of a perfect egg, but entirely of a yellow colour ; which is considered as a prodigy. Those, however, who assert that windy [or addle] eggs are the relics of preceding eggs which were produced from copulation, do not assert what is true ; for it has been sufficiently ascertained, that the young of hens and geese that have not yet copulated have brought forth windy eggs. But windy eggs are not so large as, are less sweet, and moister than, those that are prolific, but they are more numerous. These windy eggs, how ever, if they are put under the incubating bird, are not thickened in their moist part, but both the yellow and the white remain as they were before. Windy eggs, also, are produced from many birds, viz. from the hen, the partridge, the pigeon, the peacock, the goose, and the goose-fox. The young of birds, however, are more rapidly hatched by incuba tion in summer than in winter ; for hens in summer disclose their young in eighteen days ; but in winter they are sometimes five-and-twenty days before they are disclosed. The eggs, however, which are called by some cynosura [or the urine of a dog] and urina, are produced in summer more than in winter. But windy eggs are denominated by some zephyria, [or the eggs of zephyr,] because birds in the spring are seen to receive the western gales. A like effect, however, is produced by titillating the vulva of birds with the hand. Windy eggs, also, may become prolific, and those which have been now produced from coition are changed into another genus, if before the yellow is separated from the white the female which has windy eggs copulates with the male, or is pregnant from the seed of another bird ; for then the windy eggs become prolific, and the mat ter which was formed by the prior male subsists according to the nature of the male with which the female afterwards copulated. But if the female copulates after the yellow is separated from the white, then the copulation contributes nothing to the fecundity of the windy egg, or to that which was conceived by a prior copulation, passing into the genus of the other male with which the female is afterwards con nected. If, also, coition is intermitted when the eggs have begun to be formed, they do not at all increase ; but if copulation again takes place, they rapidly arrive at their proper magnitude. The yellow and the white of an egg, however, have a nature con trary to each other, not only in colour, but, also, in power. For the yellow acquires a firm consistence by the cold, but the white does not, but is rather liquefied by cold. By fire, however, the white acquires a firm consistence, but the yellow does not, but continues to be soft, unless it is burnt ; and it acquires a firmer consistence, and becomes more hard when boiled, than when exposed to a naked fire. The yellow and the white, also, are separated from each other by a membrane. But the globules which are seen near the beginning of the yellow do not contribute any thing to the generation of the young, as some are of opinion they do. These globules, also, are two ; one, indeed, in the in ferior, but the other in the superior, part of the egg. CHAPTER III. The generation, however, from an egg, as has been before observed, happens, indeed, to all birds after the same manner, but the times of its arriving at perfection differ. In hens, therefore, after three days and three nights have elapsed, indications of the future bird present themselves; but in larger hens these indications appear more slowly, and in those that are less more swiftly. In this time, therefore, the yellow ascends to the acute part of the egg, where the principle of the egg subsists, and the egg is disclosed ; and then, in the white of the egg, the heart, like a sanguineous point, presents itself to the view. But this point, as if animated, leaps and is moved ; and from it, when it is increased, two veiny avenues, sanguineous and convolved, tend to each of the surrounding tunics. About the same time, also, a certain mem brane appears, distinguished by sanguineous fibres, and which arising from the two above-mentioned avenues of the veins [surrounds the white of the egg ;] and shortly after, the body of the young bird may be distinguished, which at first is very small and white. But the head is very manifest, and the eyes especially are inflated ; and do not till after a long time decrease, and so contract themselves as to have a due proportion with the other parts of the body. At first, also, in the inferior part of the body no member is seen distinct from the rest. But

During the before-mentioned time, also, the young bird sleeps, but is sometimes excited from sleep, looks up and chirps ; and the heart is inflated, together with the navel, as if respiring. After this manner, therefore, the generation of birds from an egg subsists. Some birds, also, bring forth unprolific eggs, and these pro duced from copulation. But no bird is generated from these by incu bation. This, however, has been observed particularly to happen with pigeons. Double eggs, however, have two yolks, which sometimes that they may not be confounded are separated by a thin interstice of the white ; and sometimes the two yolks are in contact with each other without this interstice. There are, also, some hens that bring forth all their eggs double, so that in these, also, the above-mentioned circumstance happens respecting the yolk. For a certain hen having brought forth eighteen double eggs, disclosed two chickens from each, those eggs excepted which were unprolific. Two chickens, also, were disclosed from each of the double eggs, but one of the chickens was larger than the other. But the last chicken that was disclosed was a monster. CHAPTER IV. All birds, however, of the genera of pigeons, such, for instance, as the ring-dove and the turtle-dove, bring forth two eggs ; but the most which the turtle and ring-dove bring forth are three eggs. And the pigeon, indeed, brings forth, as we have before observed, at all seasons, but the ring and turtle-dove bring forth in the spring, and not oftener than twice. text: THE HISTORY OF ANIMALS. BOOK VI. 212 CHAPTER V. The vulture, however, buflds her nest in inaccessible rocks ; and on this account the nest and the young of the vulture are but rarely seen. Hence, Herodotus, the father of Brysson the sophist, says, that vultures come from another land, unknown to us ; of which, he says, this is an indication, that no one has seen the nest of the vulture, and that many of them suddenly appear following armies. Though it is difficult, however, to see their nest, yet it has been seen. Vultures, also, bring forth two eggs. All carnivorous birds, therefore, accord in this, that they are not seen to bring forth more than once in a year; except the swallow, which, though a carnivorous bird, builds her nest and brings forth twice in a year. And if any one pierces the eyes of the offspring of swallows while they are yet young, they will after wards be restored to a sane condition, and again possess the power of seeing. 5 ca As.

For, in short, all birds that have crooked claws expel their young from the nest as soon as they are able to fly, and compel them by blows to depart. Nearly, likewise, most other birds, as we have before observed, do the same thing ; and except the crow, having nourished, take no far ther care of their young. The crow, however, pays attention to them for a certain time ; for she nourishes them even when they are able to fly. CHAPTER VII. With respect to the cuckoo, some are of opinion that this bird is a transformation from the sparrow-hawk, because about the time in which the cuckoo is seen the sparrow-hawk, which resembles the cuckoo, disappears. About the time, however, in which the cuckoo begins to sing, not only the sparrow-hawk is not to be seen, but this is also the case with every other species of hawk ; except that they are only visible for a few days. But the cuckoo is seen for a short time in summer, and disappears in winter. The sparrow-hawk, however, has crooked claws, but the cuckoo has not. Farther still, neither does the head of the cuckoo resemble that of the sparrow-hawk, but both its head and its claws are more similar to those of the pigeon, and it alone resembles the sparrow-hawk in its colour, except that the colour of the latter is variegated like lines, but that of the cuckoo like points. 1 So called from having a white tail. The cuckoo, also, has been seen to be de voured by the sparrow-hawk ; though no birds of the same kind are known to do this. It is, likewise, said, that no one has ever seen the young of the cuckoo. The cuckoo, however, brings forth, indeed, but does not build a nest ; and sometimes she brings forth in the nest of lesser birds, the eggs of which birds she eats. She more particularly, however, brings forth in the nest of the ring-dove, and eats the eggs •of this bird. For the most part, likewise, she brings forth one egg, but very seldom two. She, also, brings forth in the nest of the hen linnet, who incubates the egg, and nurtures the young of the cuckoo. But the cuckoo at the time in which she brings forth is most fat, and her flesh is sweet as food. The young, likewise, of sparrow-hawks are very fat, and their flesh is very sweet. But there is a certain genus of sparroAv- hawks who build their nest on steep rocks. CHAPTER VIII. A great number of birds, however, incubate, as we have observed concerning pigeons, the males alternately succeeding the females in this employment during the time in which the female is engaged in the search of food. Among geese, however, the females alone incu bate, and when they have begun to do this, continue sitting without intermission. The nests, also, of all birds that live in marshes are constructed

BOOK VI ■2\d constructed in swampy and grassy places, on which account, being undisturbed while they incubate, they are able to impart a certain nutriment to their young, and are not entirely without food. Of crows, also, the females alone incubate, and continue sitting on their eggs without intermission. But in the mean time the males nourish the females, bring them food, and feed them with it. With respect to pigeons, however, the female beginning to incubate in the evening continues in this employment the whole night, till the hour of break fast; and the male incubates the remaining time. But partridges make two receptacles of eggs; and in one of these the female, but in the other the male, incubates. Each, also, discloses its young, and as soon as they are disclosed copulate with them. CHAPTER IX. The peacock, however, lives five-and-twenty years, and especially begins to generate at the age of three years ; at which time, also, it receives a variety of plumage ; and discloses its eggs in thirty or a few more days. But it brings forth once only in a year, and lays twelve, or a somewhat less number of eggs. It, likewise, omits two or three days in bringing forth, and does not lay its eggs in an uninterrupted succession; but its first progeny do not consist of more than eight eggs. Peacocks, also, bring forth windy or unprolific eggs. But they copu late in the spring; and bring forth immediately after copulation. They, also, lose their feathers at the same time that the leaves fall from trees, and they again begin to be replumed when the trees are in blos som. Those persons, likewise, that rear peacocks put their eggs under hens

text: BOOK VI. THE HISTORY OF ANIMALS. 217 hens to be incubated, because if the female peacock incubates her own eggs, the male flying on the female breaks them. On this account, also, among certain wild birds, the females, [when the time of bringing forth is near] flying from the males, lay and incubate their eggs [secret ly.] Two eggs, however, alone of the peacock are put under a hen, because the hen can only disclose two eggs of the peacock by incubation. Care, likewise, is taken that there is no intermission in the incubation of the hen, and that for this purpose she is supplied with food. Birds, however, at the time of copulation have their testicles manifestly larger; those, indeed, that are more salacious have them more conspicuously larger, as cocks and partridges ; but those that do not continually copulate have them less manifestly increased. CHAPTER X. After this manner, therefore, the conception and generation of birds subsist. But with respect to fishes, that all of them are not oviparous has been asserted before, for the cartilaginous kind called selache are viviparous. They first, hoAvever, conceive an egg in themselves, and nourish it in themselves, the marine frog excepted. Fishes, also, have different wombs, as we have before observed. For those that are oviparous have wombs situated in the inferior part, and divided into two cavities; but the selache have wombs more similar to the wombs of birds. They differ, however, from those of birds, because birds contain their eggs in the superior part of the womb, i. e. under the transverse septum; but certain of the selache contain their eggs in the 2 p middle

Males, however, are generated in the left part of the womb, and females in the right, and sometimes both males and females are generated in the same part. When embryos, also, are dissected, the viscera, such as the liver, Sec. in the same manner as those of quadrupeds, are found to be large and sanguineous. All the selache, however, have a multitude of eggs in the superior part of the womb, near the transverse septum, which eggs in some are larger, and in others less; but in the inferior part of the womb they contain the embryos. Hence fishes of this kind are thought to bring forth and copulate frequently in a month, because they do not bring forth all that they have conceived at once, but frequently, and for a long time ; for while they conceive eggs in the superior part of the womb, the fœtus is matured and arrives at perfection in the inferior part of it. Other sea-dogs, therefoie, and, also, the file, and the torpedo or cramp fish, emit their offspring from themselves, and again receive them into themselves. A large cramp-fish, also, has been seen which contained in itself eighty embryos. But the thorny dog is the only one of the sea-dogs which does not receive its offspring within itself, in con sequence of the thorn [with which the young are armed.] Of the broad fishes, also, neither the pastinaca nor the scate receive their young within themselves, on account of the roughness of their tail. Nor does the marine frog receive its young, on account of their thorns, and the magnitude of their head. For, as we have before observed, the marine frog is the only fish of the cartilaginous kind that is not viviparous. chap.

text: BOOK VI. THE HISTORY OF ANIMALS. 221 CHAPTER XI. Such, therefore, is the difference of these fishes with respect to each other, and such is the generation of them from eggs. The males, however, at the time of copulation have their ducts so full of genital seed, that when compressed white seed flows externally from them. But these ducts or avenues are bifidated, and originate from the transverse septum and the great vein. At the time of copulation, therefore, the ducts of the males are manifestly enlarged, though at other times they can scarcely be seen. For in some fishes they some times become entirely immanifest, as we before observed concerning the testicles of birds. The spermatic ducts, however, of the males differ from those pertaining to the womb in females in other respects, and in this, also, that the ducts of the males adhere to the kidneys, but those of the female are easily moved and involved in a thin mem brane. The mode, however, in which the ducts of the males subsist must be surveyed from anatomical descriptions. Superfetation, also, pertains to the selache, and the longest period of their conception is six months. But that sea-dog which is called the star-fish brings forth most frequently ; for it brings forth twice in a month. It, also, begins to copulate in the month of September. Other sea-dogs, however, bring forth twice in a year, the little sea-dog excepted; and this fish brings forth once in a year. All of them, like wise, bring forth in the spring ; but the file-fish brings forth the second time in autumn, towards the setting of the winter pleiades; and the first time, in the spring. After this manner, therefore, aquatic and viviparous animals gener ate, and bring forth their offspring. But oviparous fishes, as we have before observed, have their womb bifidated, and situated in the infe rior part. All fishes, however, that have scales are oviparous; such, for instance, as the wolf, the mullet, the cephalus or pollard, and the etelis; and all those that are called white, together with those that are smooth [because they are without scales], except the eel. Their egg, also, is sandy. It appears, however, to be so, because the whole womb of these fishes is full of eggs, so that in small fishes there appears to be only two eggs ; for the womb in them is immanifest, on account of its smallness and thinness. Concerning the copulation, therefore, of all fishes, we have before spoken. In most fishes, however, there is a distinction of male and female; but it is dubious whether there is this distinction in the roach and chamæ, for all that are caught of these are found to have eggs. Fishes, therefore, that copulate generate eggs from their copulation. But they, also, have eggs without copulation ; and this is evident in some

But the generation of the carp is next to that of the glanis in slowness ; and, in a similar manner, its eogs, after they are brought forth, are guarded by the male. The eggs, also, of some smaller fishes so rapidly increase, that in the space of three days they become little fishes. But the eggs which have been sprinkled with the seed of the male receive an increase, both in the day in which they were sprinkled, and, likewise, afterwards. The eggs of the glanis, therefore, increase to the size of the grains of the bitter vetch ; but those of the carp, and such like fishes, to the size of a grain of millet. These fishes, therefore, bring forth and generate after this manner. But the chalcis brings forth its eggs thick, and collected together. And the fish which they call psylon brings forth its eggs near shores, in places exposed to the wind. This fish, also, collects its eggs together in one place. But the carp, the balin, and all other fishes, as I may say, are impelled into shallow water for the purpose of bringing forth ; and frequently thirteen or fourteen males follow one female. But when the female after having brought forth her egg departs, the males sprin- kle it with their genital seed. Most of their eggs, however, perish; for, because the female as she passes through the water lays her eggs, it is necessary that the eggs being dissipated by the stream should perish, except those which adhere to some substance they may meet with. For no fish besides the glanis is a guardian of the eggs of the female except the carp, and this fish only then guards them when it finds them collected into one place. All male fishes, however, have genital seed,. except the eel ; and this fish has neither genital seed, nor an egg. Mullets, therefore, ascend from the sea into lakes and rivers ; but eels,. on the contrary descend from lakes and rivers into the sea. c II a p.

text: BOOK VI. THE HISTORY OF ANIMALS. 229 CHAPTER XV. Most fishes, therefore, as has been said, are generated from eggs. Some, however, are generated from mud and sand ; and there are some of this description even among those which are produced from copula- tion and eggs, which they say sometimes happens to be the case both in other muddy places and in the pools about Cnidos, which become dry through the heat occasioned by the dog-star, so that even all the mud remains without moisture. These places, however, begin to be filled with water with the first rain that falls, and as soon as the water com- mences, little fishes are generated in it. But these little fishes are a certain species of mullets, which are not produced from copulation, and are of the size of small mœnidia ; but in these there is neither any egg nor genital seed. In the rivers in Asia, also, where they flow into the sea, other small fishes are generated after the same manner as the before-mentioned, of the largest of which they make sauce. Some, however, assert that all mullets are generated spontaneously from putrid matter. [But this is false ;] for the females of them are seen to have eggs, and the males genital seed. There is, however, a certain genus of them which is spontaneously generated from mud and sand. That some fishes, therefore, are generated spontaneously, neither from eggs nor from copulation, is evident from what has been said. All such fishes, however, as are neither oviparous nor viviparous are generated either from mud or sand, or any putrid matter which floats on the surface of the water. Such, for instance, is the fish aphye, which is

The aphye, how ever, which is called foam, and which is unprolific, is moist and continues but for a short time, as was before observed; for at length nothing is left but its head and eyes. But fishermen that they may carry it away with them sprinkle it with salt; for by this means it continues for a longer time. CHAPTER XVL Eels, however, are neither generated from copulation, nor do they bring forth eggs, nor has any eel ever been caught which had either any genital seed or an egg. In the dissection of eels, also, no avenues have ever been found destined to the reception or emission of seed, or to performing the office of a womb; but among sanguineous animals, the whole genus of eels is neither produced from copulation nor from eggs. It is, however, evident that this is the case ; for in some muddy lakes, all the water being exhausted, and the mud extracted, when the rain falls, eels are again generated. But in dry seasons, they are not generated even in perennial lakes ; for they live and are nourished by rain-water. That they are neither generated, therefore, from copulation nor from eggs is evident. To some, however, eels appear to have the power of generating, because small worms are ingenerated in certain eels; for they fancy that eels are generated from these worms. This, however, is not true ; but they are generated from what are called the entrails of the earth ; which are spontaneously formed in mud, and in moist earth. For some eels have been seen proceeding from these entrails

And though the eggs of the conger cannot be clearly seen on account of the fat in which they are immersed, yet if fire is applied to the fat, the eggs may be sufficiently distinguished. For the satis consumed and evaporates; but the eggs leap, and, being separated, crepitate. The eggs, also, of the conger may be distinguished by the touch. For if any one handles the conger and rubs it with his fingers, he will feel that the suet is smooth, and the eggs rough. Some congers, therefore, have suet alone, but no eggs ; and others, on the contrary, have no suet, but an egg of such a kind as I have just now mentioned. And thus I have nearly considered all other animals that bring forth an egg, as well the aquatic as the winged and terrestrial ; and have, likewise, spoken concerning their copula tion, pregnancy, and generation, and other particulars similar to these. CHAPTER XVIII. Let us now direct our attention to what pertains to such pedestri ous animals as are viviparous, and, also, to man. We have already, therefore, considered what pertains to the copulation of all animals, both peculiarly and in common. But it is common to all animals to be vehemently stimulated by the desire of, and pleasure arising from, coition. Females, therefore, when they have brought forth are at first more ferocious, [through love of their offspring ;] but the males are ferocious at the time of copulation. For horses at this period bite other horses, and throw and pursue their riders ; and wild boars are most ferocious, though at this time they are most imbecil from the effect of copulation. They, likewise, give to each mare thirty stallions, or a few more. And if another horse approaches, the first horse, running in a circle about his own mares, fights with him ; and if any mare is allured by this other horse, he bites and restrains her. But the bull at the season of copulation feeds with the cows, and fights with the other bulls. At other times, however, they feed with other bulls separate from the cows, which is called a contempt of the herd. For frequently the bulls in Epirus are not seen for three months. And, in short, all savage animals, or the greatest part of them, do not feed together with the females prior to the season of copulation ; but when they become adult, the males are separated, and feed apart from the females. Swine, also, when they are impelled to copulation, which is called subation, attack even men themselves. But a passion of this kind in bitches is called catulition. In the females, likewise, when they are stimulated with lust, the genital parts swell and become wet; but mares at this period distil a certain white moisture. Females, likewise, are subject to the purifications of the menses, yet these purifications are in no female animal so abundant as in women. In sheep and goats, therefore, at the season of copulation, a certain menstrual moisture is seen, which, also, flows for some time after copu lation, and then ceases till they are about to bring forth. But then it again begins to flow, and shepherds know by this token that the time of their parturition is at hand. After delivery, however, an abundant purification follows, which at first is not very sanguineous, but is so afterwards ; and the cow, the she-ass, and the mare emit a greater quantity of this menstrual moisture, on account of their magnitude, yet less in proportion to their bulk than sheep and goats. The cow, therefore, when stimulated to copulation has but a small purification, since she only emits as much menstrual moisture as will fill the half of a cup called cotylus1, or a little more. A mare, however, brings forth the most easily of all quadrupeds, is the most free from menstrual purgations, and emits the least flux of blood, in proportion to the magnitude of her body. But the menses are especially an indication of pregnancy in cows and mares, and they cease for the space of two, four, or six months ; yet the failure of the menstrual flux cannot be known by those who are not very much accustomed to observe them, on which account some are of opinion that mares and cows are deprived of this purgation. Again, the females of mules have not this menstrual moisture, but the urine of the females is thicker than that of the males. In short, therefore, the excrement of the bladder is thicker in quadrupeds than men ; and the females of sheep and goats discharge a urine thicker than that of the males. But, on the contrary, the urine of all she-asses is thinner than that of the males ; and the urine of the ox is more acrid than that of the cow. All quadrupeds, however, after they have brought forth their young emit urine thicker than others that have a more abundant men strual purgation. Animals, also, that begin to have milk at the time of coition, at that period emit a milk which resembles pus, and which is useless; but their milk becomes useful after they have brought forth. Female sheep and goats, likewise, and in a similar manner cows and all other quadrupeds, are more fat, and eat a greater quantity of food when they are pregnant. Moreover, for the most, part, animals are more impelled to copulation in the spring. All of them, however, do not copulate at the same time of the spring, but in times adapted to the nourishment of their offspring. Domestic female swine, therefore, are pregnant during four months, but the greatest number of offspring which they bring forth is twenty ; though when they bring forth many, they are not able to nourish all of them. When they are old, also, they in a similar manner bring forth, but they copulate more slowly. They, likewise, become pregnant from one copulation; but repeatedly copulate, because after copula tion they emit that moisture which is called by some subation. This, therefore.

CHAPTER XX. Of dogs, however, there are many genera. But the Laconic dogs copulate in the eighth month of their age ; and about this time, some of the males of this species begin to lift their leg when they make water. A bitch, also, becomes pregnant from one copulation ; and this especially becomes evident in those bitches that copulate furtively ; for having once copulated they become pregnant. The Laconic bitch, however, is pregnant during a sixth part of the year; sixty-one or two, or three days at most. And her puppies when they are born are blind for twelve days. Having brought forth, also, she again copulates in the sixth month, and not before. Some bitches, however, are pregnant the fifth part of the year; i. e. seventy-two days. But the puppies of these bitches are blind during fourteen days. And there are some bitches that are pregnant a fourth part of the year; i. e. three whole months; but the puppies of these are blind for seventeen days. Bitches, also, for an equal space of time appear to possess an ardent desire of copulation. They have the menses, likewise, at this period for seven days ; and at the same time it happens that their genital parts swell. At this time, however, they do not suffer the male to copulate with them, but in the seven following days. For they appear for the most part to possess an ardent desire of copulation dur ing the whole fourteen days; and some are under the influence of this passion

But the ass more rapidly fills the mare than the horse ; and the copulation of horses is not labori ous, like that of bulls. An ass, how ever, has been known to be pregnant when but one year old, and to bring forth and rear her offspring. After copulation, likewise, she dis charges the seed she had received from the male, by making water, unless she is prevented ; and hence the keepers of asses strike and pursue the females immediately after they have copulated. The ass, also, brings forth in the twelfth month ; and, for the most part, she is delivered of only one fœtus ; for she is naturally uniparous ; but some times she brings forth two. An ass, therefore, by copulating with a mare corrupts, as we have before observed, the seed which she received from the horse ; but the horse does not corrupt the seed of the ass, when a mare has previously had connection with an ass. A pregnant ass, likewise, begins to have milk in the tenth month ; and on the seventh day after her delivery again suffers coition, and on this day especially is filled from the male, and conceives. She is, also, filled, if she co pulates after the seventh day. When he covers a mare, also, he begets a young mule. But afterwards he no longer covers her. The female mule, likewise, some times becomes pregnant, though she is unable to bring the fœtus she has conceived to perfection. The she-mules, however, in Syria, above Phœnicia, both copulate and bring forth ; but this genus of mules is different from those of which we are speaking, though it resembles them. The lives, however, of those animals, differ with respect to bringing forth and nurturing their offspring, who have a larger portion of sense, and Avho copulate on account of the pleasure Avith Avhich the act of copulation is attended. Some, there- fore, as plants, accomplish at stated times the generation appropriate to their nature; but others labour in the nurture of their offspring, and Avhen their offspring have arrived at perfection separate themselves from and have no longer any communion with them ; and others, Avho are more intelligent, and participate more of memory, conduct them- selves toAvards their offspring in a manner more sociable and political. One part, therefore, of the life of animals consists in the actions Avhich they exercise in the procreation of offspring ; but another part consists in procuring nutriment. For about these two all their attention and life are employed. All kinds of nutriment, however, principally differ according to the matter from which the beings that are nourished are composed ; for the natural increase of every animal is from the same matter as that from Avhich it consists. But that Avhich is according to nature is pleasant; and all animals pursue the pleasure which is adapted to their nature. Animals, also, are divided according to places; for some of them are pedestrious, [i. e. terrestrial,] but others are aquatic. But this difference being predicated in a twofold respect, viz. either from re ceiving air or Avater, some are called pedestrious, and others aquatic. And again, of those animals which do not receive either air or water sufficiently, but are naturally adapted to the temperament of refriger ation, some are called pedestrious, but others aquatic, though they neither respire nor receive the Avater, but derive their nutriment from and live in either of these elements. For many animals, that receive the air and bring forth their young on the land, derive their nutriment from aquatic places, and live the greater part of their time in the Avater; these animals alone, as it seems, partaking of an aquatic and terrestrial nature, and may, therefore, be considered as both pedestrious and aquatic. 2 p CHAP.
