And some, indeed, do not communicate with both natures, but others do communicate, in consequence of participating something of the matter from which they derive their nutriment in their original formation. For to every animal that which is according to nature is friendly, as we have before observed. But animals being divided into the aquatic and pedestrious triply, viz. by receiving air or water, and by the temperament of their bodies, but, in the third place, by their food, their lives are conformable to these divisions. For some are aquatic or pedestrious according to their temperament and food, and according to their receiving Avater or air; but others from their temperament or their life alone. Of testaceous animals, therefore, those which do not change their place are nourished with potable Avater. For the sea-water is perco lated through dense bodies, and the more attenuated part of it is con cocted, and receives a generation as it were from the beginning. But that sea- water by percolation may become potable is evident ; since this has been ascertained by experiment. For if a vessel made of thin Avax, to Avhich a string is fastened, is dropt into the sea empty, and re mains there for the space of a day and a night, there will be found Avithin it a considerable quantity of potable water. Sea-nettles, hoAvever, are nourished Avith any small fishes they may happen to meet with. But they have a mouth in the middle of their body, Avhich is very apparent in large sea-nettles. They have, likeAvise, in the same manner as oysters, a passage in the superior part of their body, through Avhich they discharge their excrements. For the sea-net tle, in the same manner as the oyster, appears to have a fleshy sub stance internally, and to use a rock as a shell. But the lepas frees it self from the place to which it adheres, and goes in search of nutriment. Of such testaceous animals, hoAvever, as are motive, those, indeed, that are carnivorous, as, for instance, the purple, feed on small fishes ; for this animal is carnivorous, and on this account it is caught by things of this kind ; but others feed on plants that grow in the sea. The marine tortoises, likeAvise, feed on shells ; for they have a body the most robust of all animals. For whatever they take into their mouth,

But they labour and frequently perish, Avhen swimming on the surface of the sea, they are dried by the sun ; for they cannot again easily plunge themselves in the depths of the sea. Crustaceous, also, are nourished after the same manner as testace- ous animals. Thus, for instance, crabs of the rock feed on stones wood, mud, sea-Aveed, and dung; and they are, also, carnivorous. But lobsters vanquish, indeed, large fishes, and a remarkable recipro- cation happens to some of these. For the polypi subdue the lobsters ; so that lobsters Avhen they perceive the polypi near them in the same net die through fear. Lobsters, however, vanquish the congers ; for the latter cannot escape on account of the roughness of the former ; and the congers eat the polypi; for the former, on account of their smooth- ness, cannot be caught and retained by the latter. All the mollia, like- wise, are carnivorous. Lobsters, hoAvever, feed on the little fishes,. which they hunt after near their retreats. For their habitations are in such places of the sea as are rough and stony. And whatever they catch they carry to their mouth Avith a forcipated foot, in the same manner as crabs. Naturally, likeAvise, Avhen they are nor terrified, their progressive motion is to the anterior part, letting fall their horns on their side ; but when they are terrified, they make their retreat backAvard, and extend their horns. They, also, fight Avith each other, in the same manner as rams, Avith their horns, raising these and striking Avith them. Crustaceous animals, therefore, live after this manner; but of the mollia, the small calamary and the cuttle-fish vanquish large fishes. But the polypi principally collect shell-fish, and extracting the fleshy part feed on it ; on which account, those who hunt for them knoAv their retreats by the shells [which they find in them.] That, however, which some assert, that the polypus eats itself, is false; but some of them have their arms gnaAved by the congers. Of birds, however, all such as have crooked claAvs are carnivorous; but they cannot sAvallow corn, even if it is put into their mouth ; as, for instance, all the genera of eagles, kites, and the two species of hawks, viz. the hawk which pursues the ring-dove, and that Avhich at tacks the chaffinch and the buzzard. These two species of haAvks, also, differ very much from each other in magnitude. But the buzzard is as large as the kite, and is seen at all times. Among carnivorous birds, also, are the osprey and the vulture ; but the osprey is larger than the eagle, and its colour resembles that of ashes. All the actions, however, of animals are conversant about copula tion, the nurture of their young, the means of procuring sufficient nutriment, and providing a habitation Avhich may defend them from the inconveniences arising from heat and cold, and the mutations of the seasons. And some, indeed, find the assistance of Avhich they are in Avant in the places to Avhich they are accustomed ; but others for this purpose migrate ; betaking themselves after the autumnal equinox from Pontus and other cold places, that they may avoid the approach ing winter. After the vernal equinox, however, they migrate from warm to cold places, fearing the heat; some, indeed, departing from neigh bouring places, but others, as cranes, from one extremity of the earth to another. Farther still, places near the sea-shore are Avell tempered with heat and cold ; on Avhich account the flesh of such like fishes has more consistence ; but the flesh of fishes that live in the deep sea is moist and loose. Many birds, likewise, hide themselves ; nor do all of them, as some fancy, migrate to warmer climates ; but some, indeed, being near to places of this kind in Avhich they perpetually dwell, as, for instance, kites and SAvallows, migrate to them ; and others being more remote from places of this kind, do not migrate, but conceal themselves. But this bird Avhen it begins to hide itself is very fat, and though it loses its feathers during its retreat, yet it still continues to be fat. text: BOOK VIII. THE HISTORY OF ANIMALS. 319 CHAPTER XVII. Among viviparous quadrupeds, also, porcupines and bears hide themselves. That savage bears, therefore, hide themselves is evident ; but it is dubious Avhether it is from cold, or some other cause. For both the males and females become about this time very fat, so as to be unwieldy. The female, also, brings forth at this season, and con ceals herself till the period arrives of leading forth the young bears from her retreat. But she does this in the spring, and in the third month after the Avinter solstice. The bear, likewise, is concealed for about forty days at least. And it is said, that for fourteen of these days it does not move at all, but in most of the days after these it is concealed, indeed, yet is in a vigilant state, and in motion. A pregnant bear, hoAvever, has either never been caught by any one, or by very few. It is evident, also, that the bear during the time of its concealment does not eat anything; for it does not come forth from its retreat : but when it is caught, both its belly and intestines are found to be empty. It is, likewise, said, that the intestine of the bear at that time is nearly adherent, and that on this account, as soon as it quits its retreat, it eats a certain herb Avhich is called arus, for the purpose of relaxing and separating the intestine. The dormouse, also, conceals itself in trees, and at that time becomes very fat ; and the white Pontic rat, likewise, hides itself. But of those that hide themselves, some put off what is called their old age. This, however, is their exterior skin, and the covering Avhich they received in their formation. Animals, hoAvever, do not live prosperously at the same seasons, nor similarly happy in all excesses of heat and cold. Farther still, health and disease vary according to seasons in animals of different genera, and on the Avhole are not the same in all animals. Hot and dry seasons, therefore, are advantageous to birds, both Avith respect to their health and delivery, and especially to ring-doves ; but rain is advantageous to fishes, a very feAV excepted. On the contrary, rainy seasons are disadvantageous to birds, but hot and dry seasons to fishes. For, in short, it is not advantageous towards to drink much. text: BOOK VIII. THE HISTORY OF ANIMALS, 337 CHAPTER XXIX. Places, likewise, produce a difference in the manners of animals. Thus, for instance, the manners of animals in mountainous and rude places are different from those in plains and cultivated places. For their aspect is more ferocious, and they are more robust in the former than in the latter situation ; as is evident in the swine in mount Athos. For the males of the valleys avoid the females of the mountain. Places, also, produce a great difference in the effect of the bite of savage animals. Thus, for instance, about Pharos, and other places, scorpions are not dangerous ; but in other places, and in Caria, many large and dangerous serpents are generated ; and if they bite any man or beast, the man or beast dies, and they, likewise, kill swine, though SAvine are not injured by other virulent bites. text: BOOK IX. THE HISTORY OF ANIMALS. 365 CHAPTER XIV. With respect to the halcyon, it is, indeed, not much larger than the sparrow ; but its colour is a mixture of azure, green, and purple. text: BOOK IX. THE HISTORY OF ANIMALS. 389 CHAPTER XXXIX. But of spiders, and the phalangia, there are many genera. Spiders, likewise, as soon as they are born are able to emit a thread, not from the interior part of their body, as if it were an excrement, as Democritus says it is, but from the external part, as from a rind, or after the manner of the porcupine, who hurls forth his hairs. text: BOOK IX. THE HISTORY OF ANIMALS. 391 CHAPTER XL. There is, however, a certain genus of insects which is anonymous by one name, but all the individuals of which have a congeneric form. And these are such insects as construct Avaxen cells ; such as bees, and the insects Avhich resemble them in form. Of these there are nine genera ; of which, indeed, six are gregarious bees, the kings of bees, the drone, which lives among the bees, the annual Avasp, and besides these, the hornet, and the tenthredon, [an insect resembling a Avasp.] But there are three that live alone ; the small siren, Avhich is of a brown colour; the larger siren, Avhich is black and variegated ; and a third, Avhich is called bombylius, and is the largest of these. Ants, therefore, do not hunt any thing, but collect Avhat is made by others ; but spiders neither make any thing, nor collect what is made by others, but only hunt after food. Of the before-mentioned nine genera, hoAvever, Ave shall afterwards speak about the rest; but bees hunt after no prey, but make and deposit honey, Avhich is their food. That it is their food, indeed, is evident from this, that when those that keep bees endeavour to take the honey from the hives by smoking them, the bees who suffer very much from the smoke, at that time eat more honey than usual, but at another time they are not seen to eat any great quantity of it, as reserving and depositing it for the sake of nutriment. For Avhere a pure hive is delivered to them, they construct their cells from different floAvers, and various trees ; such as the willow, the elm, and others that abound Avith rosin. With these, also, they anoint the bottom of their hives, in order to prevent other animals from entering into them ; but the keepers of bees call this work incrustation. If the avenues of the hives, likewise, are broad the bees build near it, [so as to make itnarroAver.] They, also, first fabricate the cells in which the [common] bees are born ; and afterwards the cells in Avhich those that are called the kings and the drones are born. Some of the cells, therefore, they always fabricate ; but they construct the cells of the kings Avhen there is a numerous progeny of bees, and the cells of the drones Avhen there are indications of a great abundance of honey. They, likewise, construct the cells of the kings near the cells of the [common] bees ; and these are small ; but they construct the cells of the drones near the cells of the kings ; and these are less than those of the [common] bees. But they begin the series of their cells from the roof of the hive, and form many series or Avebs of these connected Avith each other in a descending order till they reach the bottom of the hive. The cells, also, in Avhich they deposit their honey, and those in Avhich they bring forth their young, have a double entrance ; for about one basis there are tAvo avenues, after the manner of cups Avith two handles ; the one being internal, and the other exter nal. But the first cells of the honey-comb, Avhich are joined to the hive, are narrow, and void of honey, and consist of two or three circular ranges ; but those cells are fuller of honey which are constructed Avith an abundance of Avax. The first part of the entrance into the hive, likewise, is covered with an ointment called mitys ; but this is suffici ently black, being as it were a certain sediment of Avax, and of an unpleasant smell. This mitys, also, is used as a remedy for Avounds, and such like suppurations. But the matter nexi: to this with which the hive is plastered is called pitch-wax, Avhich emits a less powerful odour, and is a less efficacious remedy than mitys. The drones, also, for a great part of the time remain within the hive ; but when they fly out of it, they impetuously raise themselves on high towards the heavens, moving in an orb, and as it Avere exercising themselves. And Avhen they have done this, they again enter into the hive, and feast. The kings, hoAvever, do not fly out of the hive, except in conjunction with the Avhole swarm, neither for food, nor for any other purpose. It is, also, said that if the king of a hive Avanders from it, the Avhole swarm seeks and pursues him, till it discovers him by the smell. And it is farther said, that he is carried by the swarm, when he is unable to fly ; and if he perishes, the* swarm becomes dispersed. If, therefore, he con tinues absent for some time, the bees make honey -combs but no honey, and they themselves in a short time after perish. Bees, also, climbing along floAvers gather Avax Avith great agility with their fore-feet. Afterwards they wipe the Avax off these feet, and transfer it to the two middle feet, and from these to the curvatures of the tAvo hind feet, and thus laden fly aAvay. Hence when they return to their hives, they are seen to be heavy laden with Avax. Certain male birds, likewise, become so effemi- nate from their birth, as neither any longer to sing, nor endeavour to copulate, but suffer the males that endeavour to copulate Avith them [as if they were females.] Many birds, likeAvise, change both their voice and their colour at certain seasons. Thus, for instance, the blackbird, instead of black has a yellow colour and a various voice. For in the summer it sings, but

text: THE HISTORY OF ANIMALS. BOOK IX. 414 but in the Avinter it makes a stridulous noise, and utters tumultuous sounds. The thrush, also, changes its colour ; for in Avinter it is of an ash colour, but in summer its neck is variegated ; yet it suffers no mu tation in its voice. But the nightingale, indeed, sings continually day and night for fifteen days, during the time in Avhich the mountains are thick with foliage. After this period, likeAvise, she sings, yet no longer without intermission. But as the summer advances, she emits another and no longer an all various voice, nor a rapid and modulated, but a simple voice. She, likewise, changes her colour ; and in Italy, at this season of the year, is called by a different name. She is not, hoAvever, seen for a long time ; for she conceals herself. The robin-red-breast, likeAvise, and what is called the roach, are changed into each other. But the robin-red-breast is a bird of the Avinter; and the roach is a summer bird. They do not, however, at all differ from each other, as I may say, except in colour. In a similar manner, also, the becafigo [a bird like a wheat-ear] and the black-head are changed into each other. But the becafigo makes its appearance about the beginning of autumn, and the black head immediately after autumn. These birds, also, differ in no respect from each other, ex cept in their colour and voice. That the becafigo, however, and the black-head are the same bird is evident from this, that at the time of their change each has something which is the peculiarity of each. Nor is it at all wonderful that these birds change their voice and their colour, since the pigeon, also, is not at all vocal in Avinter, and, therefore, those who are skilled in the manners of birds are surprized if pigeons are vocal when fair Aveather succeeds a very severe winter ; but Avhen the spring commences, then the pigeon begins to be vocal. In short, birds are especially and most frequently vocal at the time of copula tion. The cuckoo, likewise, changes its colour, and its voice is not clear, when it is about to conceal itself. text: THE HISTORY OF ANIMALS. BOOK IX. 416 CHAPTER L. Some animals, also, change their forms and manners, not only accord ing to ages and seasons, but, likewise, when they are castrated. But those animals are castrated that have testicles. And some birds, indeed, and ovi parous quadrupeds, have their testicles inwardly, near the kidneys. But with respect to viviparous and pedestrious animals, the greater part have their testicles externally, and some have them internally ; but all of them have them near the end of the belly. Some birds, however, are castrated near the rump, at the part Avith Avhich they come into contact with the female when they copulate. For if any one burns this part Avith two or three hot irons, if the castrated bird is perfect, its crest will become pale, and it Avill no longer sing nor endeavour to copulate ; but if it is castrated Avhile it is yet young, it Avill never sing, nor copulate, nor have a red crest. The same thing, also, happens to men. For if they are mutilated in their private parts Avhile they are children, they will neither have hairs of posterior origin, nor will they experience a mutation of voice, but their voice will continue to be acute. But if they are castrated af ter puberty, the hairs of posterior origin will fall off, except those which are about the private parts; which, though they will be diminished, yet will not entirely fail. The hairs, however, Avhich are born with men do not fail when they are castrated ; for no eunuch becomes bald. The voice, also, of all castrated quadrupeds changes into the female voice. Other quadrupeds, therefore, if they are castrated when they are not young perish ; but in the Avild-boar alone it is of no conse quence at what period he is castrated. text: ON PHYSIOGNOM Y. CHAPTER I. JtHAT the soul follows the body, and is not itself by itself impassive ' to the body, is perfectly manifest in intoxication and sickness. For the soul is seen to suffer a great change from the passions of the body. And, on the contrary, that the body sympathizes Avith the passions of the soul, becomes evident in love, fear, pain, and pleasure. And farther still, in those things which are produced by nature, it may be more clearly seen that the soul and body are so connascently affected towards each other, as to become to each other the cause of most of their pas sions. For an animal is never so generated as to have the form of one animal, and the soul of another; but it has ahvays the body and soul 1 This is only true of the soul so far as it proceeds into body, or rather of those energies of the soul which proceed into body, and which from their union with the body may, also, he called passions. But Avhen many signs accord of one thing, it may be more confidently admitted that the signs are true. There is, also, another mode of physiognomizing, but Avhich no one has yet adopted. Thus, for instance, if it is necessary [from signs] that some one should be irascible, morose, and pusillanimous, he will, also, be envious, though he has no signs of an envious man ; but from those former signs it Avill be possible for a physiognomist to discover that he J^h^ts envious ; and this will be especially the case Avhen such a mode Avill be proper to one who philosophizes. For to be able, certain things existing, to discover Avhat is necessary, is, Ave apprehend, the peculi- arity of philosophy. We may, also, argue from a contrary ; for if from certain signs certain good things are inferred, from contrary signs we may, also, infer evils, Avhich are their contraries. With respect to voice, indeed, some one directing his attention to passion may think that an acute voice is to be considered as indicative of an irascible disposition, and this for a twofold cause. For he Avho is indignant and angry is accustomed to give intention to his voice, and to speak acutely; but he who is indolently disposed remits the tone of his voice, and speaks gravely. Again, of animals, those that are brave have a grave voice ; but those that are timid, an acute voice. The lion, indeed, the bull, and the barking dog, and the more animated cocks, emit a grave voice ; but the stag and the hare, an acute voice. Perhaps, hoAvever, in these instances, also, it is better not to consider the animals as brave or timid, because their voice is acute or grave, but to conclude that a robust voice is the sign of a brave ani mal, and that a remiss and feeble voice is the sign of a timid animal. In the proper works, therefore, of the soul, the passions, according to the body, are peculiar; but in the common Avorks of the soul, these passions are common. The common passions, therefore, are Avantonness and venereal ecstasy. Hence both of animals that have a tuft of hair on the forehead, and of those that have not, Avantonness is a common passion ; but of asses and SAvine, the common passion is venereal ecstasy. But the peculiar passion in dogs, indeed, is reviling by barking ; and in asses freedom from sorroAv. And thus Ave have shown how the common and the peculiar ought to be distinguished. Much exercise, however, and the habit acquired by exercise, are re quisite in order to be sufficiently qualified to discuss each of these par ticulars. For since the things Avhich are seen in bodies are said to be referred to the similitudes produced from animals and their actions, certain other peculiarities, also, arise from heat and cold. But some of these appearances are in bodies Avhich employ small differences, and are called by the same name; such, for instance, as the paleness arising from terror and from labour. For these have the same appellation, and differ but little fiom each other. When, however, the difference is small, it is not easy to know [what passion is signified] ; but from experience and custom, the fitness of the form (noppti) must be assumed. The swiftest and best mode, therefore, [of knowing the passions and manners of the soul by physiognomy] is that Avhich is derived from fitness [through Avhich a man resembles this or that animal.] And by thus employing this mode, many particulars may be known. It is, also, not only universally useful, but is, likewise, useful in the selection of signs. For it is requisite, that each of the selected signs should have a fitness of such a kind as is conformable to that Avhich is selected. Farther still, [we may, also, investigate the natures of men] both by the selection of signs, and by the syllogism which it is requisite to use wherever it may occur, adding things appropriate to such as are appropriate. Now, however, I shall endeavour in the first place to discuss the genera of animals, and to show Avhat those particulars in them are which it is fit should be changed, in order that they may be brave or timid, just or unjust. But the genus of animals must be divided into two forms (pootpat), i. e. into the male and female, at the same time adapting to each form that Avhich is fit. For these forms are similar. With respect to those milder animals, therefore, Avhich >ve endeavour to nurture, the females are of a softer nature than the males, and less robust ; and they are, also, more easily accustomed to the hand of man, and more readily receive nutriment from it. Hence such being the nature of the females, they are in a certain respect less irascible than the males. And this is manifest from what Ave experience in ourselves. For Avhen we are vanquished by anger, Ave yield to persuasion Avith difficulty, and are less tractable. We are, likeAvise, hurried on to vio lent conduct, and to the perpetration of Avhatever anger may impel us to do. It, also, appears to me that females are more malignant than males, more precipitate, illiberal, and imbecil. This, therefore, is very evident in Avomen, and in the females of those animals which are nou rished by us. And the same thing is testified by all shepherds and hunters of animals of the forest. This, likewise, is manifest, that the female in each genus of animals has a less head, a narroAver face, a more slender neck, a more imbecil breast,

But the knees of females are flexible, and their legs are slender. Their feet however, are more elegant than the feet of males, and the form (^<p„) of their body is more pleasing than generous (>gmtlos}. They are, also, less nervous, softer, and have moister flesh. But males, possessing the contraries to all these, are naturally braver, and more just in their kind ; and the female is naturally more timid and unjust. This being the case, the lion appears to participate the idea [i. e. form] of the male the most perfectly of all animals. For he has a very large mouth ; his face is more square, and not very bony ; his upper does not project beyond but equally corresponds to the lower jaw ; his nostrils are more thick than thin ; his eyes are yellow and concave, neither very round nor very oblong, but of a moderate magnitude. His eye-broAvs, also, are large, and his forehead is square, but more concave in the middle, and about the eye-broAvs and the nose rises up like a cloud. But in the superior part of the forehead, near the nose, he has hairs inclining [to the nose]. His head is of a moderate size ; his neck is sufficiently long, thick, and commensurate ; his hair is yellow, neither straight nor very much curled ; and the parts about the collar-bone are more detached than conjoined. His shoulders are strong, his breast is juvenile [i. e. is robust], his metaphrenon [i. e. the part opposite to the breast] is broad, and his ribs and his back are very strong. He is, also, a less fleshy animal in his hips and his thighs. His legs are robust and nervous, neither very hard, nor very moist. But he Avalks slowly, takes large steps, and vehemently agitates his shoulders as he marshes. And such r.re the particulars respecting his body. But with respect to his soul, he is disposed to give, is libe ral, magnanimous, and aspires after victory ; is mild and just, and pos sesses an affection for those Avith Avhom he associates resembling paren tal and conjugal love. The panther, hoAvever, among animals which appear to be brave, is of a more feminine form, since by reason of its legs it is inferior in its energies to all other brave animals. Its forehead is more oblong ; its ears are more round than plain j its neck is very long and thin ; its breast is not defended Avith sides; and its back is long. Its hips, also, and its thighs are fleshy; but the parts about the flank and the belly are more equable. Its colour is variegated ; and the whole of its body is without articulation, and incommensurate. Such, therefore, is the form of its body. But with respect to its soul, it is little, given to theft, and, in short, fraudulent. It is evident, therefore, how among animals which are considered as brave the lion subsists, who possesses most perfectly the form of the male, and the panther which possesses in equal perfection the form of the female. Hoav the males and females subsist in other animals it is now easy to determine. But with respect to such particulars as it belongs to physi ognomy to consider, these will be enumerated in the selection of signs. CHAPTER VI. The selection, therefore, of signs by which we may detect the nature and manners of men must be made as follows : Those whose feet are well formed and large, have articulation, and are nervous, are robust in what pertains to the soul, and are referred to the male genus. But such as have small and narrow feet, without ar ticulation, are more pleasing to the view than robust, and are effemi nate in what pertains to the soul. text: 21 No hostile sounds their horrors dart Thro' the Virgin's trembling heart, List'ning in the tranquil grove To some tender tale of love ; But Peace, and Freedom walk the hallow'd ground, And rich Abundance smiles, and Beauty blooms around On thy eternal rocks, with trophies grac'd, Above the foaming surges of the flood, Has Liberty sublime her Temple plac'd, The deep foundations stain'd with Tyrants' blood. Vast pile of adamant ! the structure stands ; To heav'ns high vault the swelling domes aspire, And shed their lustre wide — while distant lands Behold the golden glories, and admire. There native Genius, and consummate Art, Exerting each their destin'd part, Have spirit, grandeur, grace combin'd, And Gothic strength with Grecian order join'd To form one bold and regular design, Where just proportion tempers warmth divine. Around the walls, by mimic Art pourtray'd, Are Patriots, Chiefs, and mighty deeds display'd. Here the impassion'd colours tell How gentle, gen'rous Russelfell; There Sydney fierce, impatient of the yoke, Firm and undaunted meets the Tyrant's stroke : Here Eliot, ardent for her injur'd laws, With Roman spirit pleads his country's cause,

text: 38 Thus, Delia ! when, with kindred zeal infpir'd, To themes divine you consecrate your tongue, And with your Maker's praise exalt the song, We feel our breasts with new emotions fir'd ; List'ning to the heav'nly strain Common sounds intrude in vain; With sacred love our sosten'd souls o'erflow, Or with sublime enflam'd devotion glow. Tir'd Care forgets her toils, And Sorrow wipes her dewy eyes, and smiles. Fair Nymph ! proceed — the noblest hints inspire, From vulgar cares the sordid soul refine, Touch the cold bosom with a heav'nly fire, And raise our Human to Divine ! You give Religion greater grace to please, And lend her awful truths melodious ease ; Severe in others she commands, alarms, And chills with look austere the trembling breast; In you she like a tuneful Angel charms, And tempts us to be good, and wins us to be blest.

text: 59 ODE TO RELIGION, Fairest Daughter of the sky ! On whose majestic brow Divine unutterable glories glow, While round thy rosy lip, and placid eye, Love and the smiling Graces ever play, Temp'ring the blaze of thy eternal day- Religion, hail ! Thou source of hallow'd fires, Joys ever pure, and sanctified desires ! Beneath the brown-rob'd wood, Where Contemplation sits in musing mood, Sooth'd by the hollow gales, and falling flood, What time the fun to other realms is roll'd, And Eve's bright tints of purple and of gold Faint slowly from the western skies away, While Cynthia's milder face Shoots thro' th' unfolding clouds a silver ray, And o'er the landscape sheds a softer grace, Far from the world's delusive scene I fly To woo thee from thy native sphere, To catch the beamings of thy heav'n-bright eye, Thou pleasing awful Fair ! text: [ 53 ] ON RETIREMENT. Far from the cares that vex the world's repose, Here on my mossy couch I rest ; Reflection's limpid tide serenely flows, And no rough passions bluster in my breast. The vernal bloom, that purples o'er the vales, This flow'ring arbour fann'd by cooling gales, The grove's wild warblings, and the chidings shrill Of the rude streams, that Wander at their will, And hill, and dale, and forest, lake, and lawn, And light, and soade, in sweet confusion thrown, Delight the soul to pensiveness inclin'd, And sooth to solemn thought the musing mind. Here in these peaceful scenes, Daughter of God, indulgent Nature reigns, Divinely fair ! as when her infant brows From the wild waves of teeming Chaos rose, When choral Angels with a pleas'd surprize Hail'd the young lustre sparkling in her eyes, And in her radiant form, and lovely face, Saw their own heav'n with full reflected grace. Here still th' etherial Maid, In Beauty's sweet simplicity array'd, Forms her imperial crown with sylvan flow'rs, And for her palace weaves her woodbine bow'rs.

text: 91 INVOCATION TO MELANCHOLY. O Melancholy ! sad and solemn Maid ! Dost thou thro' the glimm'ring glade, Beneath the Moon's pale ray, With many a slow step stray, Far from the soothing voice of kind relief, To feed on thoughts of woe, And tell the gliding waters, as they flow, Thy oft repeated grief; And still, where'er thy weary wand'rings lead, Dread Horror stalks behind, With deeper, hoarser thunder howls the wind, And Night's grim features cast a death-like soade ? Or dost thou on the margin of the main, In melting notes complain, Beneath some craggy cliffs impending brow, Which thickets hoar, or hanging woods embrown, Whose soades tremendous frown O'er the foaming gulph below, Lull'd by the loud tumultuous waves, that swell, And beat, and break upon the bellowing soore, While hid within her hollow-sounding cell Hoarse Echo murmurs to the rough wave's roar ? Or in some defart fly the face of Men, List'ning to the raven's croak, From the mossy-fringed oak, In some Cimmerian den ; n 2

text: C in ] ON THE DEATH OF AN AMIABLE CHILD Adieu! thou soort-liv'd charm adieu ! Just soown, and raviso'd from our view ! A thousand hopes — thy Parents' pride And fondest wisoes with thee died. Ye Graces ! on her turfy bed Your blusoing soow'r of roses soed, Emblems of beauty's fading bloom ! Ye Zephyrs ! from your rosy wing Shake the freso fragrance of the spring, And waft your odours round the tomb ! Ye young-ey'd Angels ! guard her dust, for there Lies all that's soft, and sweet, and innocent, and fair. Those pallid cheeks no more we view Outvie rhe morn's vermilion hue ; No more our eager thoughts presage The beauties of her ripen'd age ; No more the soft sensations rise Within the fondling Mother's breast, When in her looks, her air, her eyes, She saw her youthful form confest; No more soe hangs upon her smiles, Her lisping lips, her mimic wiles, Nor marks the blooming graces, as they grow, With sweet conceal'd delight, till tears of transport flow.

text: 128 What tho' her eyes, too small to hurt a heart, Too artless seem, too innocent to kill, They wound like Cupid's small, yet deadly dart, Soft as the plume, but piercing as the steel. Tho' virgin coyness blusoes o'er her face, Tho' seeming Nature flows in ev'ry grace, And her mild looks ethereal sonsoine soow, She's like the surface of a soallow sea, Where heav'n's reflected beams serenely play, Yet lie the rocks and lurking Fate below. FIRST BEAUTY. Light as the breeze, and frolic as the May, Mv careless Muse her idle ditties fung ; To mortal beauty trill'd her airy lay, Round Folly's sorine her flow'ry garland hung ; 'Till Grace, kind Cherub, lighting from the sphere, To the First Beauty rais'd my fervid mind, Stamp'd the bright image of his glory there, Parent of hallow'd fires, and joys refin'd. Still, Sov'reign Fair ! th' idea deep imprest, Chears my lone musings, elevates my breast, Rules o'er my numbers, and my rapture warms ; There let the sacred passion ever glow, Sweet as thy living streams of pleasure flow, Bright as thy beams, immortal as thy charms !

text: C 133 ] TO THE NIGHTINGALE* Melodious Philomela! pleas'd I hear In the lone woods thy love-resounding lay, Where the world's din, like thunder from afar, Just mutters in the wind, and dies away. Known to a few lov'd Friends these soades among, Close treafur'd from the noisy crowd, like thee, I'd chaunt the rural, or the moral song, In native wood-notes warbling wild and free. Heav'n never form'd me for the world's affairs, Too much a foe to all its strifes and cares, Content with little in obscure repose. To Life's high storm-vext top let others rise ; Low in the vale my lot more safely lies, Nor heeds which way the raging tempest blows. PEACE. O Peace, of smiling lip, and look serene ! Whose gentle voice the breast of trouble charms, With all my soul I court thee — but in vain — While envious Care still frowns thee from my arms

Montego Bay is a thriving and pretty populous town ; but it was still more so previous to 1795, in which year it suffered very severely by a fire., which consumed two thirds of the town, and de stroyed a great deal of other property : the whole of the houses that were destroyed have not since been rebuilt, a proof that this town is not now so populous as it then was. Jamaica being situated within eighteen degrees of the equator, its climate will naturally be ex pected to be of a degree of warmth considerably above temperate. In these tropical regions it has been wisely ordained by providence, that the heat, which would otherwise be insufferable, should be tempered by appropriate causes. While the inhabitant of the mountains of Jamaica enjoys a purer and more wholesome air than he who resides near to the ocean, the latter is com forted and refreshed by the daily sea-breeze, which periodically sets in at a certain hour. Ecclesiastical affairs are here managed by a commissary court, consisting of a certain number of the clergy deputed by the king. The rectors have a seat and voice in the parochial vestries, in whatever relates to the church. Each parish is under the direction of a vestry, which consists of the oldest magistrate (who is designated honourable, and is called custos rotu lorum, from his having the custody of the paro chial records), and ten freeholders elected by the rest. All affairs relative to the parish are regu lated and settled by this body of men, and all questions are carried by a majority of voices. Besides the regulation of roads and other public works, they have the appointment to different parochial offices. In each parish there is an officer called " clerk of the peace," who is the public prosecutor in all breaches of the peace, misdemeanors, &c. He is by profession an attorney at law, and his office, in the courts of session, may be said to be like that of the attor ney-general, in miniature. There is also a co roner. The constables are appointed by the custos and other magistrates.

The professions most likely to make money here, next to attornies and the reverend clergy, are surgeons, surveyors, watch-makers, copper smiths, masons, taylors, &c. Tradesmen in ge neral can never for a moment want employment ; and, if they are skilful and industrious, their salaries are liberal. They have it much more in their power to make a speedy fortune than the planter-adventurer. The merchant, by giving long credits to hi3 customers, has an enormous profit upon his goods. But as this subject has already been touched upon, it may here only be added that the merchants of Jamaica trade either with Great Britain, or with America, and sometimes with both ; and, if they possess a tolerable capital, they soon rea lize a fine fortune. Many of them are respect able and useful characters. The shop-keepers are here called store-keepers ; they receive regu lar supplies of goods from Great Britain, for which they demand their own price, generally raising it to an unreasonable height according to the exigencies of the demand ; so that the prices seldom remain long uniform and stationary, as in the mother country. But then they consider, that they must be somehow compensated for the hazard they run with bad customers. A store-keeper, who sets up with a tolerable fund, is supported and countenanced by an able friend, and has the good fortune to procure choice customers, cannot fail of succeeding; and, without these, it would be better for him to lay out his money at lawful interest, on good security, than hazard it on so precarious a bottom. Some, however, succeed astonishingly, with few or none of these advan- tages, by dealing chiefly or solely in negro goods, or such merchandize as is adapted for the use of the negroes, for which they receive cash alone. This is a mighty advantage to them, as with ready money they are enabled to -renew their stock of goods at a very considerable discount, sometimes (at vendue sales, as they are called) even under prime cost. Specie is so scarce in the island, that extraordinary bargains may be made by a com- mand of it at times. It is by no means unusual to see various kinds of property disposed of by public sale, for cash, at one third less than they would be sold for upon credit, and at a price, in- deed, sometimes greatly under their intrinsic value. The inhabitant of the town, as well as the country (unless constantly engaged in some active employment that engrosses the whole of his time), is liable to the dull uni formity of a perpetual unvaried sameness of life and objects ; unless, happily actuated by a spirit of inquiry and taste for study, he employs the leisure hours of life in gratifying curiosity, and adding to the acquisition of knowledge. An account of a battle by land, or fight by sea, is therefore as acceptable to him as to most of our political quid-nuncs ; and one will see clusters of those politicians gathered together in the towns and villages on a Sunday or Monday morn ing waiting the coming in of the post-boy, with anxious looks, on the arrival of a packet from England ; the greater part impatient to know the

Those vicissitudes of European warfare greatly contribute to keep their minds from a stagnant languor, and give a new spring to conversation and to conjecture. There are some, tolerable good newspapers for the circulation of this sort of intelligence. The inhabitants of this country, particularly the Europeans, are peculiarly fond of convivial parties, though perhaps not so much now as for- merly. This is another source of amusement and occupation of spare time. Besides nume- rous private parties, there are frequent tavern dinners on various public occasions ; as free- masons' dinners (there are no less than seventeen lodges in the island), military dinners, vestry dinners, grand jury dinners, peace dinners, king's birth-day dinners, governor's dinners (while that officer performs his military tour), victory din- ners, &c. &c. On these occasions no expense is spared to render the entertainment costly and splendid. Every luxury is catered up for, the purpose, and copious libations of various wines, and other good things, are poured forth to the jolly god of good fellowship. Indeed, neither Hygeia nor the goddess of prudence have often a voice at these jovial meetings. It is rather to be N 3

The Creoles are not extravagantly expensive in their furniture; this is generally plain but genteel. Their side-boards and beaufets, however, display a costly brilliancy, in unison with the plentiful and splendid cheer which is spread on their din ner tables. In a large house, consisting of many apartments, the labour of six or eight female slaves is required for two or three hours every morning, in burnishing the floors, which for smoothness of polish rival even the finest ma hogany tables. These floors are either of maho gany, wild orange, or other hard wood, and acquire at length, by this daily operation, so glossy a surface that a stranger, not accustomed to tread on such smooth ground, must be heedful how he walks, in order to avoid slipping and falling down. About such a house, if the proprietor be weal thy, and have a large family (say ten or twelve in all), there are perhaps about twenty-five or thirty black and mulatto servants of all descriptions, including cooks, grooms, laundresses, Sec. and each of the females of the family has her waiting maid, besides the domestics generally attending about the house. Tbe employment of these ser vants, besides keeping the house in order, con sists in making and mending the household linen,

A certain number, who are taught sewing, sit down on the floor, under the superintendance of the ladies, to their needle, at which they are astonishingly expert. The equi page of such a family consists of a coach, and one or two covered gigs or one-horse chaises, and fifteen or twenty horses and mules, with their proper attendants, Sec. The equipage and horses, &c. may be worth about two thousand pounds sterling. When an entertainment is to be given, no expense or pains are spared to render it as sumptuous as possible. The table is spread with a profusion and variety of all the viands and delicacies which industry or money can procure. Different courses do not come in in succession, but the table is at once loaded with superabundance ; flesh, fish, fowl, game, and different vegetables appear at once to the view, in a style which rather shews the hospitality and abundance of the master or mistress of the feast, than their taste and selection. Yet here at least, whatever other sauces may give a whet to the appetite, is the zest of a free, hearty, and undisguised welcome. After the removal of the dinner, the desert is ushered in, consisting of tarts, cakes, puddings, and a profusion of sweet meats, which make a still more magnificent dis play than the dinner ; while various wines (kept cool by wet towels), liqueurs, &c. are handed

Be this as it may, the situation and treatment of the West India slaves is infinitely more mild, lenient, and comfortable, than it was twenty-five or thirty years ago. The poor slave is now no longer at the sole mercy of a barbarian master, but is pro tected by the laws from injury, insult, and wan ton and unmerited severity. His master is also compelled to furnish him with food, clothing, medical attendance, and every thing else neces sary for his comfort and support. But he must be a wretch indeed, who would require to be compelled to that which humanity, gratitude, and even interest (too often a more powerful incen tive than either) so unequivocally demands of him. The author has never heard any other hypothesis advanced on the subject than that it was owing to the atmosphere being less humid and better ventilated, from the country being now generally cleared of wood. Neither the small-pox nor the measles are native diseases of that part of Africa inhabited by the negroes, nor are some other diseases to which they are subject in the West Indies. But there are dis eases peculiar to the Africans, which are of a more terrible nature. One of these is called the cocabay ; a distemper the most horrible and re volting in its nature, and the more so as it is pecu liarly infectious, and utterly incurable. The un happy patient who is infected with it becomes soon changed in appearance, different parts of his body swell, he is covered over with a leprous scurf, his spirits sink into deep dejection, he loathes his food, and yet his miserable existence is prolonged for years, though he continually in vokes death to come and put a period to it, and to his hopeless sufferings ; at least, this is the

The other disorders that are generally most fatal among the negroes are pleurisies, inflammations of the bowels, dysenteries, and influenza : some times, too, violent fevers, proceeding from colds, are the cause of much mortality among them. The dysentery and influenza make their appear ance periodically. Some years ago the latter swept of, in the course of a few months, the tenth part of the population of many of the estates ; and 'there were few that escaped considerable loss. This disease was attended with a most violent and rapid fever, with a strong tendency to the head : in forty-eight hours the patient's strength was completely prostrated, and unless a favour able turn took place, he seldom survived long beyond that time. In the rapidity of its opera tion, it resembled the yellow or malignant bili ous fever among the whites : but as the negroes are exempt from the attacks of this latter disorder, so are the whites not at all liable to the influenza during its prevalence among the negroes. The appearance of dysentery among the negroes is most to be apprehended in the latter end of sum mer, when the new yams are begun to be got in, and the avagata pear (a favourite article in the negroes' meals) still remains unripe, but which they will yet use. Hear, mighty Lord ! thy servant's pray'i And if thou deign'st her life to spare, Add to this mighty gift — one more, To mental light her sight restore : Then shall each tender babe be taught To sing thy praise in word and thought To moral duties not confin'd, Enlarge their views, exalt their mind ; And early be they taught to know, From God alone all blessings flow.

Terms, then, it appears, are not to be im plicitly relied on ; so that it may be prudent, where they exist, not only to take an assign ment of them, but to look out for some more effectual method of barring the purchaser's wife's dower. Where terms do not exist, the neces sity of doing the latter is rendered the more imperious. By considering what it is that gives a wife a title to her dower or thirds, we shall more ea sily discover the best method of preventing it from attaching. Before a widow can claim dower out of her deceased husband's estates, it must appear 1st, that he was possessed of an es tate of inheritance in fee simple or fee tail in possession. 2dly, That he was solely seized of such an estate ; and 3dly, That he was so sei zed in possession. Dower may therefore be barred or prevented three ways : first, by crea ting a trust ; secondly, by conveying the estate to the purchaser and a trustee jointly, thereby creating a joint tenancy ; or, thirdly, by put ting the fee in remainder or reversion. Any form of limitation, therefore, that embraces ei ther of those objects may be deemed safe, and they will be more or less desirable or approv ed of, as they meet the wishes of the parties interested, and agree with their ideas of con venience.
